        @rwlocked(read=["deps", "outs"])
        def run(
            self,
            dry=False,
            no_commit=False,
            force=False,
            allow_missing=False,
            no_download=False,
            **kwargs,
        ) -> None:
            if (self.cmd or self.is_import) and not self.frozen and not dry:
                self.remove_outs(ignore_remove=False, force=False)
    
            if (self.is_import and not self.frozen) or self.is_partial_import:
                self._sync_import(dry, force, kwargs.get("jobs"), no_download)
            elif not self.frozen and self.cmd:
                self._run_stage(dry, force, **kwargs)
            elif not dry:
                args = ("outputs", "frozen ") if self.frozen else ("data sources", "")
                logger.info("Verifying %s in %s%s", *args, self)
                self._check_missing_outputs()
    
            if not dry:
                if no_download:
                    allow_missing = True
    
                no_cache_outs = any(
                    not out.use_cache
                    for out in self.outs
                    if not (out.is_metric or out.is_plot)
                )
                self.save(
                    allow_missing=allow_missing,
                    run_cache=not no_commit and not no_cache_outs,
                )
    
                if no_download:
                    self.ignore_outs()
                if not no_commit:
                    self.commit(allow_missing=allow_missing)
    
        @rwlocked(read=["deps"], write=["outs"])
        def _run_stage(self, dry, force, **kwargs) -> None:
            return run_stage(self, dry, force, **kwargs)

## Assistant

`frozen: true` prevents the stage’s command from executing, but DVC still checks that its declared outputs exist. Our historical stage declares `data/raw/fine-news`, which hasn’t been created here. Plain `just dvc repro` includes that stage and fails validation. This is an oversight in the scaffold. See [DVC’s freeze documentation](https://doc.dvc.org/command-reference/freeze).

For the comparison, use:

```bash
just dvc repro compare_sources
```

This runs its required preparation and sampling stages while excluding the unrelated historical acquisition.

To make bare `just dvc repro` work cleanly, the historical recipe should live in a separate DVC pipeline file outside the default root targets.

    # Fine News acquisition
    
    `filter_fine_news` documents the historical staging selection from
    [Fine News](https://huggingface.co/datasets/ksolovev/fine-news) at the revision
    in [acquisition.json](acquisition.json). It selects `eng_Latn` capture-month
    shards and the exact 115-hostname [allowlist](domains.csv), including subdomains.
    The hostname comes from `metadata.url_hostname`, falling back to `metadata.url`
    when blank. One query reads the input glob and writes `text`, `id` and `metadata`
    to `data/raw/fine-news/articles.parquet`.
    
    This is the historical source filter, not a reviewed publisher list or a
    research-ready article corpus. Fine News applies its own filters and
    deduplication; capture month is not necessarily publication month. The upstream
    dataset card describes content rights and usage restrictions. No full output has
    been built, verified or cached here, and no DVC lock entry is claimed.
    
    The stage is frozen: `dvc repro` will not execute it, even with `--force`.
    Since the declared output is absent, targeting it currently reports missing data.
    After obtaining or rebuilding and verifying the output, track its actual state
    before relying on it downstream. Unfreezing or invoking the command directly can
    run the acquisition and requires network access and substantial resources.
    DuckDB may download its `httpfs` extension on first remote access.
    
    For a local trial, provide `--config` with a local source glob, domain CSV and
    fresh output directory. The script refuses to overwrite an existing output.
    Output layout, order and Parquet bytes differ from
    the staging shards; selected rows have not been compared with that dataset.

    # CCFinance
    
    CCFinance is a data engineering project for filtering and enriching public
    Common Crawl News (CC-News) copies for research into language in finance.
    
    ## Start
    
    Exordio supplies the Python and LaTeX toolchains, a pinned Nix environment and CI.
    Copier answers record Exordio `v0.1.1-alpha` (the documented `v0.1.0` tag was not
    available in the local source).
    
    ```bash
    bash infra/nix/install-devenv.sh
    devenv shell
    just setup
    just python::run --help
    just python::run stages list
    just check
    ```
    
    Shared agent instructions and Codex configuration are maintained in
    [`.agents/`](.agents/README.md). `just setup` applies them; use
    `just agents::preview` to preview link changes and `just agents::check` to
    verify the generated links.
    
    `just check` validates Justfile syntax and formatting alongside the other
    quality gates. Run `just fmt` to format Justfiles and other source files.
    
    For Python alone, with Python 3.13, uv and just installed:
    
    ```bash
    just python::setup
    just python::check
    ```
    
    ## Data and reproducibility
    
    DVC is initialized at the repository root with analytics disabled. Use:
    
    ```bash
    just dvc status
    just dvc dag
    ```
    
    Semflow tracks the executable Python dependencies of DVC stages. When adding a
    stage, run `just semflow-patch` to review its proposed fingerprints, then
    `just semflow-apply` to materialize them. Commit the generated
    `.semflow/hashes/` files with the DVC definition. After semantic source changes,
    run `just semflow-refresh`; `just semflow-check` detects stale fingerprints.
    The frozen [Fine News acquisition stage](data/inputs/fine-news/README.md) documents
    the staging dataset's historical selection. The
    [source comparison](data/inputs/source-comparison/README.md) prepares small
    probability samples using Parquet metadata before acquiring article payloads.
    Keep data, configuration and environment dependencies explicit in DVC: Semflow's
    static analysis cannot discover string-driven dynamic imports.
    
    See [Python commands](src/python/README.md), [LaTeX commands](src/latex/README.md)
    and [infrastructure](infra/README.md). The scaffold's Apache-2.0 license covers
    code; it does not grant rights to upstream article content.

    ## Unreleased
    
    ### Added
    
    - Source-comparison DVC stages with metadata preparation, selective Parquet reads
      and exploratory estimates of publisher-filter yield.
    - Statsmodels LaTeX summaries and individual yield and population tables for papers.

    - pytest-layout-enforcer for source-aligned test paths.

    # DVC Pipeline for Pricing Perspective Analysis
    
    params:
    - params.yaml
    
    metrics:
    
    - data/papers/paper1/dyadic_confound/results.json
    - data/papers/paper3/certificate_validation/results.json
    - data/papers/paper5/post_corpus_qmle/results.json
    vars:
    - py_pipeline: uv run --project src/python pipeline
    - py_semflow: uv run --project src/python semflow
    - shared: data/shared
    - p1: data/papers/paper1
    - p3: data/papers/paper3
    - p5: data/papers/paper5
    - p6: data/papers/paper6
    - p1_tex: src/latex/projects/01_continuous_bounds/src
    - p3_tex: src/latex/projects/03_distance_implied_mpt/src
    - p5_tex: src/latex/projects/05_spatial_pricing/src
    - p6_tex: src/latex/projects/06_information_motion/src
    stages:
    
      # ====================================================================
      # SEMFLOW CONTROL PLANE
      # ====================================================================
    
      semflow_refresh:
        desc: >-
          Refresh semantic entrypoint fingerprints after source changes. This
          control-plane stage owns JSON only; semflow instrumentation of dvc.yaml
          remains an explicit human-reviewed patch.
        cmd: >-
          ${py_semflow} refresh --apply
        deps:
        - semflow.toml
        - src/python/pyproject.toml
        - src/python/uv.lock
        - src/python/apps/pipeline/src
        - src/python/apps/hotelling/src
        outs:
        - .semflow/hashes:
            cache: false
    
      # ====================================================================
      # SHARED SUBSTRATE
      # ====================================================================
    
      jcor_qualification:
        desc: >-
          Qualify JCOR fitting, covariance, supplied refits, dynamic geometry,
          weighted transport and checked QP, plus Hotelling composition, against
          deterministic witnesses with separate CPU timing and compiled-memory
          evidence. This is package qualification, not a paper result.
        cmd: >-
          ${py_pipeline} qualify-jcor
          --output-dir ${shared}/jcor_qualification
          --sample-size 64
          --benchmark-size 512
          --repeats 3
        deps:
        - .semflow/hashes/entrypoints/pipeline/qualify-jcor.json
        outs:
        - ${shared}/jcor_qualification
    
      ## corpus & embeddings
    
      normalize_corpus:
        desc: >-
          Deduplicate, date-parse, and filter the raw NASDAQ corpus to the configured
          ticker universe; output articles.parquet + summary.yaml.
        cmd: >-
          ${py_pipeline} normalize-corpus
          --input data/raw/nasdaq.jsonlines
          --output-parquet ${shared}/corpus/articles.parquet
          --output-summary ${shared}/corpus/summary.yaml
          --params params.yaml
        deps:
        - .semflow/hashes/entrypoints/pipeline/normalize-corpus.json
        - data/raw/nasdaq.jsonlines
        params:
        # The roster reaches this stage through `--params params.yaml`, not through
        # the interpolated `cmd`, so without this declaration a universe change
        # leaves the stage falsely clean and the corpus silently stale.
        - symbols
        outs:
        - ${shared}/corpus/articles.parquet
        - ${shared}/corpus/summary.yaml
      co_mentions:
        desc: >-
          Build a Ge--Linton--Li-style news co-mention graph from exact-two company
          tags in the normalized corpus; emit article edges, yearly pair counts,
          persistent weighted edges, and a JSON audit summary. The source taxonomy has
          no RavenPack topic IDs, so analyst, rating, and index-topic exclusions from
          the paper are not applied.
        cmd: >-
          bash src/python/apps/pipeline/src/pipeline/stages/substrate/co_mentions.sh
          ${shared}/corpus/articles.parquet data/universe.csv ${shared}/co_mentions
          ${start_date} ${end_date} ${co_mentions.min_persistence_years}
        deps:
        - ${shared}/corpus/articles.parquet
        - data/universe.csv
        - src/python/apps/pipeline/src/pipeline/stages/substrate/co_mentions.sh
        params:
        - start_date
        - end_date
        - co_mentions.min_persistence_years
        outs:
        - ${shared}/co_mentions/events.parquet
        - ${shared}/co_mentions/pair_year.parquet
        - ${shared}/co_mentions/adjacency.parquet
        - ${shared}/co_mentions/summary.json
      subsample:
        foreach: ${symbols}
        do:
          frozen: true
          desc: >-
            Subsample normalized corpus articles for a ticker using DuckDB with date and
            body-length filtering; deterministic md5-ordered sampling.
          cmd: >-
            ${py_pipeline} subsample
            --symbol ${item}
            --input-path ${shared}/corpus/articles.parquet
            --output ${shared}/subsampled_headlines/${item}.parquet
            --start-date ${start_date}
            --end-date ${end_date}
            --min-body-chars ${min_body_chars}
            --n-samples ${n_samples}
          deps:
          - .semflow/hashes/entrypoints/pipeline/subsample.json
          - ${shared}/corpus/articles.parquet
          outs:
          - ${shared}/subsampled_headlines/${item}.parquet
      generate_embeddings:
        matrix:
          symbol: ${symbols}
          embedding_model: ${embedding_models}
        frozen: true
        desc: >-
          Generate embeddings for subsampled articles via OpenRouter
          (OpenAI-compatible).
        cmd: >-
          ${py_pipeline} generate-embeddings
          --symbol ${item.symbol}
          --parquet-path ${shared}/subsampled_headlines/${item.symbol}.parquet
          --model-key ${item.embedding_model}
          --output-file ${shared}/embeddings/${item.embedding_model}/${item.symbol}.parquet
          --params-file params.yaml
        deps:
        - .semflow/hashes/entrypoints/pipeline/generate-embeddings.json
        - ${shared}/subsampled_headlines/${item.symbol}.parquet
        params:
        - embedding.models
        - embedding.base_url
        - embedding.batch_size
        - embedding.concurrency
        - embedding.max_chars
        outs:
        - ${shared}/embeddings/${item.embedding_model}/${item.symbol}.parquet
    
      chronobert_embeddings:
        foreach: ${encoder_vintage_ablation_specs}
        do:
          desc: >-
            Materialize raw document vectors from one pinned annual ChronoBERT
            checkpoint on the unchanged shared article sample, separately from
            the seven-cell base representation roster.
          cmd: >-
            ${py_pipeline} generate-chronobert-embeddings
    ✓ • 0ms

    """Preserve the historical Fine News publisher acquisition command."""
    
    import os
    from pathlib import Path
    from tempfile import TemporaryDirectory
    from typing import Annotated
    
    import duckdb
    import typer
    from pydantic import BaseModel, ConfigDict
    
    from pipeline.stages.raw.publishers import PUBLISHER_MATCH, SOURCES, write_parquet
    
    
    class FineNewsConfig(BaseModel):
        """Versioned inputs and output for the Fine News selection."""
    
        model_config = ConfigDict(extra="forbid")
    
        source: str
        domains: Path
        output: Path
    
    
    def filter_fine_news(
        config: Annotated[
            Path, typer.Option(help="Historical acquisition configuration.")
        ] = Path("data/inputs/fine-news/acquisition.json"),
    ) -> None:
        """Select English publisher shards from a pinned Fine News revision."""
        settings = FineNewsConfig.model_validate_json(config.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
        target = settings.output / "articles.parquet"
        if target.exists():
            raise FileExistsError(f"Output exists: {target}")
        target.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
        with TemporaryDirectory(dir=target.parent) as staging, duckdb.connect() as con:
            if settings.source.startswith("hf://"):
                con.execute("INSTALL httpfs; LOAD httpfs")
            temporary = Path(staging) / "articles.parquet"
            write_parquet(
                con,
                f"""WITH articles AS (
                    SELECT {SOURCES["fine_news"].projection} FROM read_parquet($source)
                ) SELECT text, id, metadata FROM articles WHERE {PUBLISHER_MATCH}""",  # noqa: S608 - authored projection and predicate.
                {"source": settings.source, "domains": str(settings.domains)},
                temporary,
            )
            os.link(temporary, target)
        typer.echo(f"Wrote: {settings.source} -> {target}")

    ## Common options
    
    - `--format` — Output format: `--format json` (or `--json`) or `--format table` (default).
    - `-q / --quiet` — Quiet output (one ID per line).
    - `--revision` — Git revision id which can be a branch name, a tag, or a commit hash.
    - `--token` — Use a User Access Token. Prefer setting `HF_TOKEN` env var instead of passing `--token`.
    - `--type` — The type of repository (model, dataset, or space).
    
    ## Mounting repos as local filesystems
    
    To mount Hub repositories or buckets as local filesystems — no download, no copy, no waiting — use `hf-mount`. Files are fetched on demand. GitHub: https://github.com/huggingface/hf-mount
    
    Install: `brew install hf-mount`, or download a binary from https://github.com/huggingface/hf-mount/releases
    
    Some command examples:
    - `hf-mount start repo openai-community/gpt2 /tmp/gpt2` — mount a repo (read-only)
    - `hf-mount start --hf-token $HF_TOKEN bucket myuser/my-bucket /tmp/data` — mount a bucket (read-write)
    - `hf-mount status` / `hf-mount stop /tmp/data` — list or unmount
    
    ## Tips
    
    - Use `hf <command> --help` for full options, descriptions, usage, and real-world examples
    - Authenticate with `HF_TOKEN` env var (recommended) or with `--token`
    - Update the CLI with `hf update` (uses the correct command for the detected install method)

## Activity

    $ cat src/python/README.md
    # Python workspace
    
    `apps/pipeline` is an installable Typer application in a Python 3.13 uv workspace.
    Run from the repository root:
    
    ```bash
    just python::setup
    just python::run --help
    just python::run version
    just python::run stages list
    just python::run stages raw --help
    just python::layout
    just python::check
    ```
    
    Data processing is organized into three layers, matching `dvc.yaml`:
    
    | Module and CLI group | Purpose | Data location |
    | --- | --- | --- |
    | `pipeline.stages.raw` / `stages raw` | Preserve source snapshots and provenance | `data/raw/` |
    | `pipeline.stages.processed` / `stages processed` | Build reusable cleaned and enriched tables | `data/processed/` |
    | `pipeline.stages.research` / `stages research` | Curate coverage panels, cohorts and release datasets | `data/research/` |
    
    The raw layer includes the frozen historical Fine News publisher filter described
    in [its acquisition configuration](../../data/inputs/fine-news/README.md), alongside
    `prepare-comparison` and `sample-comparison`. The research layer provides
    `compare-sources` for weighted estimates from the resulting manifests and counts.
    Experimental implementations live under each layer's `experiments` package.
    They share Pydantic artifact contracts through `pipeline.experiments`; the raw
    `publishers` module owns source mappings and extraction. DVC passes artifact
    paths explicitly, while statistical and source parameters live under
    `experiments.source_comparison` in the root parameter file. Reporting follows
    the configured dataset keys and can run a deliberate subset of sources.
    See the [source comparison](../../data/inputs/source-comparison/README.md) before
    running acquisition. Python setup installs DuckDB's `httpfs` extension so the
    local HTTP integration check can run offline. Add other stage commands under their owning layer,
    with explicit inputs and outputs, and declare their dependencies in `dvc.yaml`.
    DVC connects layers through artifacts; Python modules need not import earlier
    layers to read their outputs. Importing a module performs no dataset access.
    
    Setup installs the committed lock. Checks run offline with frozen dependencies.
    Ruff checks formatting, annotations, docstrings and common correctness/security
    issues; strict Pyrefly checks all app code and tests. Tach enforces module
    boundaries, rejects unused dependency declarations and forbids cycles. The CLI
    imports the stage router, which registers the three independent layer modules.
    
    `pytest-layout-enforcer` checks test paths against their owning source modules
    both during pytest collection and with `just python::layout`. Test paths mirror
    `apps/pipeline/src/pipeline` under `apps/pipeline/tests`: for example,
    `cli.py` maps to `test_cli.py`, and `stages/raw/loader.py` maps to
    `stages/raw/test_loader.py`. Feature variants use `__`, as in
    `test_loader__empty.py`; `include-packages` also allows tests for package
    initializers. This checks existing test placement, not test coverage. Tach checks
    imports and does not enforce this layout.
    
    `just python::test` runs all tests. `test-changed` is a local optimization only.
    `build` builds a wheel and source archive. `fmt` explicitly repairs formatting.
    Ruff and Pyrefly run from the same uv lock locally and in CI.
    ✓ • 0ms

    $ sed -n '1,120p' /home/marcussky/Git/fine-news-financial-publishers/README.md
    ---
    configs:
      - config_name: default
        data_files:
          - split: train
            path: "data/01_intermediate/*/eng_Latn/*.parquet"
    ---
    
    # Fine News Financial Publishers
    
    Tools for cleaning and enriching the monthly financial news Parquet shards in
    this repository. `data/00_raw/domains.csv` records the acquisition allowlist.
    The raw article source is upstream Fine News; publisher- and
    language-filtered shards live in `data/01_intermediate/YYYY-MM/eng_Latn/`.
    Cleaned records belong in `data/02_primary/`, with derived attributes in
    `data/03_feature/`. Generated primary/feature files and `outputs/` are ignored;
    the intermediate shards stay tracked with Git LFS. See [data stages](data/README.md).
    
    ## Development
    
    Use Linux x86-64 or ARM64 with Nix and Git LFS installed:
    
    ```bash
    bash infra/nix/install-devenv.sh
    devenv shell
    just setup
    just check
    ```
    
    The environment pins Python 3.13, uv, Git LFS, Ruff and Pyrefly. Setup installs the
    locked Python workspace and repository-local pre-commit hooks. `hf` is available
    through `cd src/python && uv run --frozen hf --help`.
    
    ## Restore data from the Hugging Face cache
    
    After an `hf download marcusinthesky/fine-news-financial-publishers --type dataset`,
    reuse its cache without another download:
    
    ```bash
    just data-restore --dry-run
    just data-restore
    ```
    
    The helper checks every indexed LFS object's cached size, copies each blob into
    `.git/lfs/objects` with `cp --reflink=auto`, verifies SHA256, and runs the offline
    `git lfs checkout`. Reflinks share disk blocks when supported and keep the cache
    independent from working files; other filesystems fall back to copying. Checkout
    preserves locally modified data. The helper honors `HF_HOME` and `HF_HUB_CACHE`,
    or accepts `--cache-dir /path/to/datasets--owner--repo` (the directory containing
    `blobs/`). `--dry-run` checks availability and sizes without hashing or writing.
    No cache files are moved, changed or deleted. Incomplete blobs fail explicitly.
    It follows the Git index, so staged shard renames are restored at their new paths.
    
    If the cache is missing files, fetch those through `hf download` first, or use
    `git lfs pull` to download the missing LFS objects from the configured remote.
    
    ## Build intermediate data
    
    The concise [acquisition pipeline](data/00_raw/README.md) reads the pinned Fine
    News revision through DuckDB's `hf://` support, filters by the 115-domain CSV and
    English capture paths, and writes the original monthly shard layout.
    
    ```bash
    just python::run intermediate build --month 2016-08 --dry-run
    just python::run intermediate build --month 2016-08 --output .tmp/intermediate-trial
    ```
    
    Omit `--month` for all English capture months. This requires network access.
    The default output is `data/01_intermediate`; existing shard paths are refused.
    Use a fresh directory for a rebuild.
    
    ## Clean and enrich
    
    Run from the repository root inside `devenv shell`:
    
    ```bash
    just python::run intermediate inspect
    just python::run primary build data/01_intermediate/2016-08/eng_Latn/part-000000.parquet --output data/02_primary/2016-08.parquet
    just python::run feature build data/02_primary/2016-08.parquet --output data/03_feature/2016-08.parquet
    ```
    
    The Typer root attaches separate `intermediate`, `primary` and `feature` command
    modules. Each stage supports `inspect` and `build`.
    The former top-level `inspect` and `clean` commands are replaced by these stage
    commands. Pass `.` to `intermediate inspect` to discover the intermediate shards
    from the repository root. Repository-root scans exclude generated stages. Polars uses lazy scans and a
    streaming Parquet sink. Cleaning preserves original text, IDs and metadata,
    adds whitespace-normalized `clean_text`, and drops null or blank articles.
    Enrichment adds character and word counts, the lowercased publisher hostname
    (with an initial `www.` removed), publication date and source file path.
    Invalid dates become null. Output creation refuses to overwrite existing files.
    These cleaning stages do not deduplicate or resolve entities. The separate
    [company tagging pipeline](src/python/apps/fine_news_cli/docs/company-tagging.md)
    extracts candidate companies and evidence; its completed 14.81M-row run and
    the Nasdaq coverage comparison are documented alongside the command.
    
    All Python workflows live in the `fine-news` Typer application; see
    [Python](src/python/README.md).
    Explore the historical candidate comparison in the
    [marimo notebooks](src/python/notebooks/candidate_datasets/README.md).
    Run `just fmt` to format and `just check` to lint, typecheck, test and build.
    
    ## Template updates
    
    This project adopts [Exordio](https://github.com/marcusinthesky/template) from the
    local `~/Git/template` checkout, pinned in `.copier-answers.yml`. Commit local
    work before using Copier 9.16.0 to update; review conflicts in the renamed
    Python packages and project documentation. The existing LFS attributes are
    project-owned and must be preserved when merging template updates.
    
    The configured `origin` is the Hugging Face dataset repository. The included
    GitHub Actions workflow is ready for a GitHub remote; publishing is separate.
    ✓ • 0ms

    # Data workspace
    
    Data follows the same layers as `dvc.yaml` and `pipeline.stages`:
    
    - `raw/`: versioned source snapshots and provenance.
    - `processed/`: reusable cleaned, deduplicated and enriched tables.
    - `research/`: coverage panels, study cohorts and release datasets.
    - `inputs/`: small, Git-tracked inputs to pipeline stages.
    
    Experiments use the same name within each layer. Source-comparison manifests
    and samples live in `raw/experiments/source-comparison/`; estimates and paper
    tables live in `research/experiments/source-comparison/`. Later processing
    experiments can use `processed/experiments/<name>/`. DVC connects these artifacts;
    an experimental result does not become a release dataset merely by moving it.
    
    Stage commands create their output directories when implemented. Git ignores
    large data payloads; track reproducible data with DVC. Keep small input files,
    `.dvc` pointer files and documentation in Git.

    # Raw acquisition inputs
    
    [domains.csv](domains.csv) is the exact 115-hostname allowlist used by the
    original Colab publisher filter. It contains domains rather than individual
    article URLs. Matching includes each listed host and its subdomains, preserving
    specific hosts such as `fortune.cnn.com` without admitting all of `cnn.com`.
    
    The article source remains upstream `ksolovev/fine-news`, pinned to commit
    `7a841090e69f3c58a9e04b0c39213d879af68e8a` in
    [`_filter_config.json`](../../_filter_config.json). Raw article/media files are
    queried remotely and are not duplicated in this directory. The CSV is the
    builder's filter input; the root JSON records the historical dataset filter.
    
    Run from the repository root inside `devenv shell`:
    
    ```bash
    just python::run intermediate build --month 2016-08 --dry-run
    just python::run intermediate build --month 2016-08 --output .tmp/intermediate-trial
    ```
    
    Omit `--month` to select all English capture months. Without `--output`, the
    builder targets `data/01_intermediate`; it refuses any existing destination
    shard before scanning articles. Use a fresh output directory for a rebuild.
    `--source` accepts an explicit `hf://` or local glob with the same
    `YYYY-MM/eng_Latn/*.parquet` layout; `--domains` selects another domain CSV.
    
    The builder runs the [filter SQL](../../src/python/apps/fine_news_cli/src/fine_news_cli/intermediate/filter.sql.j2)
    once per source shard and retains its month/language/filename layout. It
    prefers nonblank `metadata.url_hostname`, falling back to the URL hostname,
    then normalizes case, whitespace and trailing dots. It projects only `text`,
    `id` and `metadata`, excluding separate media columns. Text, IDs and metadata
    values are retained; row ordering and encoded Parquet bytes need not match.
    
    This is the Colab filtering operation without Google Drive mounting, runtime
    package installation, quota monitoring or resume machinery. DuckDB uses two
    threads, a 2 GiB memory limit, a 4 GiB spill limit and Zstandard level 9, as in
    the original. Completed shards are published atomically; failed temporary files
    are removed. A later failure can leave earlier completed shards in place.
    
    The dependency environment can be prepared with `just setup`. Remote builds and
    remote dry runs need network access; a dry run only lists paths. DuckDB installs
    and loads its `httpfs` extension on first remote use. Local source globs work
    offline and are used by the regression tests.

    $ cat > /tmp/ccfinance_restore_fine_news.py <<'PY'
        """Restore the published Fine News snapshot from verified local Parquet files."""
        import hashlib
        import json
        import subprocess
        from pathlib import Path
        from tempfile import TemporaryDirectory
        
        import pyarrow.parquet as pq
        
        workspace = Path('/home/marcussky/Git/CCFinance')
        repository = Path('/home/marcussky/Git/fine-news-financial-publishers')
        source = repository / 'data/01_intermediate'
        target = workspace / 'data/raw/fine-news'
        revision = '3168f32f57107eac95a2c53f024e5e340c91ef2e'
        local_revision = subprocess.check_output(['git', '-C', str(repository), 'rev-parse', 'HEAD'], text=True).strip()
        assert not target.exists(), f'Output already exists: {target}'
        files = sorted(source.rglob('*.parquet'))
        assert len(files) == 168, f'Unexpected shard count: {len(files)}'
        config = json.loads((workspace / 'data/inputs/fine-news/acquisition.json').read_text())
        domains = workspace / 'data/inputs/fine-news/domains.csv'
        assert domains.read_bytes() == (repository / 'data/00_raw/domains.csv').read_bytes()
        expected = {}
        for path in files:
            relative = path.relative_to(source).as_posix()
            published = subprocess.check_output(['git', '-C', str(repository), 'show', f'{revision}:{relative}'], text=True)
            local = subprocess.check_output(['git', '-C', str(repository), 'show', f'{local_revision}:data/01_intermediate/{relative}'], text=True)
            assert published == local, f'Published and local LFS pointers differ: {relative}'
            lines = published.splitlines()
            assert lines[0] == 'version https://git-lfs.github.com/spec/v1', relative
            expected[relative] = {'sha256': lines[1].removeprefix('oid sha256:'), 'bytes': int(lines[2].removeprefix('size '))}
        published_paths = subprocess.check_output(['git', '-C', str(repository), 'ls-tree', '-r', '--name-only', revision], text=True).splitlines()
        assert {path for path in published_paths if path.endswith('.parquet')} == set(expected), 'Published shard inventory differs'
        target.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
        with TemporaryDirectory(prefix='.fine-news-restore-', dir=target.parent) as temporary:
            staging = Path(temporary) / 'snapshot'
            print(f'Copying {len(files)} verified published shard paths...', flush=True)
            subprocess.run(['cp', '-a', '--reflink=auto', str(source), str(staging)], check=True)
            records = 0
            manifest = []
            for number, (relative, identity) in enumerate(expected.items(), 1):
                path = staging / relative
                assert path.stat().st_size == identity['bytes'], f'File size differs: {relative}'
                with path.open('rb') as handle:
                    digest = hashlib.file_digest(handle, 'sha256').hexdigest()
                assert digest == identity['sha256'], f'SHA256 differs: {relative}'
                metadata = pq.read_metadata(path)
                assert metadata.schema.to_arrow_schema().names == ['text', 'id', 'metadata'], relative
                records += metadata.num_rows
                manifest.append({'path': relative, **identity, 'records': metadata.num_rows})
                if number % 20 == 0 or number == len(expected):
                    print(f'Verified {number}/{len(expected)} shards', flush=True)
            provenance = {
                'repository': 'marcusinthesky/fine-news-financial-publishers',
                'revision': revision,
                'source_pattern': f'hf://datasets/marcusinthesky/fine-news-financial-publishers@{revision}/*/eng_Latn/*.parquet',
                'local_repository_revision': local_revision,
                'local_source_directory': 'data/01_intermediate',
                'upstream_source': config['source'],
                'domains_sha256': hashlib.sha256(domains.read_bytes()).hexdigest(),
                'files': len(manifest),
                'records': records,
                'parquet_bytes': sum(file['bytes'] for file in manifest),
                'layout': 'Published capture-month shards; a fresh filter run writes articles.parquet.',
                'verification': 'Every restored file matches its published Git LFS SHA256 and size; rows and columns checked from Parquet metadata.',
                'shards': manifest,
            }
            (staging / 'provenance.json').write_text(json.dumps(provenance, indent=2) + '\n')
            staging.rename(target)
        print(json.dumps({key: provenance[key] for key in ('repository', 'revision', 'files', 'records', 'parquet_bytes')}), flush=True)
        PY

## Activity

    $ cat ARCHITECTURE.md
    # Architecture
    
    CCFinance separates code and research artifacts. Git stores source, configuration,
    locks, provenance definitions and documentation. DVC defines data dependencies
    and will track large data and experiment outputs once they are materialized.
    
    - `src/python/apps/pipeline` owns the CLI and data stage implementations.
    - `src/python/uv.lock` locks runtime, quality, testing, packaging and DVC tools.
    - `src/latex` owns the manuscript source and bibliography.
    - `data` holds ignored data payloads and versioned DVC pointer files.
    - `infra/nix` and `devenv.lock` own the reproducible system environment.
    
    Tach enforces module boundaries; Ruff and strict Pyrefly check Python source.
    pytest-layout-enforcer checks test file placement during collection and CI.
    Semflow fingerprints the Python code used by DVC stages, allowing DVC to
    invalidate tracked results when executable behavior changes.
    CI executes those checks, tests and builds through the same just recipes as local
    work. Setup may download dependencies; ordinary checks use cached dependencies
    and do not repair authored content. LaTeX uses a versioned Tectonic asset bundle.
    
    The Hugging Face dataset is staging, and the bucket is intended for intermediate
    and experiment artifacts. The frozen raw acquisition stage documents the
    historical selection without fetching its output. Company-level coverage,
    enrichment and remote artifact transport remain future work. The raw comparison stages prepare
    sampling manifests from Hub listings and Parquet footers, then acquire only the
    selected row groups through the shared publisher filter. Research aggregation
    reads those artifacts without importing raw-stage modules. DVC connects these
    steps; pinned source revisions and recorded draw probabilities define the
    experiment's population and sampling design.
    
    Each data layer groups experimental artifacts beneath `experiments/<name>/`.
    Experimental stage code follows the same grouping under its owning layer.
    `pipeline.experiments.source_comparison` defines shared parameters and artifacts;
    Tach permits raw and research to depend on these contracts without importing one
    another. Raw publisher extraction owns one source-field registry, deriving both
    SQL projections and projected column sizes from it. DVC supplies artifact paths
    explicitly. Research uses statsmodels for survey-estimate summaries and LaTeX
    tables; it preserves the probability-sampling design.
    
    Copier answers record the source and tag for future template updates. Review
    update conflicts and preserve project-specific code and configuration. The
    upstream template is [Exordio](https://github.com/marcusinthesky/exordio).
    ✓ • 0ms

    # Dataset Comparisons Summarized
    
    **Date:** 2026-11-16
    **Source:** chatgpt.com
    
    ---
    
    ### **You** · Mon 16 Nov, 11:10
    
    In the appendix of [https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.23447](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.23447) what are the other dataset the authors discuss and compare theirs against?
    
    ---
    
    ### **ChatGPT** · Mon 16 Nov, 11:10
    
    <small><strong>Reasoning / progress:</strong><br>
    I’ll check the paper’s appendix and identify the datasets it explicitly discusses in comparison with the authors’ own.</small>
    
    In **Appendix A, Table 5** of <Link url="https://arxiv.org/html/2410.23447v3#Sx1" title="Systematic Covariance Envelopes from Wasserstein Geometry"/>, the authors compare their Nasdaq-hosted financial-news dataset against **four other financial-news datasets**.
    
    | Dataset | Reference | Coverage |
    |---|---|---|
    | **RavenPack Equity – Dow Jones Edition** | Ge et al. (2023) | Large proprietary archive; 2004–2015 in the cited study |
    | **Thomson Reuters News Analytics (TRNA)** | Scherbina & Schlusche (2013) | Approximately 5.5 million stories, 1996–2012 |
    | **Raw Reuters financial-news corpus (Ding et al. corpus)** | Schwenkler & Zheng (2020) | 106,521 full-text articles, 2006–2013 |
    | **RESET Financial Text Intelligent Analysis Platform + Juyuan** | Ge et al. (2026) | 1,138,247 relevant Chinese financial-news articles, 2006–2021 |
    
    <Cite refs={["turn302746view1"]}/>
    
    ### How they compare
    
    The authors evaluate these datasets along six dimensions: geographical/language coverage, availability of full article text, entity annotations, scale, accessibility/reproducibility, and researcher control over text processing.
    
    Their own dataset is the **Nasdaq-hosted public per-symbol news archive**, which provides full article bodies and permits independent embedding and text processing. Its main limitation is narrower, coverage-conditioned sampling compared with proprietary archives.
    
    ### One additional dataset worth noting
    
    Appendix A also discusses the **Hoberg–Phillips ETNIC-All product-market similarity dataset** (Hoberg & Phillips, 2016; 2025). This is not one of the four news-corpus comparisons in Table 5, but it is used as an empirical benchmark.
    
    ETNIC measures firm similarity from 10-K business descriptions using doc2vec embeddings. The authors compare it with their news-embedding Wasserstein distances for 81 firms. <Cite refs={["turn302746view2"]}/>
    
    **Source:** <Link url="https://arxiv.org/html/2410.23447v3" title="Paper HTML, Appendix A, Table 5"/>. Note that this is version 3, revised November 5, 2026.
    
    ---
    
    ### **You** · Mon 16 Nov, 11:11
    
    What metadata do these datasets contain?
    
    ---
    
    ### **ChatGPT** · Mon 16 Nov, 11:11
    
    <small><strong>Reasoning / progress:</strong><br>
    I’ll distinguish metadata documented for each dataset from fields that may be available only in particular versions or licensing arrangements.</small>
    
    The datasets differ substantially in the **article-level metadata** they provide, particularly company identifiers, timestamps, sentiment scores, event classifications, and entity mentions.
    
    The key distinction is that **RavenPack and Thomson Reuters News Analytics provide structured, vendor-generated metadata**, whereas the raw Reuters and Nasdaq datasets offer greater control over the article text but fewer precomputed annotations.
    
    ## 1. Metadata comparison
    
    The paper's Appendix A, Table 5, confirms which datasets have entity annotations and full text, but it does **not** provide exhaustive field-level schemas. The comparison below therefore distinguishes documented features from metadata that depends on the particular dataset version or processing pipeline. <Cite ref="turn287435view0"/>
    
    | Dataset | Article metadata | Entity metadata | Analytical metadata | Full text |
    |---|---|---|---|---|
    | **RavenPack Equity – Dow Jones** | Timestamp, story ID, source | Company ID, ticker/ISIN mappings | Sentiment, relevance, event category, novelty | No, in standard analytics files |
    | **Thomson Reuters News Analytics (TRNA)** | Timestamp, story ID, source | Company identifiers, firm mentions | Sentiment, relevance, novelty, volume measures | Requires companion archive |
    | **Raw Reuters (Ding et al.)** | Article text and associated records; exact fields vary | Automatically extracted company mentions | Derived co-mentions and network relationships | Yes |
    | **RESET + Juyuan** | Financial news records; exact schema not established | Chinese listed-company mentions | Text-derived firm relationships | Partial, licence-dependent |
    | **Nasdaq archive (authors' dataset)** | Article date, URL/identifier, ticker association | Source-level ticker association | Researcher-generated embeddings and distances | Yes |
    
    These are not all equivalent types of metadata: the sentiment and event scores in commercial analytics products are typically vendor-produced, while the embeddings and network measurements in the research datasets are created by researchers.
    
    ## 2. Detailed metadata by dataset
    
    ### RavenPack Equity – Dow Jones Edition
    
    RavenPack is especially rich in **company-level and event-level metadata**. Documented fields in RavenPack analytics products include:
    
    - **Identification:** story ID, timestamp, company name, company identifier, ticker, ISIN, source.
    - **Entity relevance:** how strongly a story concerns a particular company.
    - **Sentiment:** event sentiment and composite sentiment scores.
    - **Event classification:** event category or taxonomy, such as earnings or corporate developments.
    - **Novelty:** whether similar information has appeared previously.
    - **Other analytics:** story-event counts and related measures.
    
    An academic description of RavenPack News Analytics 3.0 reports 39 fields for the Global Equities edition. The exact schema depends on the product version. <Cite refs={["turn983798search14","turn983798search0"]}/>
    
    ### Thomson Reuters News Analytics (TRNA)
    
    TRNA is also highly structured. Historical documentation describes more than 80 metadata fields, including:
    
    - **Identification:** item ID, timestamp, Reuters instrument code (RIC), source, feed.
    - **Entity information:** companies mentioned, number of companies, first-mention position.
    - **Sentiment:** positive, negative and neutral probabilities.
    - **Relevance:** a numerical company-specific relevance score.
    - **Novelty:** counts and links to similar previous stories across several lookback windows.
    - **Topics:** subject categories, broker actions and market commentary classifications.
    - **Volume and structure:** news intensity, word counts, sentence counts, story type.
    
    Importantly, TRNA can generate **different relevance and sentiment metadata for different companies mentioned in the same article**. <Cite refs={["turn657501search1","turn657501search39","turn657501search37"]}/>
    
    ### Raw Reuters financial-news corpus
    
    The appendix confirms that this corpus contains full article text and was processed using automated named-entity recognition (NER).
    
    This makes it possible to derive company mentions, co-mentions, sentence-level relationships and news networks.
    
    However, the appendix does **not** establish a complete original-record schema for timestamps, article IDs, publisher fields or entity identifiers. Those should be checked against the historical corpus documentation rather than assumed to be available as standardized columns. <Cite ref="turn287435view1"/>
    
    ### RESET + Juyuan
    
    The documented relevant features are Chinese financial-news text and company mentions, used to infer financial relationships among China A-share firms.
    
    The exact company-annotation pipeline, field names and availability of full-text exports are not established in the appendix. In particular, I would not assume that it supplies standardized sentiment, relevance or event-category fields without inspecting the licensed product documentation. <Cite ref="turn287435view1"/>
    
    ### Nasdaq news archive
    
    For the authors' own dataset, the paper confirms:
    
    - Article identifiers used for deduplication.
    - Article dates for window filtering.
    - URLs used for deterministic sampling.
    - Full article bodies.
    - Source-level ticker associations, rather than manually validated article-level entity annotations.
    - Firm names and sector labels obtained from separate Nasdaq summary metadata.
    
    The authors subsequently calculate document embeddings and firm-pair distances. Those are **derived research variables**, not metadata supplied by Nasdaq. <Cite ref="turn287435view2"/>
    
    ## 3. Additional comparison: Hoberg–Phillips ETNIC-All
    
    This dataset is structurally different because its unit of observation is a **firm pair in a given year**, rather than a news article.
    
    Its principal information is firm identification, year and an embeddings-based product-market similarity score. ETNIC-All includes similarity measures for all firm pairs, not just close competitors. <Cite ref="turn657501search0"/>
    
    ## Which dataset is most useful?
    
    For research requiring **timestamped, company-specific news with ready-made sentiment and event metadata**, RavenPack and TRNA are the strongest of these options.
    
    For research requiring **raw text, custom entity extraction or independently generated embeddings**, the raw Reuters corpus and the Nasdaq archive are more suitable, subject to accessibility and coverage limitations.
    
    One particularly important distinction for constructing firm networks is whether a dataset identifies **every company mentioned in an article**, rather than merely associating the article with one primary ticker. The former is much more useful for building reliable co-mention networks, while the latter may require a separate NER pipeline.

    **Neither dataset uses free-form event classifications.** Both use predefined, controlled taxonomies, but they organize information differently.
    
    - **RavenPack Equity – Dow Jones Edition:** A hierarchical event taxonomy, with increasingly specific categories such as `acquisitions-mergers → acquisition → acquisition-acquirer`.
    - **Thomson Reuters News Analytics (TRNA):** A controlled set of Reuters topic codes, such as `MRG` (mergers and acquisitions), `RES` (financial results), and `DIV` (dividends). These cover events but also industries, geographies, asset classes, and broader subject matter.
    
    The distinction matters because RavenPack's taxonomy is more explicitly designed to identify **what happened to a company**, while Reuters topic codes describe **what an article is about**. <Cite refs={["turn765275search5","turn572709search21","turn572709search25"]}/>
    
    ## 1. RavenPack: Hierarchical event classification
    
    A documented historical RavenPack taxonomy (2016) contains four levels:
    
    <box border radius="lg" padding={3} gap={2}>
      <box background="surface-secondary" radius="md" padding={3} align="center">
        <text color="secondary" weight="medium" size="xs">TOPIC</text>

      </box>
      <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="tertiary"/></row>
      <box background="surface-secondary" radius="md" padding={3} align="center">
        <text color="secondary" weight="medium" size="xs">GROUP</text>
        **Acquisitions–Mergers**
      </box>
      <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="tertiary"/></row>
      <box background="surface-secondary" radius="md" padding={3} align="center">
        <text color="secondary" weight="medium" size="xs">TYPE</text>
        **Acquisition**
      </box>
      <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="tertiary"/></row>
      <box background="rgba(16,130,90,0.07)" border={{size:1,color:"subtle"}} radius="md" padding={3} align="center">
        <text color="secondary" weight="medium" size="xs">CATEGORY — MOST GRANULAR</text>
        **Acquisition-acquirer**
      </box>
    </box>
    
    <text color="secondary" size="xs">Historical taxonomy: 5 topics, 51 groups, 412 types and 2,064 categories. The taxonomy has since expanded; RavenPack currently advertises more than 7,000 event topics. <Cite refs={["turn765275search26","turn765275search1"]}/></text>
    
    Some actual category examples include:
    
    | Event group | Example classifications |
    |---|---|
    | Earnings | Earnings announcements, earnings above expectations, earnings guidance |
    | M&A | Acquisition acquirer, acquisition acquiree |
    | Products and services | Product release, product recall |
    | Workforce | Layoffs, executive resignation, strike |
    | Regulatory and legal | Regulatory investigation, litigation, sanctions |
    | Financial markets | Analyst ratings, credit ratings, price targets |
    | Corporate operations | Facility openings, supply-chain disruptions |
    
    These are representative labels, not an exhaustive taxonomy export. In RavenPack, the exact event classification can also vary by company within a single story.
    
    The full taxonomy is a versioned lookup rather than a field that accepts arbitrary text. RavenPack provides taxonomy mapping files through WRDS, and its API supports taxonomy queries. <Cite refs={["turn765275search4","turn765275search5","turn765275search27"]}/>
    
    ## 2. Thomson Reuters News Analytics: Topic codes
    
    Reuters uses a predefined set of codes, but unlike RavenPack's event hierarchy, the taxonomy mixes several kinds of classification.
    
    Here are examples documented in the Reuters taxonomy and historical TRNA materials:
    
    | Code | Classification | Meaning |
    |---|---|---|
    | `MRG` | Mergers & acquisitions | Takeovers, mergers, acquisitions |
    | `RES` | Results | Corporate financial results |
    | `RESF` | Results forecast | Forecast financial results |
    | `DIV` | Dividends | Dividend announcements and forecasts |
    | `IPO` | Initial public offerings | New public stock offerings |
    | `ISU` | New issues | New debt or equity issuance |
    | `RCH` | Research | Research-related coverage |
    | `JOB` | Labour/personnel | Employment and labour issues |
    | `AAA` | Credit/debt ratings | Creditworthiness assessments |
    | `CEN` | Central banks | Central-bank activity |
    | `ECI` | Economic indicators | Economic data releases |
    | `GDP` | Economic output | GDP and GNP data |
    | `INT` | Interest rates/policy | Central-bank rate policy |
    | `ESG` | ESG | Environmental, social and governance issues |
    | `TECH` | Technology | Broad technology subject |
    | `SOFW` | Software | Technology subcategory |
    
    <Cite refs={["turn572709search21","turn572709search23","turn572709search0"]}/>
    
    A few important characteristics:
    
    - **Multi-label:** One news article can have several topic codes.
    - **Hierarchical:** Some codes have parent–child relationships, such as `TECH` and `SOFW`.
    - **Not exclusively events:** Codes can represent industries, asset classes, geographic regions or economic subjects.
    - **Controlled vocabulary:** Codes are drawn from a maintained reference list, not freely generated by an LLM or written independently for each story.
    
    The Reuters feed documentation represents topic codes as `N2:` identifiers, for example:
    
    
    
    The corresponding archive field can contain a space-delimited list of topic codes. <Cite refs={["turn572709search22","turn572709search25"]}/>
    
    You can explore the public code directory here:
    
    <Link url="https://liaison.thomsonreuters.com/tools/topic-codes" title="Reuters Topic Codes — Official taxonomy browser"/>
    
    Note that the live directory can contain codes added after the historical TRNA dataset was compiled, so it should not automatically be treated as the exact historical codebook.
    
    ## 3. Practical comparison
    
    | Property | RavenPack | TRNA |
    |---|---|---|
    | Controlled vocabulary | Yes | Yes |
    | Free-form event labels | No | No |
    | Hierarchical | Yes, explicit event hierarchy | Yes, parent–child topic codes |
    | Company-specific event roles | Yes, for applicable events | Not generally encoded in topic codes |
    | Multiple classifications per article | Yes | Yes |
    | Granular event distinctions | Strong | More limited |
    | Broad subject/industry tagging | Yes | Strong |
    | Taxonomy reference available | Via vendor/WRDS mapping | Public topic-code directory, plus versioned reference files |
    
    ## 4. Implication for your research
    
    If you're interested in **grouping articles by the economic event they describe**, RavenPack is generally the closer match.
    
    For example, with a merger article:
    
    - RavenPack may distinguish the acquiring company from the acquired company through event categories.
    - TRNA may simply assign `MRG` alongside other relevant topic codes, without representing those transaction roles in the topic classification itself.
    
    Conversely, if you want to group articles into broad subjects such as technology, banking, energy, monetary policy or corporate results, Reuters topic codes provide a useful controlled vocabulary.
    
    **One important caveat:** Neither taxonomy is a universal set of mutually exclusive event classes. A single article can discuss several subjects or events, and a category alone may not capture every relationship expressed in the text.
    
    For reproducible academic analysis, I would use the **historical taxonomy mapping corresponding to the actual data release**, not today's vendor taxonomy, because classifications and code coverage can change over time.

    # Architecture
    
    The raw source is upstream Fine News, pinned by `_filter_config.json`.
    `data/00_raw/domains.csv` is the acquisition allowlist. The intermediate builder
    uses a short parameterized DuckDB SQL query over `hf://` files, selecting English
    paths and retaining only text, IDs and metadata. It preserves the original
    Colab hostname predicate, without the Drive/quota/resume runtime machinery. Monthly
    publisher- and language-filtered shards live under
    `data/01_intermediate/YYYY-MM/eng_Latn/`, tracked with Git LFS. Hugging Face's
    README configuration selects only these shards for the default dataset split.
    
    `data/02_primary` holds cleaned articles; `data/03_feature` holds enriched
    records. Each directory retains a tracked `.gitkeep`, with generated contents
    ignored. Model-input and later stages are deferred until their contracts exist.
    See [data stages](data/README.md) for current transformations and boundaries.
    
    The `fine-news` Typer application owns the data workflows and transformations
    under `src/python/apps/fine_news_cli`. Its root registers `intermediate`,
    `primary`, `feature`, `eval` and `company` command groups. Intermediate building
    queries the upstream files, while inspection reads the
    filtered shards; primary building cleans text; feature building derives the existing
    publisher/date/count attributes. Scans preserve `source_path` lineage across
    stages and repository-root scans select only intermediate inputs.
    
    Tests cover the stage workflow, whitespace, missing values, enrichment, LFS
    pointer detection, source lineage and overwrite protection. Lazy scans and
    streaming writes support both single-shard trials and the full intermediate set.
    
    The standalone `scripts/restore-lfs-cache.py` uses Python's standard library,
    Git LFS and GNU cp. It seeds verified objects from existing Hugging Face cache
    blobs without network requests. It reads LFS paths from the index so staged
    renames are respected during checkout. Independent reflinks protect the cache from
    working file edits; checksum verification precedes checkout.
    
    Devenv pins system tools in `devenv.lock`; `src/python/uv.lock` pins Python
    runtime, build and test dependencies. Setup prepares dependencies and local Git
    hooks. Formatting is explicit; checks do not repair tracked source files.
    
    The project was rendered from `~/Git/template` with Copier 9.16.0, selecting only
    Python. `.copier-answers.yml` records the source revision. The package names,
    project documentation and original LFS attributes are project customizations;
    review these when merging a template update.

    # Full-corpus company candidates
    
    The production CPU runner tags every source row with candidate companies from
    the annual US top-1000 panel and the fixed Gawronsky–Huang roster. It extracts
    mentions and publisher evidence; it does not claim substantive relevance,
    primary-company truth or calibrated probabilities.
    
    Install the [CPU extra](company-cpu.md) before running from the repository root
    inside the development environment:
    
    ```sh
    src/python/.venv/bin/python -m fine_news_cli company tag-corpus
    ```
    
    Defaults are six processes, one native thread per process, 128 input rows per
    batch, and compressed Parquet output chunks of 8,192 rows. The default run first
    processes a 100,000-row pilot distributed proportionally across source files,
    then continues to the full corpus. Both stages enforce an 8 GiB combined process
    memory ceiling. Pilot ranges are deterministic contiguous ranges for bounded
    Parquet reads, not a random sample suitable for prevalence inference. Reported
    throughput includes source reads, matching and durable output; preflight source
    hashing and final reports are separate.
    
    The initial successful 100,000-row pilot covered all 168 local files and took
    13.0 seconds (about 7,700 rows/second), with 3.3 GiB peak combined resident memory.
    The reader uses a 512 MiB DuckDB budget per process; the aggregate ceiling also
    accounts for Python objects and output buffers. All 322 CLI tests passed before
    the production run. The optimized matcher produced identical evidence on all
    2,000 checked raw rows,
    and its cased projection matched the frozen policy on all 1,135 clean supported
    evaluation rows.
    
    ## Completed production run
    
    The 2026-11-04 run completed all **14,807,287 source rows in 168 files** with
    exit code zero. Processing took **1,643 seconds (27 minutes 23 seconds)**,
    averaging **9,012 articles/second**, including source reads, matching and durable
    writes. Preflight hashing and final report generation are outside that timing.
    Peak combined process-tree resident memory was **7,533,608,960 bytes (7.02 GiB)**,
    below the 8 GiB guard. Six CPU workers ran on the Ryzen 5 9600X; the GPU was not
    used. No per-core utilization trace was collected, so these measurements do not
    establish exact CPU saturation.
    
    | Universe | Source rows with candidates | Rows with cased name evidence | Rows with publisher evidence |
    | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
    | Annual US top-1000 | 12,159,551 | 8,365,194 | 512,169 |
    | Fixed GH roster | 3,764,426 | 1,569,478 | 139,298 |
    
    Evidence categories overlap. Candidates include ambiguous and lowercase aliases;
    these counts are not estimates of substantive coverage, precision or recall.
    The independent [2,000-row prevalence audit](company-prevalence.md) addresses
    substantive coverage with a different procedure and remains provisional.
    
    The committed [findings snapshot](company-tagging-findings.json) retains run
    metrics, contract and artifact fingerprints, the GH minimum, and the Nasdaq
    comparison below. Generated predictions remain in the local output directory.
    
    Use `--phase preflight`, `--phase pilot` or `--phase run` for individual stages.
    Use `--resume` to verify and continue a run. `--limit` restricts the processing
    frame in source-file order for development. Configuration, registry, code,
    dependencies and source fingerprints must match the frozen manifest on resume.
    
    ## Evidence and identities
    
    One Rust Aho–Corasick DFA searches the union of registry names and aliases.
    Extended legal suffixes follow the existing tested policy, with separate alias
    ownership and overlap selection for each universe. Publication year controls
    top-1000 eligibility; the GH roster is fixed across years. Current registry
    names and fixed GH ticker spellings are not certified historical identities.
    
    Rows retain all candidate companies. Single-token lowercase matches, shared
    aliases, ambiguous symbols and incomplete catalogs have explicit flags.
    `cased_name_match_count` distinguishes evidence that survives the tested case
    policy; lowercase evidence remains available rather than becoming a negative.
    Neither a complete catalog nor a no-candidate result proves irrelevance.
    
    Publisher exchange annotations, cashtags and conservative standalone ticker
    tags are extracted separately. Explicit annotations are masked in the name
    matching view. Ordinary prose and complete company names remain intact; the
    evaluation sanitizer that could remove parts of company names is not applied.
    No bare ticker search is added to prose unless that spelling already appears
    as a catalog name or alias. Publisher evidence is unverified and must not be
    used as independent evaluation truth for predictions derived from that evidence.
    
    Top-1000 issuer IDs are `top1000:PERMCO`; GH IDs are `gh:CIK` with padded CIKs.
    Their identities remain separate, including when a company belongs to both.
    The output retains catalog CIK link status without inferring a crosswalk.
    Tickers are labels from the relevant catalog, not additional issuer identities.
    
    ## Output and recovery
    
    The destination defaults to `data/02_primary/company_tags/dfa-v1/`:
    
    - `manifest.json` freezes source SHA-256 fingerprints and the run contract.
    - `shards/NNNNN/part-NNNNN.parquet` stores every source row with native nested
      candidate/evidence structs. Each source directory has a `completed.json`.
    - `pilot/` contains separate pilot predictions and timing.
    - `progress.jsonl` records progress, resource observations and failures.
    - `summary.json` reconciles rows and counts by year, universe and evidence.
    - `company-year-counts.csv` counts candidate and publisher-supported source rows.
    - `gh-company-year-2018-2022.csv` includes zero-count cells for all GH companies;
      `gh-floor-2018-2022.json` identifies the minimum candidate count and ties.
    
    Read production predictions with `shards/*/part-*.parquet`; a recursive glob over
    the entire run directory would also include the separate pilot predictions.
    For the launched background run, `background-job.json` and `worker-process.json`
    identify the processes, `runner.log` captures errors, and `background-exit.json`
    records the eventual exit code. A final `summary.json` with `status=complete`
    confirms successful processing and report generation.
    
    `row_key` hashes the relative source path and zero-based physical row number.
    Original article IDs remain nullable and are not assumed unique. Duplicate or
    syndicated source rows are retained. Article text is not copied into outputs.
    Each candidate has full occurrence counts and at most four representative spans
    per field; offsets describe the NFKC/casefold matching view, not raw text.
    
    Workers commit a source directory atomically after row-count reconciliation and
    durable writes. Incomplete `.partial` source directories are rebuilt on resume.
    Completed chunks are checksum-verified and reused; corruption or changed inputs
    causes an error. Source failures prevent successful completion. An output lock
    prevents concurrent writers. A failed row is never silently dropped.
    
    Company-year counts describe source rows with candidate evidence, not unique
    stories or adjudicated substantive company coverage. In particular, the GH
    candidate floor is not a validated academic coverage floor.
    
    ## GH annual floor and Nasdaq comparison
    
    Across the fixed 100-company GH roster and the five publication years 2018–2022,
    the minimum among all 500 company-year cells is **CDNS in 2018: 16 candidate
    source rows**. Fifteen have cased company-name evidence and two have publisher
    ticker evidence; one row has both. None of the 500 candidate cells is zero.
    These source rows have not been deduplicated or adjudicated for substantive
    company coverage.
    
    The local `pricing-perspective` Nasdaq archive is a separately acquired,
    ticker-directed source. Its `main` revision
    `c8a4bd69cf26c87163d5db3c0a2de7b0d8b14cef` documents collection through
    `api.nasdaq.com/api/news/topic/articlebysymbol` in December 2022–January 2023.
    The immutable raw archive contains 397,041 rows; the current normalized local
    artifact contains 214,480 records across 100 symbols. Its global article-ID
    deduplication keeps one scrape-symbol assignment, potentially losing other
    article–symbol memberships. Nasdaq assignments and our extracted candidates
    therefore measure different things.
    
    | Publication year | Nasdaq normalized CDNS records | Fine News CDNS candidates | Fine News Nasdaq-hosted rows, all companies |
    | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
    | 2018 | 123 | 16 | 0 |
    | 2019 | 97 | 126 | 74,258 |
    | 2020 | 69 | 275 | 212,834 |
    | 2021 | 57 | 134 | 174,027 |
    | 2022 | 381 | 314 | 241,988 |
    
    There are also 123 distinct CDNS article IDs in the raw Nasdaq archive for 2018,
    so deduplication does not explain that year's 123-versus-16 difference. The
    historical `annual_raw_article_floor: 47` admission rule precedes normalization;
    it is not a guaranteed deduplicated annual floor. The realized normalized
    archive's minimum is SNPS in 2018 with 34 records. Its documented minimum of
    449 per ticker concerns the entire recovered history, rather than one year.
    
    The Fine News host counts use publication year from `metadata.publish_date`,
    and the normalized URL hostname with URL fallback. They include `nasdaq.com`
    and its subdomains across all 168 source files. None of the 123 Nasdaq CDNS
    URLs from 2018 matches a Fine News source URL after stripping the Nasdaq
    scheme/hostname and query/fragment components. This establishes a source URL
    coverage gap; it does not rule out copies hosted by original publishers.
    Title matching alone is insufficient: repeated earnings and market-summary
    headlines also occur in different years. The snapshot retains this diagnostic
    with its dates rather than treating repeated titles as duplicate stories.
    
    ## Confirmed recall gaps and next experiment
    
    The frozen GH catalog supplies `Cadence Design Systems` and the branded
    `cādence`, plus the legal name. Suffix expansion adds `CADENCE DESIGN SYSTEMS`;
    neither normalization nor that expansion produces plain `Cadence` or
    `Cadence Design`. Bare `CDNS` in prose is also outside the current ticker policy.
    
    A case-sensitive whole-word search for `Cadence` or `CDNS` in 2018 titles and
    bodies finds 75 source rows, of which 15 already have CDNS candidates. The
    remaining 60 are not all false negatives: they include Cadence Bank, Aerospace,
    Minerals, personal names, ordinary prose and an unrelated CDNS acronym.
    Three inspected untagged examples do identify the semiconductor/EDA company:
    
    | Source and date | Article | Missing spelling |
    | --- | --- | --- |
    | Korea Herald, 2018-02-28 | [Samsung's non-memory chips at MWC](http://www.koreaherald.com/view.php?ud=20180228000675) | Cadence |
    | Business Day, 2018-08-17 | [SA is on wrong side of global shift towards new industries](https://www.businesslive.co.za/bd/opinion/2018-08-17-sa-is-on-wrong-side-of-global-shift-towards-new-industries/) | Cadence Design |
    | Forbes, 2018-11-01 | [Simulation Becomes Increasingly Important For Self-Driving Cars](https://www.forbes.com/sites/davidsilver/2018/11/01/simulation-becomes-increasingly-important-for-self-driving-cars/) | Cadence |
    
    These are confirmed missed name mentions from local extracted text, not new
    human gold labels for substantive relevance. Their source IDs and excerpts are
    retained in the snapshot. Consequently, 16 undercounts available mentions and
    cannot establish the academic coverage floor. Both acquisition coverage and
    matching recall require attention.
    
    The next experiment should combine the Nasdaq archive with Fine News while
    preserving provenance and all article–company memberships through deduplication.
    Test provenance-backed aliases and contextual handling of ambiguous names on
    independent data before changing the production dictionary. Then recompute the
    company-year table and review its low-count cells. The completed run and its
    catalog remain frozen; this comparison does not merge sources or revise tags.

    $ cat /home/marcussky/Git/fine-news-financial-publishers/src/python/apps/fine_news_cli/docs/company-eval.md
    # Company matching evaluation pilot
    
    This pilot produces article-level company matching data, using publisher ticker
    markup as partial reference evidence. It does not produce exact NER span labels.
    The sample and article text are local generated data under ignored
    `.tmp/company-eval-v2/`; they are not automatically licensed for redistribution.
    
    From the repository root, in `devenv shell` after workspace setup:
    
    ```sh
    src/python/.venv/bin/python -m fine_news_cli eval build \
      --background-publishers src/python/apps/fine_news_cli/docs/company-eval-publishers.json
    src/python/.venv/bin/python -m fine_news_cli eval status
    ```
    
    `build` refuses to overwrite a nonempty output directory; `--output`, `--input`,
    `--membership` and `--seed` are configurable. Background articles are drawn
    from all available capture months in 2016–2025, restricted to publishers named
    in the policy, with nonempty retained tags and no detected ticker annotation
    in tags, title or body. It selects up to 200 per publication year, then fills
    any shortfall from other eligible years to reach 2,000. The signal stratum
    draws up to 100 articles per year from one seed-selected capture month per year.
    The background is selected first and the signal sample is disjoint. The
    manifest records file hashes, DuckDB version, membership hash, publisher policy,
    counts, pool limits and seed. Each candidate pool is capped at 4,000 per year.
    Build fails if it cannot find 2,000 qualifying background articles.
    
    The policy is based on the strongest *observed* agreement in a preliminary
    screen, not a guarantee that a publisher always annotates every company. It
    records its evidence and limitations. An article without a detected annotation
    is a candidate negative, not a confirmed negative. The filter conservatively
    rejects known exchange-qualified symbols and uppercase ticker-shaped tag tokens;
    it can reject unrelated acronyms and miss unrecognized ticker formats. A human
    review is needed to establish the actual in-scope companies.
    
    Documents must have at least 200 body characters after trimming and a parseable
    publication date in the capture year. Exact duplicate bodies or normalized URLs
    are removed. The corpus is already filtered to selected publishers, so scores
    and prevalence are not representative of unfiltered news. Press releases are
    not separately excluded. Publication dates are source metadata, not crawl-date
    substitutions. Full article text may include publisher navigation or other
    extraction artifacts.
    
    The membership CSV is a security-year panel. A publisher exchange-qualified
    symbol found in title, body or tags is recorded even if it is not in the panel.
    The automated resolver produces `unique_year_ticker_candidate` only when its
    symbol maps to one PERMCO in the publication year. This is evidence for review,
    not a verified exchange, issuer, CIK or company mention: the panel does not
    itself contain exchange identifiers, CIK links may be candidate-only, and
    symbols can be reused. Ambiguous and out-of-universe signals are retained.
    The data itself does not establish whether a publisher tag was created by a
    person or automation, or whether its list is exhaustive.
    
    The output contains:
    
    - `articles.jsonl`: original body, title, tags, URL, publisher, date, source path,
      source ID, stable article ID, publication year and sampling stratum.
    - `signals.jsonl`: source string, exchange, symbol, tag index or character
      offsets in title/body, candidate PERMCO, issuer keys and link status.
    - `review.jsonl`: a pending queue for 250 independently sampled background
      articles and all sampled signal articles, ordered deterministically within
      each group. No entry is considered a human-reviewed label until explicitly
      completed.
    - `manifest.json`: frozen inputs, output hashes and aggregate counts. The review
      hash is the initial blank queue and will differ once review has begun.
    
    ## Review protocol
    
    Join an article and its signals to a queue row using `article_id`. Review the
    **whole title and body** for all companies in that publication year's top-1,000
    security panel, not just the extracted tickers. Consult the signals and the
    membership CSV as aids; resolve ambiguous tickers and share classes from dated
    source evidence. `text_company_permcos` is the complete list of distinct
    in-scope PERMCO strings explicitly mentioned in title or body. Put additional
    in-scope companies supported only by publisher metadata in
    `metadata_company_permcos`; use `[]` when there are none. Record evidence and
    ambiguities in `notes`. Do not equate a metadata tag with a text mention.
    
    Set `reviewer` to the reviewer's identifier. Set `review_status` to `reviewed`
    only when both lists are complete and `unresolved` is empty. Use `uncertain`
    for ambiguous cases and keep their unresolved details in that list. Keep
    `pending` entries unscored. Review the 250 background rows and keep reviewing
    signal rows until at least 250 articles have confirmed positive matches. The
    `status` command reports progress. More than one company can occur in an
    article; GOOG and GOOGL may resolve to the same PERMCO and should appear once.
    
    Example completed queue record (IDs and evidence are illustrative):
    
    ```json
    {"article_id":"...","stratum":"publisher_signal","review_status":"reviewed","reviewer":"reviewer-id","text_company_permcos":["8048"],"metadata_company_permcos":[],"unresolved":[],"notes":"Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT) in the first paragraph"}
    ```
    
    ## Scoring
    
    A tool adapter should produce UTF-8 JSONL with one line per predicted article:
    
    ```json
    {"article_id":"...","company_permcos":["8048"]}
    ```
    
    Use an empty list for an article with no predictions. Predictions must cover
    all reviewed articles; unknown or duplicate article IDs are rejected. Supply
    only title and body to a text-only tool. For a metadata-aware tool, document its
    inputs and run separately:
    
    ```sh
    src/python/.venv/bin/python -m fine_news_cli eval score \
      --predictions /path/to/predictions.jsonl --mode text
    src/python/.venv/bin/python -m fine_news_cli eval score \
      --predictions /path/to/predictions.jsonl --mode metadata
    ```
    
    Scores are micro-aggregated issuer precision, recall and F1 over completed,
    fully reviewed articles, separately by sampling stratum. The metadata-aware
    reference is the union of text and metadata labels; the text reference excludes
    metadata-only labels. The report also provides alignment with unreviewed
    publisher signals for predicted articles, deduplicated by article and PERMCO.
    Those signals are partial and may be wrong: alignment is **not** precision,
    recall or a substitute for human review. No reviewed labels means there is no
    measured precision or recall. Retain reviewer and source evidence when comparing
    tools, and document any overlap between tool development and this sample.
