    # Define dataset requirements
    
    ## Goal
    
    Specify a public, reproducible financial news dataset for firm-level text,
    co-mention networks and market research.
    
    ## Requirements
    
    - **Coverage:** Report distinct usable articles per company-year, including zero
      counts for a declared universe, and firms meeting selectable annual thresholds
      over consecutive years. Compare with 47 raw articles per year over 2018–2022
      for the 100-firm Pricing Perspective frame; report raw and usable counts separately.
    - **Articles:** Provide stable IDs, source and publisher, URL, title, article text,
      language, publication and capture times with precision, quality flags, and
      traceable capture provenance where available.
    - **Companies:** Preserve all article–company links, dated issuer identifiers,
      supporting evidence, ambiguity and substantive relevance. Distinguish mentions
      from company-focused coverage and retain unresolved identities.
    - **Sources:** Maintain versioned publisher selection criteria and distinguish
      original reporting, syndicated material and press releases where possible.
      Deduplicate stories without discarding source records or company links.
    - **Research validity:** Evaluate extraction, deduplication, dates, company links
      and relevance against human-adjudicated samples. Report precision, recall,
      uncertainty and coverage gaps across years, publishers and firms.
    - **Reproducibility:** Publish a versioned schema, data dictionary, lineage,
      checksums, methods, coverage reports and examples for firm-year panels and
      co-mention networks. Document article-text access and redistribution conditions.
    - **Extensions:** Treat company-specific sentiment and events, article topics and
      novelty as separately versioned, evaluated enrichments.
    
    Numerical coverage and quality targets remain provisional until the staging audit.
    Publication dates before CC-News began do not establish when text was observable.
    See the [Pricing Perspective comparison](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.23447v3#Sx1)
    for the baseline and its limitations.
    
    ## Acceptance
    
    - [ ] Review these requirements against staging evidence and intended studies.
    - [ ] Set evidence-based coverage and quality targets for a first release.

    # Random-source company coverage estimate
    
    This experiment estimates the fraction of source rows that substantively cover
    at least one company in the article-year universe. It accepts multiple central
    companies, including product, operational and legal stories without stock-market
    discussion. It does not require a unique primary company or attempt exhaustive
    company extraction. Passing examples, analyst employers, author holdings,
    advertisements and fund-sponsor attribution alone do not qualify.
    
    ## Completed result
    
    All 2,000 sampled rows have outcomes. Eight failed requests were retried once in
    a separate ledger; all retries completed. The effective outcomes are 310 positive
    (15.5%), 1,333 negative (66.65%) and 357 unknown (17.85%). Unknowns comprise 320
    historical catalog gaps and 37 unsupported years, rather than outstanding requests.
    
    The weighted AI-assisted audit estimates **18.06–20.56%** substantive eligible
    company coverage. The range spans seven unresolved review labels. The approximate
    95% interval for source sampling and review subsampling is **14.12–24.50%**;
    systematic AI-review error and corpus-coverage error are additional uncertainties.
    This corresponds to **2.67–3.04 million** of the observed 14.81M local source rows,
    or **3.61–4.11 million per 20M** if the larger source has the same mix.
    
    | Output | Estimated source articles with at least one correct returned company |
    | --- | ---: |
    | DFA candidates | 16.75% |
    | Tev1 final choice | 10.73% |
    | Either method | 17.45% |
    
    These are valid-link yields, not company-set precision, recall or F1. DFA emits
    candidates on 1,127/2,000 rows (56.35%), including many incidental matches. Its
    larger valid-link yield does not make all those candidate links acceptable.
    
    Every one of the 82 Tev1-positive cases whose selected company is absent from
    DFA's candidates was reviewed. Tev1's proposed company is accepted in 17 cases;
    DFA already has a different accepted company in three of those. Tev1 therefore
    adds **14/2,000 articles (0.70 percentage points)** with a valid association.
    Six of these have no DFA candidate at all: **6/2,000 (0.30 percentage points)**.
    The remaining eight have DFA candidates, all incidental or otherwise incorrect.
    
    Preparation accounts for part of that apparent advantage. A separate DFA-only
    sensitivity check preserves distinctive symbols inside complete registry-derived
    multiword company names, while still removing standalone symbols and explicit
    annotations. It changes 31 article views and recovers two of the 14 incremental
    links (CF Industries and Sirius XM). The residual is 12/2,000 (0.60 points).
    Original model inputs/results remain frozen. This diagnostic is not a new gold
    sanitizer certification; full company-name spans should be protected before a
    production labeling run.
    
    Other incremental cases suggest registry/normalization improvements to test on
    independent data: Wal-Mart/Walmart, Papa John's/Papa Johns, Uber/Uber Technologies,
    Wells Fargo's `/MN` legal-name suffix, and subsidiary names such as Janssen and
    OneMain Financial. The experiment supports high-recall dictionary retrieval plus
    better name preservation, identity data and semantic filtering. It does not
    establish a fast CPU routing policy that captures Tev1's marginal benefits.
    
    ## Source sample and preparation
    
    The frozen draw contains 2,000 uniformly hash-selected Parquet rows from all
    14,807,287 rows in the 168 local English intermediate files. Selection happens
    before annotation, dictionary, date, ID or length filtering. A physical source
    row is the sampling unit: syndicated copies count separately. The seed, exact
    query paths, DuckDB version, SQL hash, source file sizes/mtime and output hashes
    are saved in `sample.json`. The source Parquet files are not fully checksummed.
    The local source population is smaller than the user's 20M+ target, so larger
    corpus projections require the same publisher, language and date mix.
    
    The separate `company-prevalence-text-1` profile strips explicit exchange/ticker
    annotations, cashtags, metadata markup and distinctive bare symbols. Publisher
    tags and expected labels never enter the decision state. Ambiguous prose and
    company names remain, with an audit warning: 890 inputs are clean and 1,110 are
    usable with ambiguity. All 2,000 rows remain in the denominator. This is unlabeled
    prevalence inference; the profile does not certify leakage-free gold evaluation
    inputs or replace the existing frozen evaluation sanitizer.
    
    ## Frozen model protocol
    
    Tev1 runs locally through Docker/SGLang on the RTX 5060 Ti in BF16, using its
    pinned checkpoint and image, FlashInfer and radix caching. The checkpoint
    revision and runtime arguments are in `runtime.json`; the actual sample-client
    configuration is `inference-config.json`. The container startup manifest retains
    older benchmark input-path defaults, which the client configuration overrides.
    
    Every named issuer in the article-year catalog is scored, without a DFA candidate
    restriction. Groups contain at most 22 companies plus none/unclear. Each group
    nominates its highest-scoring company; intermediate reductions lead to a final
    company-or-none choice. Any substantive co-central company is accepted. Full
    title/body text is preserved; context failures are recorded rather than truncated.
    Group probabilities are conditional and uncalibrated.
    
    The `substantial-company-presence-4` protocol was fixed before the independent
    sample inference. Earlier canaries used the previously reviewed 60 disagreements
    to reveal logical-OR false positives and excessive model abstention; those cases
    are not independent validation of the new protocol. No sample audit labels were
    used to tune its prompts or thresholds.
    
    A negative requires a complete catalog and successful inference. Missing
    historical company names, unsupported years and request failures remain unknown.
    There are 37 sampled rows outside the available annual membership panel. Some
    older display names and aliases also disagree with historical tickers; catalog
    completeness alone does not establish semantic identity correctness.
    
    Transient group-request failures are retried separately after the main pass.
    The original predictions remain frozen. Complete retries can supply a separate
    effective result, with provenance linking each replacement to its original.
    
    The client first saved 567 rows before exiting with code 137 during severe host
    memory pressure. A four-article concurrency resume reached 939 saved rows;
    growing native tokenizer memory then prompted bounded 128-article subprocesses
    with `MALLOC_ARENA_MAX=2`. Each chunk releases its memory and resumes only missing
    IDs. Execution segments and chunk logs record these operational changes. The
    model, article inputs and question protocol remain fixed; this mixed execution
    is not a controlled throughput benchmark.
    
    ## Audit and interpretation
    
    An independent random base audit contains 200 articles selected without viewing
    model outcomes. Three AI reviewers read full prepared texts, with Tev1, DFA and
    publisher annotations hidden, and checked annual membership. Fifty articles,
    prioritizing uncertain cases, received a second blinded review. One binary
    disagreement was reconciled from the full text; this targeted cross-review is
    not a representative inter-rater agreement estimate.
    
    The audit then adds randomly selected unreviewed articles within final Tev1
    positive, negative and unknown strata, targeting at least 100, 100 and 50 reviews
    respectively. The 82 additions bring this random audit to 282 rows: 100 positive,
    132 negative and 50 unknown outcomes. Existing base reviews are retained.
    
    A further 57 targeted reviews complete a census of all 82 potential new-link
    cases, giving **339 unique reviewed articles**. The enhanced estimate separates
    the model-positive population into 228 overlap cases (75 randomly reviewed) and
    82 potential new-link cases (all reviewed). Negative and unknown samples retain
    their original design. Conditional on these cell counts, the non-census reviews
    remain uniform within each cell. The original three-stratum estimate is also
    retained, without mixing targeted additions into its random positive sample.
    
    Estimates weight each cell by its share of the full 2,000-row draw, rather than
    averaging an oversampled positive review set. Unresolved review labels span bounds.
    Approximate intervals include source-sampling and review-subsampling variation,
    but exclude systematic reviewer errors and source-coverage errors.
    
    Review is **AI-assisted, not human gold**. It supplies a provisional planning
    estimate. Article-level valid-link yield means that at least one returned PERMCO
    is accepted. It is distinct from complete company-set precision, recall or F1.
    The DFA candidate rate is also distinct from substantive company coverage.
    
    ## Reproduction and artifacts
    
    Run from the repository root, using the installed CLI environment:
    
    ```sh
    fine-news eval prevalence \
      --output .tmp/company-prevalence-tev-v1 \
      --source data/01_intermediate --phase sample
    
    # Start the pinned local Docker runtime before inference.
    fine-news eval prevalence \
      --output .tmp/company-prevalence-tev-v1 --phase infer \
      --runtime-config .tmp/company-prevalence-tev-v1/inference-config.json \
      --concurrency 4
    
    fine-news eval prevalence-audit \
      --output .tmp/company-prevalence-tev-v1 \
      --reviews .tmp/company-prevalence-tev-v1/audit/all-reviews.jsonl \
      --predictions .tmp/company-prevalence-tev-v1/effective-predictions.jsonl \
      --reviewer-type ai_assisted --census-additions
    ```
    
    `prevalence_sample.sql.j2` is packaged with the eval module. Resume validates
    frozen sample/config/protocol hashes and article IDs/input hashes. The source
    archive and dependency hash sidecar retain the inference implementation. The
    primary resume contract checks the orchestrator, preparer and presence module;
    additional serving dependencies are recorded separately rather than all enforced
    by that resume check.
    
    Artifacts under `.tmp/company-prevalence-tev-v1/` include the raw sampled rows,
    prepared inputs and sanitization sidecars, annual universe, group distributions,
    final decisions, DFA candidates, blinded dossiers, review judgments, cross-review
    reconciliation and weighted summaries. Original and post-retry results remain
    separate. The GPU runtime is removed after inference and retries finish.
    
    The main result is `audit-census-summary.json`; `audit-effective-summary.json`
    retains the original 282-row random audit. `audit/all-reviews.csv` contains the
    339 judgments, and `audit/routing-census.json` lists every potential addition.
    `name-sensitivity-summary.json` records the separate preparation diagnostic.
    The final Docker log and cleanup confirmation are retained. The original runtime
    helper session was unavailable at teardown, so no complete GPU-monitor trace
    was recovered; the owned container was removed explicitly after preserving logs.

    # Text adjudication of DFA–Tev1 disagreements
    
    All 60 disagreements between `extended_cased` Rust DFA and the saved Tev1
    predictions were reviewed against full sanitized titles and bodies. This is
    **AI-assisted adjudication**, not independently reviewed human gold. It supplies
    case evidence and provisional labels; no original publisher labels were changed.
    
    Three reviewers received disjoint 20-article batches, balanced by text length.
    Prediction identities were randomized as A/B per article; publisher annotations
    and the A/B model key were withheld during their initial judgments. The final
    reconciliation applied the user's ticker-conditioned embedding requirement:
    multiple substantively central, year-eligible issuers can all be accepted.
    Incidental examples, author disclosures, advertisements, analyst employers and
    fund sponsors without substantive company coverage do not qualify. Company-year
    membership was checked separately from current display names and historical
    aliases. Eleven cases have medium rather than high confidence, including
    extraction failures and boundary-of-scope judgments.
    
    ## Adjudication result
    
    | Acceptable output on the disagreement | Articles |
    | --- | ---: |
    | Tev1 only | 26 |
    | DFA only | 15 |
    | Both select valid companies | 10 |
    | Neither output is acceptable | 9 |
    
    Twenty articles have multiple eligible central associations, twenty have one,
    and twenty have no eligible central association. `Both valid` means each model's
    single selection is acceptable; it does not imply either returns the complete
    company set. Abstention counts as valid when there is no eligible central company.
    
    Tev1 produces 36 acceptable outputs here, versus 25 for DFA. Its advantage is
    largest on articles with no eligible central company: Tev1 alone is correct on
    12, DFA alone on one, and neither on seven. On multi-company articles, DFA alone
    is valid on seven, Tev1 alone on three, and both on ten. Accepting ties therefore
    preserves useful associations rather than manufacturing a unique primary label.
    
    These findings revise the earlier conclusion drawn from publisher ticker overlap:
    Tev1 is useful on some semantic errors, especially incidental matches and
    out-of-universe subjects. They do not establish full-corpus model accuracy or a
    beneficial routing policy. The 161 agreeing reference articles were not adjudicated
    here, this subset was selected for disagreement, and the reviewers are models.
    Identifying disagreement itself also requires both predictions; a production
    CPU-only gate must identify useful fallbacks before running Tev1.
    
    ## Examples
    
    - The Leidos earnings story maps to Leidos; Amazon appears in an unrelated stock
      service advertisement. Tev1 selects Leidos and DFA selects Amazon.
    - The equal-weight ETF discussion uses Apple as a portfolio example. Tev1's
      abstention is accepted and DFA's Apple selection is incidental.
    - The blockchain applications article has meaningful Amazon, Walmart and
      Microsoft business examples. DFA's Amazon selection is accepted; abstention
      loses useful associations under the embedding scope.
    - The J&J/Lilly clinical-development comparison supports both company links.
    - The Spirit Airlines article has neither selected company as an eligible central
      subject. Neither Alpha Metallurgical nor Spire is an acceptable replacement.
    - An article can name a company clearly but have no eligible issuer in that
      article-year universe, including some IPO-period and non-US issuer examples.
    - Target, Amazon, Boot Barn and Disney title-only/incomplete-body cases retain
      explicit extraction/medium-confidence notes; they do not become clean gold.
    
    ## How many articles may receive ticker links?
    
    The independent source sample has 30,000 rows selected by a uniform hash,
    independent of ticker presence. Its eligibility frame requires a non-null ID,
    at least 200 text characters and a publish year inside the membership panel.
    It samples the 168 local English Parquet files containing 14,807,287 rows; it
    is not an observed census of the user's full 20M+ target corpus.
    
    | Measurement | Observed count | Rate | Conditional equivalent per 20M |
    | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
    | Detected exchange-qualified or standalone publisher ticker evidence resolving to the universe | 1,032 / 30,000 | 3.44% | 688,000 |
    | Refined DFA returns at least one company candidate, clean supported cohort | 4,205 / 8,267 | 50.86% | 10,172,977 |
    
    The annotation rate covers only recognized formats and unique article-year
    symbol resolutions. It is not the fraction of all company-related articles.
    The 3.44% sample proportion has a Wilson interval of 3.24–3.65%, describing
    sampling uncertainty only, not annotation completeness or correctness.
    
    The DFA figure is a **candidate rate**, not a validated relevant-company rate.
    There are 7,277 candidate article–company pairs; 1,702 of the 8,267 articles have
    multiple candidates. A primary is selected on 4,195 articles, leaving ten tied
    candidate-bearing articles. Future association output should retain accepted
    multiple central issuers rather than drop those articles.
    
    The broader sample has 20,090 sanitizer-blocked articles, 9,910 clean articles,
    and 1,643 clean articles outside the current 2016–2025 scoring cohort. Those
    unscored rows are not negatives. The clean cohort is selected: 826 of the 1,032
    articles with detected in-universe ticker evidence are blocked. Consequently the
    50.86% rate cannot yet be treated as a reliable full-corpus forecast, and the
    60 deliberately selected disagreements cannot estimate population precision.
    
    The current evidence suggests substantial candidate volume, potentially millions
    of articles. A validated count of accepted ticker associations requires resolving
    coverage gaps and auditing a random sample of matches and no-matches.

    # Company reference universes
    
    These are frozen research inputs collected on **2026-11-02**:
    
    | File | Rows | Coverage |
    | --- | ---: | --- |
    | [nasdaq_100.csv](nasdaq_100.csv) | 203 | Historical Nasdaq-100 ticker/issuer entries since August 2016; 190 distinct SEC CIKs |
    | [gawronsky_huang_2026.csv](gawronsky_huang_2026.csv) | 100 | Exact tickers and row order of the pricing-perspective study roster |
    
    The historical window starts **2016-08-01**, the first month in our CC-News
    collection, and ends **2026-11-02**. The historical roster combines the
    [current constituent list](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_NASDAQ-100_companies)
    with additions and removals in the
    [historical changes table](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Historical_components_of_the_Nasdaq-100)
    within that window. Historical symbols `FB`, `FISV`, `PCLN`, `CTRP`, `SYMC`,
    `WLTW` and `QVCA` are retained alongside the tables' later symbols. The tables
    sometimes use later tickers retrospectively, so this is a company search
    universe, **not a dated membership panel** or proof that every listed symbol
    traded in the index throughout the window.
    
    The study CSV preserves `~/Git/pricing-perspective/data/universe.csv` exactly
    at the ticker level, including `FISV` and `GOOG`; it is not replaced by today's
    Nasdaq-100. The local file hash, repository commit, source order, Wikipedia
    list revisions and output hashes are recorded in
    [company_references.provenance.json](company_references.provenance.json).
    
    ## Identity and aliases
    
    `company_legal_name` comes from the annual-report cover where recoverable,
    otherwise the SEC submissions name. `legal_name_source` identifies which.
    `cik` is a **zero-padded string**, and `ticker` retains the roster's symbol.
    Use **`(ticker, cik)`**, rather than ticker alone, as the historical row key:
    `FOX` and `FOXA` each occur for both Twenty-First Century Fox and the separate
    Fox Corporation issuer. Share classes and ticker changes can also share a CIK.
    
    `other_names` is a JSON-encoded `List[str]`, for example
    `["Meta Platforms", "Facebook, Inc.", "Facebook"]`. Names come from the
    constituent tables, study names, Wikipedia lead names and SEC former names,
    with shortened legal suffixes and case-insensitive deduplication. The legal
    name remains in its own column. `other_names_source_urls` provides the
    Wikipedia revision and SEC identity record. Obvious product names and generic
    business categories were removed; this is not an exhaustive brand dictionary.
    Aliases are unversioned search candidates: short names and former names need
    context before assigning an article to an issuer.
    
    ## SEC descriptions
    
    `sec_business_description` contains extracted source text, **not a generated
    summary**. The selected report is the latest original annual report found in
    the retrieved SEC submissions history, filed on or before the access date:
    
    - Form **10-K**, **Item 1: Business**.
    - Form **20-F**, **Item 4: Information on the Company**, for foreign issuers.
    - Thomson Reuters' Form **40-F**, **Exhibit 99.1**, the annual report's complete
      Business section (printed pages 2–18).
    
    Reports are retrieved from official `sec.gov/Archives` URLs using Exa's full
    rendered-text fetch. SEC identity and filing metadata come directly from
    `data.sec.gov/submissions`. The rendered text retains tables in Markdown;
    layout, headings and page folios can differ from the original HTML. Body
    boundaries were checked against the rendered report; exceptions use recorded
    line boundaries rather than silently matching the contents page.
    
    Four integrated reports—**ASML, CCEP, INTC and VOD**—incorporate their business
    disclosures from multiple page ranges. For these, `sec_referenced_pages`
    records the ranges in the filing's Item 1/4 cross-reference index. Extraction
    retains the surrounding rendered-page intervals to avoid truncating a
    referenced page when folios are missing. These cells therefore include
    adjacent material, sometimes substantial; they are explicitly marked
    `cross_referenced_pages_with_context`. Their exact retained line windows are
    in the provenance JSON. Other populated rows are marked `extracted_section`.
    
    **HONA and SPCX have no annual report in the retrieved SEC histories.** Their
    SEC description, filing URL and report dates are empty, with status
    `no_annual_report_available`; their company identity, SEC search link and
    Wikipedia description are retained. A registration statement or parent
    company's annual report has not been substituted for an unavailable report.
    All 100 study rows have a populated annual-report description.
    
    Each row provides:
    
    - `sec_form`, `sec_section`, `sec_report_date`, `sec_filing_date` and accession.
    - `sec_filing_url`, the actual text source; `sec_primary_document_url` points
      to the filing cover when the text comes from an exhibit.
    - `sec_search_url`, a CIK/form-filtered EDGAR search, and `sec_submissions_url`.
    - `sec_accessed_date`, extraction method/status and text SHA-256 hashes.
    
    The document hash identifies the **rendered UTF-8 text**, not original filing
    HTML bytes. The description hash identifies the exact decoded CSV cell.
    Historical tickers may point to a later annual report and later legal name
    for the same issuer. These latest-access descriptions and aliases are **not
    point-in-time features** for historical prediction; report dates must govern
    any such use.
    
    ## Wikipedia descriptions and attribution
    
    `wikipedia_description` contains the company article's lead paragraphs with
    reference markers removed. It is separate from the SEC description and is
    not presented as a filing disclosure. Each row records the article URL,
    permanent revision URL, access date, language and description SHA-256.
    
    Insmed's available page is in **German** (`wikipedia_language=de`); its text
    is retained without translation. The United Airlines Holdings article URL
    redirects to the operating airline article; that scope difference is noted
    in the row. Other row-specific limitations appear in `notes`.
    
    Wikipedia text is attributed to the linked article's contributors and is
    available under [CC BY-SA 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/).
    Permanent revision links identify the relevant text and provide access to its
    history. The extraction changes formatting and removes citation markers.
    This attribution does not assign the same licence to company-authored SEC
    filing text or assert a licence for the whole dataset.
    
    ## Reading the CSVs
    
    Both files use UTF-8, RFC-style CSV quoting and multiline text cells. Decode
    `other_names`, `other_names_source_urls`, `membership_evidence` and
    `sec_referenced_pages` as JSON; do not split list cells on commas. Preserve
    CIK leading zeros when loading:
    
    ```python
    import polars as pl
    
    companies = pl.read_csv(
        "data/00_raw/gawronsky_huang_2026.csv",
        schema_overrides={"cik": pl.String},
    ).with_columns(
        pl.col("other_names").str.json_decode(pl.List(pl.String))
    )
    ```
    ✓ • 0ms

    # Primary-company pilot
    
    The OpenRouter method sends all issuer groups together in one Decisions API
    request per article and model; there is no runoff. A separate local Kev runner
    uses grouped choices followed by a final runoff. Keep each method's outputs and
    provenance separate when comparing results.
    
    All commands run from the repository root through the single Typer application.
    Install optional dependencies from `src/python` with
    `uv sync --locked --all-packages --extra decisions` for OpenRouter, or
    `uv sync --locked --all-packages --all-extras` for GPU QC as well.
    
    ```sh
    just python::run eval prepare-inputs
    just python::run company extract --dry-run
    just python::run company extract --canary-only
    just python::run company extract
    ```
    
    Preparation verifies the frozen sample and membership hashes. It removes tags,
    URLs, source metadata, exchange-qualified ticker annotations, cashtags, marked
    bare symbols and HTML from the title/body input. Normalized shadow text retains
    offsets into the originals for the removal audit. Every publisher annotation
    used as inline label evidence must be covered by removal spans. Unresolved
    known bare symbols quarantine the article, including symbols collected across
    the dataset's ticker annotations and ticker-shaped tags. Parenthesized uppercase
    ticker-shaped strings are removed even outside the universe. This can also remove
    ordinary acronyms. The vocabulary is dataset-wide, not article-label-specific.
    Uppercase prose and initialisms need careful handling. This is a conservative
    automated boundary, not proof that every
    possible annotation format has been recognized. Inspect `sanitization.jsonl`
    before relying on the sample.
    
    As an additional safeguard, each article is quarantined if one of its own
    publisher ticker signals or standalone ticker-shaped tags remains visible as a
    bare token after preparation. This check does not add labels to model input,
    but using source evidence to exclude articles can bias the retained sample.
    The original, unsanitized source should remain available for separate human
    review of removals and ambiguous quarantine decisions.
    
    The default input directory is `.tmp/company-eval-text-v1`. Its manifest records
    the sanitizer version and immutable input hashes. `articles.jsonl` contains only
    identifiers, year, sanitized title/body and preparation status. Strata, original
    text hashes and removal evidence remain in the separate audit. Prepared output
    refuses overwrites; keep prior versions when regenerating.
    
    The decision backend receives only task instructions and sanitized title/body.
    The publication year selects the eligible Top 1,000 security panel, deduplicated
    by PERMCO. It does not enter the article state. Identity supplements provide
    missing display names with source evidence; they do not certify CIK links or
    historical aliases.
    
    Every eligible issuer appears in exactly one Choice question in a single
    request. Perplexity's models use groups of up to 253 issuers plus two null
    options; Clef uses at most 24 plus two nulls; other models use 32 plus two.
    If exactly one group selects an issuer and the others choose no match, it is
    selected. Multiple winners or an unclear answer trigger abstention; probabilities
    from different groups are not compared. This aggregation needs independent
    validation: a model may disagree with itself across groups, and context or
    option effects can bias its choices. No NER shortlist is used.
    
    One HTTP request does not guarantee one internal forward pass or a shared-state
    billing rate. Perplexity documents joint requests for v1.2, whereas its Flash
    route currently bills state per question. Some runtimes also split large
    requests. This pilot records the provider and actual usage and never splits a
    request in client code. Articles exceeding the conservative full-request byte
    bound are recorded as context-exceeded rather than truncated or split.
    The default is standard `perplexity/pplx-decider-v1.2`; the other models remain
    available for explicitly selected compatibility experiments. The byte bound is
    conservative and may exclude inputs that would fit the provider tokenizer.
    
    The configured models use OpenRouter's native
    [Decisions API](https://openrouter.ai/docs/api/api-reference/alphadecisions/submit-a-decisions-request),
    not token-generating chat completions. A synthetic tail-reading and typed-answer
    probe precedes article inference. Clef excludes Workers AI because its
    [documented text truncation](https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/community/multimodal-decisions#limits)
    would silently omit article content. Model context overflow is recorded instead
    of shortening the article. The UTF-8 byte bound deliberately overestimates token
    counts and can reject articles that a provider tokenizer would fit.
    
    SecretSpec resolves the `openrouter` profile in the repository's
    `secretspec.toml`, using the existing `OpenRouter` GCP Secret Manager item.
    Credentials are retrieved lazily for an uncached paid request and are not
    written to artifacts. An explicit `OPENROUTER_API_KEY` environment override is
    also supported.
    
    The run directory `.tmp/company-decisions-single` contains per-model CSV/JSONL,
    combined predictions, probes, the catalog snapshot, request cache, manifest,
    summary and durable budget records. Cache keys include the prepared-input,
    universe and question-version contract. Resume with the same directory. The
    configured cumulative limit covers all models and retries. The default is
    USD 5; the current pilot's authorized ceiling is USD 5.39867 against its
    existing shared ledger. Keep the immutable
    `cost_ledger.json` baseline together with its adjacent `.journal` file. New
    reservations and settlements append to the fsynced journal; the run summary
    reports current charges and commitments. Reservations are written before
    requests; unaccounted errors and interrupted requests retain their
    reservation. Costs are reconciled against returned usage, and potentially
    exceeded reservations stop paid work. Never reset the ledger to resume a test.
    Changing directories creates a separate ledger and must not be used to bypass
    the cumulative test budget. To run a revised input contract in a new output
    directory while retaining prior charges and reservations, pass the existing
    ledger with `--budget-ledger .tmp/company-decisions-v1/cost_ledger.json`.
    The ledger's lock serializes runs that share it. The default concurrency is four
    articles and 24 requests, configurable with `--article-concurrency` and
    `--request-concurrency`.
    
    The ten-article canary spans publication years and sampling strata. Only clean
    inputs proceed. API errors, context overflow and unavailable models are distinct
    from a model's null answer. Outputs are predictions, not human labels.
    `primary_review.jsonl` is a separate pending queue for human primary-company
    review. The existing `eval score` command measures **all-company mentions** and
    cannot measure this task's primary-company accuracy.
    
    ## Independent QC
    
    ```sh
    just python::run eval qc --backend dictionary --backend spacy --backend gliner \
      --device cuda:0 --batch-size 32 --limit 10 --output .tmp/company-eval-qc-smoke
    ```
    
    QC uses the same verified sanitized title/body. The dictionary, spaCy transformer
    NER and native GLiNER produce independent suggestions with character offsets,
    candidate PERMCOs and disagreements for review. GPU inference uses one process
    and overlapping bounded text windows; the GLiNER revision and model versions are
    recorded. Failed partial inference is not published as an empty prediction.
    QC suggestions never gate the decision models or become gold automatically.
    
    `eval link` reuses frozen spaCy and GLiNER v2.1 mention spans and replaces their
    exact-alias candidates with a shared pretrained contextual linker. It uses
    [`knowledgator/gliner-linker-large-v1.0`](https://huggingface.co/knowledgator/gliner-linker-large-v1.0)
    directly through GLiNER; the GLinker framework is not a dependency. The checkpoint
    and software versions are recorded in the output summary. The model's native
    span representation and label-scoring head classify the original spans. Entity
    label embeddings are computed once, and every named registry issuer is scored
    for each mention. No exact-name, fuzzy-name or NER-derived candidate shortlist
    is used. Canonical names and aliases are embedded separately, following the
    documented default name-label format. Each issuer receives its highest native
    alias logit; aliases shared across issuers remain competing identities. Names
    exceeding encoder limits are explicitly clipped and counted. Registry
    descriptions are retained for audit but excluded from inference: the current
    metadata includes unreviewed matches and disambiguation-page text, and combining
    names, alias lists and long descriptions degraded the pilot. Article context is
    bounded around the original mention without discarding any part of that mention.
    
    ```sh
    just python::run eval link --prepared .tmp/company-eval-text-v4 \
      --qc .tmp/company-eval-qc-v4 --output .tmp/company-eval-linked-v2
    just python::run eval score-signals --prepared .tmp/company-eval-text-v4 \
      --decisions .tmp/company-decisions-single-v3 --qc .tmp/company-eval-linked-v2
    ```
    
    Linking uses the model's default 0.5 threshold, without fitting it to publisher
    signals. At most one company is accepted per mention. Ties, below-threshold
    scores, unalignable spans and excessive contexts are explicit unresolved states.
    Year eligibility is checked after scoring: an ineligible winner is not replaced
    by the next eligible company. Noneligible named registry issuers serve as
    distractors, but the registry does not represent every outside company. The
    threshold is not a trained open-world NIL classifier. Registry aliases are not
    all reviewed or historically valid; modern names can postdate articles. These
    limitations remain material for academic use. This is an exploratory pilot:
    changing the label representation after inspecting initial errors means a
    fresh, independently reviewed holdout is needed for confirmatory results.
    
    The linked output keeps source file hashes, raw spans, previous alias candidates,
    top model candidates, scores and link states. It has the same article format as
    QC, so `score-signals` can compare before and after linking on the identical
    common reference subset. The resolver never receives publisher reference
    signals. Its output still represents company mentions, not primary-company
    labels.
    
    The alias-aware pilot relinked all 1,135 clean articles. On the same 224
    signal-bearing articles (311 observed article/issuer pairs), descriptive overlap
    F1 changed from 0.631 to 0.352 for spaCy, and from 0.666 to 0.373 for GLiNER
    v2.1. Observed-signal recall was 0.842 for both linked systems; many additional
    predictions lacked observed publisher signals. The incomplete reference cannot
    establish that every such prediction is false. These results do not support
    promoting the default 0.5 acceptance threshold to an automatic enrichment policy.
    The new command remains explicit; the frozen baseline is retained. Reports,
    model provenance and link audits are in `.tmp/company-eval-linked-v2/`.
    `--limit 0` processes all clean inputs; choose a fresh output directory.
    
    `fine-news eval score-signals` reports overlap with the observed publisher ticker
    signals—including uniquely resolved standalone uppercase ticker tags—on
    signal-bearing articles for which every decision model and both NER
    systems completed. Its apparent precision and F1 treat unobserved companies as
    unmatched, even though the publisher annotations can be incomplete or wrong.
    The reference includes secondary and metadata-only companies; NER proposes all
    resolved mentions while each decision model predicts at most one primary
    company. These scores are descriptive and must not be presented as validated
    primary-company accuracy or as a fair ranking of unlike tasks.
    
    For the revised sample created during this pilot, run:
    
    ```sh
    just python::run eval score-signals --prepared .tmp/company-eval-text-v4 \
      --decisions .tmp/company-decisions-v4 --qc .tmp/company-eval-qc-v4
    ```
    
    On NixOS, the NVIDIA driver libraries must be visible to PyTorch and CuPy, for
    example by including `/run/opengl-driver/lib` in `LD_LIBRARY_PATH` alongside the
    devenv C++ runtime. The GPU extra supplies CUDA 13 CuPy for the RTX 5060 Ti.
    
    ## Local Kev with SGLang Docker
    
    `company local-extract` uses the native `/v1/systemone` pointer-head API of
    `jaredpalmer/kev-0.8b`, with the model's fitted temperature and no text generation.
    It asks one Choice question per group of 32 year-eligible issuers, retaining each
    group's highest-probability company even when its null option won. A final Choice
    over these company finalists includes no-match and unclear options. Probabilities
    from separate groups are never compared. This covers every eligible issuer
    without a NER shortlist and avoids losing all finalists to first-stage nulls.
    The grouping seed matches the earlier grouped pilot; this local prompt contract
    is versioned separately.
    
    The [upstream Kev recipe](https://docs.sglang.io/cookbook/autoregressive/Kev/kev)
    explicitly disables radix caching, chunked prefill and CUDA graphs. Each question
    prefills the article separately. SGLang batches these prefills, but this run does
    not demonstrate prefix-cache reuse. The running server's resolved settings are
    recorded in the runtime provenance. No unsupported cache override is applied.
    
    The pilot pins SGLang 0.5.23 and the Kev adapter, pointer head, tokenizer and Qwen
    base revision. Model hashes are retained in `.tmp/kev-runtime/`. Its Docker
    launch script binds port 30000 only to localhost, mounts the adapter read-only,
    uses a separate model cache, and attaches the local RTX 5060 Ti through NVIDIA
    CDI. The base model is cached before launch; the container runs with
    `HF_HUB_OFFLINE=1`.
    
    ```sh
    # Download the exact adapter and its required base into the Docker cache.
    hf download jaredpalmer/kev-0.8b \
      --revision bf75a6a8848ea6960ff2ed108d9ed44c2941174f \
      --local-dir .tmp/models/kev-0.8b
    hf download Qwen/Qwen3.5-0.8B-Base \
      --revision dc7cdfe2ee4154fa7e30f5b51ca41bfa40174e68 \
      --cache-dir .tmp/kev-runtime/hf-cache
    bash .tmp/kev-runtime/launch.sh
    
    # Use the frozen article-ID-only selection for the existing comparison.
    just python::run company local-extract \
      --runtime-provenance .tmp/kev-runtime/runtime.json \
      --article-ids .tmp/kev-runtime/comparison-article-ids.jsonl \
      --output .tmp/company-decisions-kev-v1
    ```
    
    Omit `--article-ids` to process all clean prepared articles in a new run directory.
    The runner verifies sanitized inputs and membership, sends only task/title/text,
    requires a localhost endpoint, bypasses environment proxies, validates complete
    answer distributions, and saves every completed article and response. It refuses
    changed contracts on resume. A resource or API failure stops the run with an
    explicit error rather than producing an apparent negative label. No articles
    are truncated. The local command does not resolve OpenRouter credentials or
    consume the paid pilot's ledger.
    
    On 2026-11-04, the local pilot completed the frozen 221-article comparison
    (304 observed article/issuer pairs) without inference failures or truncation.
    Kev's observed-signal precision/recall/F1 were 0.935/0.566/0.705, compared with
    0.994/0.523/0.685 for the earlier Span-02 grouped pilot. Kev selected a company
    for 184 articles and returned unclear for 37. It recovered 172 observed pairs,
    made 12 predictions without an observed signal, and left 132 pairs unpredicted.
    These are partial-reference overlap counts, not independently verified errors.
    
    The run took 423.8 seconds including local orchestration, with 405.4 seconds
    inside HTTP inference calls and 12,080,196 counted input tokens across 7,072
    question prefills. There were 442 localhost HTTP requests and zero paid API
    charges. The measured run used BF16 on the RTX 5060 Ti, with 16 maximum running
    requests and a 16,384-token prefill batch limit. Four separate synthetic controls
    (weather, public library, outside-universe workshop, equally central companies)
    all returned no company; the weather and library controls chose unclear rather
    than no-match. These controls do not validate performance on real background
    articles.
    
    Kev's F1 advantage over Span-02 was 0.020. An exploratory paired article
    bootstrap (10,000 resamples) gave a 95% interval of -0.017 to +0.058 for that
    difference, so this sample does not establish superiority. The bootstrap does
    not account for publisher clusters, near duplicates, incomplete reference labels
    or exploratory model selection. Results and provenance are in
    `.tmp/company-method-comparison-kev-v1/`, with predictions in
    `.tmp/company-decisions-kev-v1/`. The GPU container was stopped after the run.
    
    ## Reproducible local optimization trials
    
    `company benchmark` now manages pinned SGLang or vLLM Docker servers, queues
    articles concurrently, and measures the complete extraction policy. It records
    actual HTTP requests and question prefills separately: putting several questions
    in one HTTP request does not turn them into one model forward pass. Every first
    stage covers the full article-year issuer universe. No NER shortlist is used.
    
    The model contracts are pinned in `company/profiles.py`. Available paths are:
    
    | Profile | Engine/API | Maximum options | Prefix reuse |
    | --- | --- | ---: | --- |
    | Kev 0.8B | SGLang native `/v1/systemone` | 255 | Disabled by native pointer path |
    | OneJev 1.6 0.8B | SGLang `/v1/score`; vLLM one-token completions | 255 | Supported |
    | Tev1 0.8B experimental | SGLang `/v1/score`; vLLM one-token completions | 24 | Supported |
    | D3-edge, D3-lite | vLLM native `/v1/systemone` classifier | 255 | Disabled: bidirectional attention |
    
    The SGLang D3 checkpoint-loading canary produced missing-parameter warnings and
    an unusable answer. That path is refused; only vLLM's native D3 classifier is
    enabled. Kev 0.5B and Liquid d1-omni-600M do not have a verified native path in
    these pinned images and are not substituted with a different checkpoint or a
    custom integration. The native D3 head stays in its trained FP32 representation.
    See [vLLM's D3 contract](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/models/structured_decisions_models/#decision-30)
    and [SGLang's Kev recipe](https://docs.sglang.io/cookbook/autoregressive/Kev/kev).
    
    Download the immutable checkpoint revisions before running. For example:
    
    ```sh
    hf download OmniJev/OneJev1.6-0.8B \
      --revision c89933c277629b707895bff752c61d2b0664c85e \
      --local-dir .tmp/models/onejev-0.8b
    hf download vllm-sr/d3-edge \
      --revision bee5e872f75b9c5d1405767bf244a6948b95c0af \
      --local-dir .tmp/models/d3-edge
    hf download vllm-sr/d3-lite \
      --revision 6c01fba14e74f63b70e1ef442b0b6d1b934339d5 \
      --local-dir .tmp/models/d3-lite
    hf download togethercomputer/Tev1-0.8B-experimental \
      --revision 6bb2dff14b38fea90ddb14d870166ccaf77374e9 \
      --local-dir .tmp/models/tev-0.8b
    ```
    
    The example configurations pin both images by digest. Pull them explicitly if
    they are not cached. Allow sufficient disk space for extraction and checkpoint
    weights; the two installed engine images report approximately 56 GB and 33 GB.
    Containers mount checkpoints read-only, reuse a persistent compilation cache,
    bind only localhost, and run offline. An exclusive GPU lock prevents overlapping
    benchmark processes. Cleanup removes the owned container even if saving its log
    fails.
    
    ```sh
    just python::run company benchmark \
      --config src/python/apps/fine_news_cli/examples/company-benchmark.json \
      --output .tmp/company-model-benchmark
    just python::run company benchmark \
      --config src/python/apps/fine_news_cli/examples/company-cache-benchmark.json \
      --output .tmp/company-cache-benchmark
    ```
    
    Each suite consists of `base` RunConfig fields and named `trials` with
    `overrides`. Keep inputs, selection and reference identical between trials.
    Tune `article_concurrency`, `max_sequences`, `token_budget`,
    `chunked_prefill_size`, `attention_backend`, `precision` and `group_size` explicitly.
    OneJev supports BF16 and an online FP8 canary in the pinned SGLang image. NVFP4
    requires a supported quantized checkpoint; the runner does not manufacture one
    from BF16 weights. Engine support and F1 must be rechecked after precision changes.
    
    The default `exhaustive` policy asks about every group, keeps one company from
    each, and recursively reduces finalists to a final choice. Group sizes can
    shrink when a complete prompt would exceed context. An article that cannot fit
    even with one issuer stops the run; text is never truncated. Intermediate
    `outside_group` and final `no_primary_match` have distinct meanings.
    
    `layout=catalog_first` places the complete trusted issuer catalog before article
    text to permit reuse across different articles from the same year.
    `compact_options=true` refers back to catalog identifiers instead of repeating
    names in the question. The optional `catalog` policy first routes among catalog
    pages, then decides among companies in the selected pages. Every issuer appears
    in the routing state. Uncertain or null routes fall back to exhaustive scoring.
    This policy can still miss the correct company through a confident routing
    error; it must pass the same frozen reference test before promotion.
    
    `prime_prefix=true` performs an additional prefix-only score call before
    parallel SGLang questions, allowing the shared article prefix to enter the
    cache before fan-out. This extra call is included in work and timing counters.
    Cache effectiveness is measured from before/after Prometheus counters, rather
    than inferred from the presence of a launch flag. Per-question distributions
    are normalized within each question only; normalized confidence above uniform
    chance is a routing heuristic, not a calibrated correctness probability.
    
    Outputs include source snapshots, model and input hashes, resolved server
    settings, GPU samples, engine cache counters, traces, SQLite checkpoints and
    bounded Parquet shards. Reuse is limited to exact sanitized text and year under
    the same run contract, with separate article lineage. `local-extract --config`
    resumes a matching contract; benchmark timing requires a fresh directory.
    
    Quality passes only when **every** frozen reference article completed and its
    observed-signal F1 exceeds 0.68. Incomplete screening runs report no passing F1.
    Reports include exploratory article bootstrap intervals and, for suites with
    multiple complete policies, five-fold policy selection with identical input
    hashes kept together. Reusing this previously inspected publisher-reference
    sample does not create an independent primary-company gold evaluation.
    
    For timing independently of annotation presence:
    
    ```sh
    just python::run company prepare-throughput \
      --input data/01_intermediate --limit 30000 \
      --output .tmp/company-throughput-corpus
    ```
    
    The SQL resource samples source rows by a seeded hash without a ticker or NER
    filter, retains duplicates, and passes them through the existing leakage audit.
    Use its `prepared` directory in a RunConfig and set `article_ids` to null. The
    sample's year, length, duplicate and quarantine counts are recorded. Missing
    historical issuer names stop extraction with details in `universe.json`.
    Quarantined articles are never counted as completed labeling.
    
    30 million articles in one day requires 347.2 articles/s before overhead; the
    sample runtime gate uses 400/s for headroom. Two to three days requires
    173.6 to 115.7 articles/s. A sample projection is always labeled unverified.
    After a candidate passes quality, coverage and throughput screening, use at
    least 10,000 fresh eligible documents, three fresh-output repetitions and a
    one-hour stream of distinct documents to test sustained throughput. Replaying
    the 221-article comparison would inflate cache reuse and is not a corpus test.
    
    The independent 2026-11-04 sample at `.tmp/company-throughput-corpus-v1`
    contained 30,000 source articles: 9,910 passed the strict leakage boundary and
    20,090 were quarantined. It exposed 229 missing historical year/issuer names
    before the 2016–2025 pilot window. Its body-length median/p90/p99 were
    2,826/6,240/21,463 characters, with a maximum of 89,539. These are source-sample
    lengths, not tokenizer counts. The full-corpus timing gate remains unmet;
    excluding old years or quarantined articles would change the task's coverage.
    
    ### Measured results on the frozen comparison
    
    The following trials each completed all 221 articles and use the same 304
    observed publisher article/issuer pairs. F1 is partial-reference overlap, not
    adjudicated primary-company accuracy. All paths used groups of up to 253
    companies, a final runoff, 16 concurrent articles and 64 server sequences,
    except Tev, whose trained option limit requires groups of 22 companies.
    These compare complete policies, not model architecture in isolation.
    
    | Model / engine | Precision | F1 | Articles/s | Pilot projection for 30M (days) |
    | --- | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
    | Tev1 experimental / SGLang | BF16 | 0.729 | 0.85 | 410 |
    | Kev / SGLang | BF16 | 0.708 | 1.05 | 331 |
    | OneJev / SGLang | BF16 | 0.700 | 1.05 | 332 |
    | OneJev / SGLang, primed | FP8 | 0.696 | 1.42 | 244 |
    | D3-edge / vLLM | BF16 | 0.577 | 1.78 | 195 |
    | D3-lite / vLLM | BF16 | 0.593 | 1.04 | 334 |
    
    The BF16 Kev/OneJev observations are earlier exploratory trials in
    `.tmp/company-optimization-v2-quality-clean`. The native D3 and FP8 trials in
    `.tmp/company-optimization-v4-quality` also retain frozen source ZIPs. The
    fastest passing configuration is FP8 OneJev: P/R = 0.949/0.549, with an
    exploratory F1 bootstrap interval of 0.644–0.746. Its point estimate passes
    0.68; this interval does not establish F1 above 0.68 with 95% confidence.
    
    Tev's full run is in `.tmp/company-optimization-v5-tev-quality`, with
    P/R = 0.924/0.602 and exploratory F1 interval 0.681–0.776. Its F1 advantage
    over the earlier Kev policy was 0.022; a paired article bootstrap gave
    [-0.009, 0.052], so this comparison does not establish superiority. Its smaller
    trained option limit required 10,943 question prefills, versus approximately
    1,100 for the 253-company BF16 policies. The combined six-method report and
    source-summary hashes are in `.tmp/company-optimization-report-v1`.
    
    D3-edge processed 48,294 input tokens/s at mean GPU utilization of 95.1%, while
    FP8 OneJev averaged 96.2% GPU utilization. These results are consistent with
    prefill throughput in the tens of thousands of tokens/s. D3-edge used 27,172
    input tokens per article; FP8 OneJev counted 30,328 including priming, with
    16.1% of prompt tokens cached. The company choices and repeated reads make
    article throughput much lower than a short, one-question synthetic benchmark.
    
    On a separate 40-article screen, placing the complete catalog first and using
    compact options achieved 81.9% aggregate prompt-token reuse, but only 0.56
    articles/s and exploratory F1 0.129. A high cache-hit rate alone does not
    establish either quality or throughput. The catalog policy was not promoted.
    Those outputs are in `.tmp/company-optimization-v4-catalog-tev`. The earlier
    catalog router fell back on 35 of 40 articles and was also slower.
    
    The independent clean-input profile in `.tmp/company-optimization-v4-input-profile`
    contained 9,910 distinct sanitized year/text pairs, averaging 580 title/body
    tokens (p50/p90/p99 = 504/1,036/1,716). It excludes quarantined source rows,
    instructions, options and serialization overhead. Even hypothetical single
    prefill at 50,000 new tokens/s would take about four days for 30 million such
    articles. This conditional sample is not a full-corpus runtime estimate.
    
    The 10,000-document repeated throughput test and hour-long soak were not run:
    the independent-input coverage preflight failed and all measured policies
    missed the runtime screening target by a large margin. No one-day or
    two-to-three-day completion claim is supported. All owned containers are
    removed after trials; no paid API requests are involved.
    
    ### Evaluating a learned fast stage
    
    A fast classifier followed by selective decision-model inference is a separate
    production candidate. A useful first stage must resolve confident matches as
    well as irrelevant documents, since merely rejecting some background articles
    does not remove enough GPU work at the measured decision-model rate. It should
    read the full sanitized article and preserve the unique-primary-company,
    no-match and unclear outcomes. No such gate is enabled by these experiments.
    
    Benchmark TF–IDF with a linear model as an inexpensive learned baseline, and a
    fine-tuned encoder such as ModernBERT for full-text decisions. Treat spaCy,
    GLiNER and linking as mention/identity components; primary-company salience
    requires its own task labels and validation. Independently maintained aliases
    can aid discovery. Publisher ticker annotations used as reference must stay
    stripped before every learned or matching stage. A no-alias-hit result does not
    by itself establish a negative label.
    
    The [ModernBERT paper](https://aclanthology.org/2025.acl-long.127/)
    supports testing efficient encoders for classification. The
    [entity-salience study](https://aclanthology.org/2024.findings-naacl.28.pdf)
    reports RoBERTa cross-encoder F1 of 0.811 on abstract-aligned NYT labels, but
    0.606 and 0.630 on human-annotated SEL and EntSUM. These different tasks and
    datasets do not establish expected primary-company F1 on this corpus. The
    [credit-news funnel](https://aclanthology.org/2022.naacl-industry.40.pdf)
    discarded 70% using a classifier trained on over 30 million Reuters-coded
    documents; its credit-relevance definition is different from ours.
    
    If a fraction `f` reaches a decision stage sustaining `r` articles/s, that
    stage alone needs `30,000,000 * f / r` seconds. At the observed FP8 rate,
    two days permits at most 0.82% fallback and three days at most 1.23%, ignoring
    the first stage, I/O and retries. Retaining 30% would require about 73 days of
    decision-model work. CPU/GPU overlap can hide some first-stage time, while
    stages sharing the one GPU compete for its capacity.
    
    Before claiming an improvement, split training/calibration/test documents by
    time and duplicate group, audit rejected/no-hit articles, and measure the
    entire cascade on the same primary-company reference. A sufficiently fast
    first stage, a measured fallback fraction, and preserved end-to-end recall
    are all necessary; a paper's F1 or a model's raw confidence is insufficient.

    # Company reference universes
    
    These are frozen research inputs collected on **2026-11-02**:
    
    | File | Rows | Coverage |
    | --- | ---: | --- |
    | [nasdaq_100.csv](nasdaq_100.csv) | 203 | Historical Nasdaq-100 ticker/issuer entries since August 2016; 190 distinct SEC CIKs |
    | [gawronsky_huang_2026.csv](gawronsky_huang_2026.csv) | 100 | Exact tickers and row order of the pricing-perspective study roster |
    
    The historical window starts **2016-08-01**, the first month in our CC-News
    collection, and ends **2026-11-02**. The historical roster combines the
    [current constituent list](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_NASDAQ-100_companies)
    with additions and removals in the
    [historical changes table](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Historical_components_of_the_Nasdaq-100)
    within that window. Historical symbols `FB`, `FISV`, `PCLN`, `CTRP`, `SYMC`,
    `WLTW` and `QVCA` are retained alongside the tables' later symbols. The tables
    sometimes use later tickers retrospectively, so this is a company search
    universe, **not a dated membership panel** or proof that every listed symbol
    traded in the index throughout the window.
    
    The study CSV preserves `~/Git/pricing-perspective/data/universe.csv` exactly
    at the ticker level, including `FISV` and `GOOG`; it is not replaced by today's
    Nasdaq-100. The local file hash, repository commit, source order, Wikipedia
    list revisions and output hashes are recorded in
    [company_references.provenance.json](company_references.provenance.json).
    
    ## Identity and aliases
    
    `company_legal_name` comes from the annual-report cover where recoverable,
    otherwise the SEC submissions name. `legal_name_source` identifies which.
    `cik` is a **zero-padded string**, and `ticker` retains the roster's symbol.
    Use **`(ticker, cik)`**, rather than ticker alone, as the historical row key:
    `FOX` and `FOXA` each occur for both Twenty-First Century Fox and the separate
    Fox Corporation issuer. Share classes and ticker changes can also share a CIK.
    
    `other_names` is a JSON-encoded `List[str]`, for example
    `["Meta Platforms", "Facebook, Inc.", "Facebook"]`. Names come from the
    constituent tables, study names, Wikipedia lead names and SEC former names,
    with shortened legal suffixes and case-insensitive deduplication. The legal
    name remains in its own column. `other_names_source_urls` provides the
    Wikipedia revision and SEC identity record. Obvious product names and generic
    business categories were removed; this is not an exhaustive brand dictionary.
    Aliases are unversioned search candidates: short names and former names need
    context before assigning an article to an issuer.
    
    ## SEC descriptions
    
    `sec_business_description` contains extracted source text, **not a generated
    summary**. The selected report is the latest original annual report found in
    the retrieved SEC submissions history, filed on or before the access date:
    
    - Form **10-K**, **Item 1: Business**.
    - Form **20-F**, **Item 4: Information on the Company**, for foreign issuers.
    - Thomson Reuters' Form **40-F**, **Exhibit 99.1**, the annual report's complete
      Business section (printed pages 2–18).
    
    Reports are retrieved from official `sec.gov/Archives` URLs using Exa's full
    rendered-text fetch. SEC identity and filing metadata come directly from
    `data.sec.gov/submissions`. The rendered text retains tables in Markdown;
    layout, headings and page folios can differ from the original HTML. Body
    boundaries were checked against the rendered report; exceptions use recorded
    line boundaries rather than silently matching the contents page.
    
    Four integrated reports—**ASML, CCEP, INTC and VOD**—incorporate their business
    disclosures from multiple page ranges. For these, `sec_referenced_pages`
    records the ranges in the filing's Item 1/4 cross-reference index. Extraction
    retains the surrounding rendered-page intervals to avoid truncating a
    referenced page when folios are missing. These cells therefore include
    adjacent material, sometimes substantial; they are explicitly marked
    `cross_referenced_pages_with_context`. Their exact retained line windows are
    in the provenance JSON. Other populated rows are marked `extracted_section`.
    
    **HONA and SPCX have no annual report in the retrieved SEC histories.** Their
    SEC description, filing URL and report dates are empty, with status
    `no_annual_report_available`; their company identity, SEC search link and
    Wikipedia description are retained. A registration statement or parent
    company's annual report has not been substituted for an unavailable report.
    All 100 study rows have a populated annual-report description.
    
    Each row provides:
    
    - `sec_form`, `sec_section`, `sec_report_date`, `sec_filing_date` and accession.
    - `sec_filing_url`, the actual text source; `sec_primary_document_url` points
      to the filing cover when the text comes from an exhibit.
    - `sec_search_url`, a CIK/form-filtered EDGAR search, and `sec_submissions_url`.

    # DFA alias and evidence refinement
    
    A subsequent [blinded text adjudication](company-dfa-adjudication.md) reviews all
    60 disagreements and accepts multiple central ticker associations. It finds
    semantic benefits from Tev1 that the publisher-overlap proxy does not capture;
    the original F1 tables below remain unchanged.
    
    The experiment preserves the original dictionary implementation and adds opt-in
    policies, shared evidence features, and grouped training experiments. It uses
    complete sanitized text and article-year membership. No additional neural
    inference or publisher ticker metadata enters the matching features.
    
    ## Reproduce
    
    From the repository root, after installing the CPU extra:
    
    ```sh
    src/python/.venv/bin/python -m fine_news_cli eval cpu-refine \
      --config src/python/apps/fine_news_cli/examples/company-cpu-benchmark.json \
      --output .tmp/company-dfa-refinement-v2
    ```
    
    Use `--phase quality` or `--phase timing` separately. Quality requires a fresh
    output directory. The timing phase reads the fitted bundles and checks their
    checksums before loading trusted local joblib files. It tests one/six workers,
    batches of 128, and three repetitions on the same 8,267 supported clean articles
    as the earlier benchmark. Startup is separate from prediction and durable writes.
    
    ## Diagnostic evidence
    
    On the frozen 221-article reference, the original DFA retrieves 270 of 304
    publisher-observed issuer pairs. Of Tev1's 198 company selections, 171 already
    appear among DFA candidates. Twenty-four selected-company disagreements can be
    addressed by ranking existing candidates; another 27 involve a missing candidate.
    Tev1 abstains on 23 articles for which the original DFA selects a company.
    
    Generic single-word aliases account for substantial extra matches: `price`
    appears on 105 articles lacking that publisher annotation, `new` on 35 and
    `people` on 30. Missing publisher annotations do not prove those companies are
    absent. Historical display names and PERMCO mappings can also be misleading, so
    teacher output is not automatically converted into new aliases or identities.
    
    ## Methods and safeguards
    
    Typography normalization canonicalizes Unicode apostrophes, dashes and
    whitespace. An additional punctuation experiment removes apostrophes and treats
    hyphens as spaces symmetrically in text and aliases. Legal suffix expansion
    removes generic suffixes; the extended variant also strips Company/Co. Derived
    roots must have at least four alphanumeric characters, be non-generic and have
    one owner within the year. Capitalization filtering rejects lower-case evidence
    for single-token aliases. This can miss legitimately lowercase company names;
    it is an accuracy experiment rather than a universal proper-name rule.
    
    Evidence models share one logistic regression across all issuers. Features are
    counts, title/lead placement, case, alias length, legal-name matches, owner
    ambiguity and relative frequency. They contain no issuer/alias identifiers,
    publisher metadata, article IDs or Tev confidence. Numeric scaling, regression
    weights and mention/primary thresholds are fit within grouped folds. Inner
    three-fold predictions select thresholds; outer five-fold predictions supply
    quality scores. Duplicate groups remain together. A second training source uses
    only existing Tev1 decisions; articles without teacher coverage never enter its
    fitting or threshold selection. Tev1 is an imperfect teacher.
    
    All alias policies are generic and label-independent, but choosing among policies
    uses this previously inspected sample. Results are exploratory, not an untouched
    confirmation test. Candidate mention overlap, primary-company proxy overlap and
    binary relevance remain separate tasks. Publisher annotations are incomplete;
    annotation-free backgrounds are provisional negatives. Learned scores are not
    calibrated probabilities. Deployment bundles use all training rows and median
    outer-training thresholds; their quality is reported from held-out models,
    not these deployment bundles.
    
    Evidence offsets explicitly identify transformed text coordinates. Frozen
    article IDs and input hashes remain unchanged. The original DFA baseline and
    previous benchmark artifacts remain available for comparison.
    
    ## Results on the same 221 articles
    
    | Method | Mention-overlap F1 | Primary-proxy F1 | Independent articles/s, six workers |
    | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
    | Original DFA | 0.477 | 0.659 | 103,301 |
    | Extended legal suffixes | 0.482 | 0.693 | 106,526 |
    | Cased single-token evidence | 0.607 | 0.719 | 20,801 |
    | Extended suffixes + cased evidence | 0.623 | 0.752 | 23,372 |
    | Punctuation fold + extended suffixes + case | 0.616 | 0.756 | 14,006 |
    | Extended suffixes + publisher-trained evidence | 0.763 | 0.690 | 51,499 |
    | Extended suffixes + Tev-trained evidence | 0.730 | 0.713 | 50,415 |
    | Saved Tev1 | — | 0.729 | Previously measured 0.85 |
    | Saved GLiNER v2.1 | 0.661 | — | Not remeasured |
    | Saved spaCy | 0.625 | — | Not remeasured |
    
    The extended+cased policy retrieves 287/304 publisher-observed pairs (94.4%)
    versus 270/304 (88.8%) originally. It emits 331 unobserved pairs versus 559
    originally. Primary selections hit the publisher set on 196 articles versus
    172 originally. Punctuation folding adds one primary hit but loses five observed
    mention pairs, so it is not a clear improvement over the simpler combination.
    Typography normalization alone leaves the measured predictions unchanged;
    conservative suffix stripping alone slightly reduces primary-proxy F1.
    
    The original-to-extended+cased primary F1 difference is +0.093; its descriptive
    paired group-bootstrap 95% interval is +0.060 to +0.131. Against Tev1, the
    +0.023 difference has interval −0.016 to +0.062. These intervals do not account
    for choosing among inspected policies. The experiment therefore does not
    establish superiority over Tev1 or academic primary-company accuracy.
    
    The publisher-trained model improves mention overlap substantially by trading
    recall for precision: 212 true observed pairs, 40 unobserved predictions and
    92 missed observed pairs (precision 0.841, recall 0.697). That mention score
    must not be interpreted as primary-company performance. Its deployment timing
    uses a full-fit bundle, while reported quality uses grouped outer predictions.
    
    The timings are medians of three complete prediction-and-durable-write passes
    on 8,267 clean supported articles, with startup excluded. All predictions agree
    between one/six workers. The original DFA's 103,301 articles/s here is a fresh
    measurement, compared with the earlier pilot's roughly 110,000. No preparation,
    quarantine resolution or unsupported historical catalog work is included.
    
    ## Recommended next default for testing
    
    Use **extended suffixes + cased evidence** as the next primary-ranking candidate:
    it provides nearly the best observed primary proxy, better mention recall and
    higher speed than the punctuation variant. Keep the original matcher as the
    comparison and fallback for lowercase-only evidence; such cases should be marked
    uncertain rather than automatically declared irrelevant.
    
    ```python
    from fine_news_cli.eval.cpu.alias_policies import POLICIES, PolicyMatcher
    
    matcher = PolicyMatcher(universe, POLICIES["extended_cased"], backend="rust_dfa")
    predictions = matcher.predict(prepared_articles)
    ```
    
    The combined policy retains 98.7% of all 224 known-positive evaluation articles,
    below the earlier 99% filtering target. It retains 50.9% of the independent clean
    throughput sample. It is therefore not validated as a permanent negative gate,
    and it does not make the GPU cascade fit within one day. Models optimized for
    mention F1 are also not calibrated high-recall rejection gates.
    
    Confirm these improvements on a fresh, manually reviewed sample covering
    lowercase brand names, ambiguous aliases, multi-company stories, no-hit articles
    and historical identity changes before promoting the policy for final labels.
    
    ## Artifacts and checks
    
    The complete comparison is in `.tmp/company-dfa-refinement-v2/summary.json` and
    `quality.json`, with per-article predictions, fold memberships, paired intervals,
    source snapshots, trusted local model bundles and timing reports beside them.
    The initial diagnostic cases remain in
    `.tmp/company-dfa-refinement-v1/diagnostics.json`. No prior prepared input or
    benchmark output was overwritten. All 242 workspace tests pass; Pyrefly reports
    zero errors.
