    # TypeSafe
    
    > How to use TypeSafe's System One API
    
    - [Introduction](https://docs.typesafe.ai/introduction.md): Jev is TypeSafe's flagship model and the first System One model. Send state and typed questions; get structured answers your code can use directly.
    - [Quick start](https://docs.typesafe.ai/introduction/quickstart.md): Get up and running with Jev in 5 minutes.
    - [Jev with coding agents](https://docs.typesafe.ai/introduction/coding-agents.md): What Jev is (and isn't) when you're using a coding agent.
    - [Use cases](https://docs.typesafe.ai/concepts/use-case-map.md): Build business workflows where Jev makes the judgments and your code acts on them.
    - [System One](https://docs.typesafe.ai/concepts/system-one.md): System One models make fast, structured decisions for software. Jev is TypeSafe's flagship model and the first System One model.
    - [State](https://docs.typesafe.ai/concepts/state.md): What state is, how to structure it, and how to give a System One model the context it needs.
    - [Primitives (Questions)](https://docs.typesafe.ai/primitives.md): The System One question types, the typed answers they return, how to choose between them, and how to ask several at once.
    - [Choice](https://docs.typesafe.ai/primitives/choice.md): A Choice is a System One question type for selecting one option from a defined set. The answer includes the selected option, a probability for each option, and confidence.
    - [Score](https://docs.typesafe.ai/primitives/score.md): A Score is a System One question type for rating content against ordered, descriptive levels. The answer includes a score, a probability for each level, and confidence.
    - [Noul](https://docs.typesafe.ai/primitives/noul.md): A Noul question asks Jev to evaluate a yes/no question and return the probability that the answer is yes.
    - [Box](https://docs.typesafe.ai/primitives/box.md): A Box is a System One question type for finding where something is in an image. The answer is the four edges of a box around it, as fractions of the image's width and height.
    - [Advanced: structure](https://docs.typesafe.ai/primitives/advanced.md): Instructions, Choice options, Score levels, and Noul criteria all accept JSON structure.
    - [Images](https://docs.typesafe.ai/images.md): Send images in a System One request: in the state, inside a question's instructions, and as the criteria a question is judged against.
    - [Confidence](https://docs.typesafe.ai/confidence.md): How Jev reports certainty, how it differs from probability, and how to use it to control system behavior.
    - [How to build with TypeSafe](https://docs.typesafe.ai/concepts/how-to-build-with-system-one.md): Design AI-powered software by keeping code in control and giving Jev narrow, structured decisions.
    - [AI primer](https://docs.typesafe.ai/introduction/machine-learning-primer.md): Why TypeSafe trains decision models with calibrated probabilities instead of optimizing for generated text.
    - [Patterns](https://docs.typesafe.ai/patterns.md): Architectural patterns for building systems with TypeSafe.
    - [Speculative fan-out](https://docs.typesafe.ai/patterns/fan-out.md): Send many questions in a single request, including speculative ones, and let your code decide what's relevant.
    - [Screen with a Noul first](https://docs.typesafe.ai/patterns/noul-screen.md): Ask one yes/no question first, and run the expensive step only when the answer is a clear yes.
    - [Companion Noul](https://docs.typesafe.ai/patterns/companion-noul.md): Pair a Choice with a Noul that asks whether any option fits, so your code can tell when none does.
    - [Routing by confidence](https://docs.typesafe.ai/patterns/confidence-routing.md): Use confidence as a second axis. The score tells you what; confidence tells you whether to act on it.
    - [Routing by probability](https://docs.typesafe.ai/patterns/probability-routing.md): Give riskier actions a higher probability threshold. The answer says what to do, and its probability says whether to do it.
    - [Composite scoring](https://docs.typesafe.ai/patterns/composite-scoring.md): Break a complex judgment into atomic scores, combine with weights you control in code.
    - [Cookbooks](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks.md): End-to-end recipes that show TypeSafe in real problems, from a few questions to full pipelines.
    - [Function calling](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/function_calling.md): Turns natural-language trading requests into calls to ordinary typed functions by mapping function names and closed-set arguments to confidence-aware System One questions.
    - [Skill suggestion](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/skill_suggestion.md): Picks at most one skill for an agent turn out of the 194 in Nous Research's Hermes catalog, using two TypeSafe requests to rank and re-check the top candidates.
    - [Guardrails for LLMs](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/llm_guardrails.md): Screens every message into and out of an LLM app with one TypeSafe request, then passes, reviews, blocks, or sends it to support by thresholds you set.
    - [Double-checking citations](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/citation_check.md): Catch wrong or hallucinated citations by checking against the source document. One Choice question decides whether the quote's context supports the claim.
    - [Verifying LLM answers against their source](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/verify_llm_outputs.md): Check whether an LLM's answer follows from the paragraphs it was given, using three Noul questions in one request, and send the doubtful answers to review.
    - [Classifying RAG passages](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/classifying_rag_passages.md): Score each retrieved passage with one TypeSafe request, then decide in code which ones reach the answering model.
    - [Simple memory system](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/basic_memory.md): Let Jev decide which requests and answers are worth remembering, then wrap the Jev call in a small function that adds memories to later calls.
    - [Hierarchical classification](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/hierarchical_classification.md): Uses parallel beam search over Jev's Choice probabilities to classify documents in deep patent, retail product, and biomedical hierarchies.
    - [Classification using confidence](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/classification_using_confidence.md): Classify SEC annual reports into 75 industry groups with one Choice each, then read the answer's own confidence to decide whether to report that group or the broader division above it.
    - [Twitch chat filter](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/twitch_chat_filter.md): Hides insults, spam, and unasked-for gameplay tips in Twitch chat, blurs spoilers, and highlights questions. Each message gets one TypeSafe request with three questions, requests run concurrently, and plain rules in code turn the answers into what the viewer sees.
    - [SDE cascade](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/sde_cascade.md): Extracts structured data with a cheap model, checks each field with Jev, and escalates to a reasoning model only when a check fires.
    - [Date extraction](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/date_extraction_cookbook.md): Extracts absolute and relative dates by asking Jev for the parts named in a document, then resolving and validating them in code with confidence-based review.
    - [Pre-parsed value extraction](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/pre_parsed_value_extraction_cookbook.md): Finds candidate emails, phone numbers, and amounts with a regex, has Jev pick the one you ask for, and normalizes that exact span in code.
    - [Structure recovery](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/autoformat.md): Reconstructs Markdown from plain text that lost its formatting in two requests: one stitches hard-wrapped lines back together, one classifies every block (heading, list, code, callout).
    - [Shopping cart](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/cart_from_primitives.md): Turns a natural-language cafe order into a structured cart: a shrinking-options loop of Choice questions finds every item, then one batched request per item fills its known fields.
    - [Reading a scanned vaccination record](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/reading_scanned_documents.md): Find each vaccine on a scanned travel record with a Noul and a Box, read the year of each dose with a Choice that can answer unreadable, and check each dose still covers the trip in a text-only request.
    - [OCR confidence and bounding boxes](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/ocr_confidence_bounding_boxes.md): Check the values an OCR extractor read from invoice photos: Jev boxes each value, scores it against the page and against a crop of its box, and flags low scores for review.
    - [Feeder-cam visit log](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/feeder_watch.md): Send frames from bird feeder camera footage to Jev with five questions, one of them a Box that finds the bird, then use plain code to turn the answers into a visit log per species.
    - [Re-ranking](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/rerank_typesafe.md): Builds 30-passage BM25 shortlists for 40 CLERC legal queries, then uses one System One question per query-candidate pair to raise top-1 accuracy from 5% to 30% and top-10 accuracy from 38% to 65%.
    - [Infinite cardinality choice](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/infinite_cardinality_choice.md): From someone's own description, find the film they half-remember among 5,000: one Noul per film on a short plot, again on a long plot for the top eighty, and one Choice over the top twenty. The right film comes first 78% of the time, against 33% when embedding search builds the shortlist.
    - [Line-by-line search](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/semantic_find.md): Build semantic search for GitHub's Terms of Service. In one request, score 218 line ids against a plain-language query with a Choice question, and use a Noul question to check whether the document contains an answer.
    - [Knowledge graph entity alignment](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/entity_alignment.md): Route candidate record pairs from two sources to a merge recommendation, manual review, or no link, using one Score question.     - [Intelliprompter](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/intelliprompter.md): Tick off a presenter's notes as they speak: Jev scores the live transcript against each note not yet covered, and a note stays ticked once its score passes the threshold.
    - [Self-consistency: choices](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/consistency_choice_cookbook.md): Ask a model the same moderation question twice: how often does the decision change? A test of reliability that needs no answer key, comparing LLMs and Jev on borderline posts.
    - [Self-consistency: nouls](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/consistency_noul_cookbook.md): Ask a model about the same insurance claim twice: how often does the decision change? A test of reliability that needs no answer key, comparing LLMs and Jev on borderline claims.

    # Speculative fan-out
    
    > Send many questions in a single request, including speculative ones, and let your code decide what's relevant.
    
    Because Jev answers many questions in a single API call, we recommend putting all of the questions your system needs in a single request, and then using code to decide what is relevant after the fact. All questions are evaluated in parallel, so adding more questions usually has little effect on response time.
    
    ## Example: triaging support tickets
    
    Let's imagine you are building a support system that needs to triage support tickets. You need to classify the ticket into a category. If it's a bug report, you also need to determine the severity of the bug.
    
    Instead of asking for the category first and then the severity in a follow-up call, you can ask for both at the same time. If the ticket is not a bug report, you simply ignore the results of the bug severity question.
    
    ```mermaid
    %%{init: {"fontFamily": "Inter, sans-serif", "flowchart": {"rankSpacing": 35, "wrappingWidth": 300, "subGraphTitleMargin": {"top": 8, "bottom": 60}}}}%%
    flowchart LR
        t["support ticket"]
    
        subgraph req["Jev evaluates each question<br/>against the ticket in parallel"]
            direction TB
            c["<b>Choice:</b> category"]
            b["<b>Score:</b> bug severity"]
            r["<b>Noul:</b> reproducible steps?"]
            f["<b>Noul:</b> refund requested?"]
            s["<b>Score:</b> frustration"]
            %% invisible links: without an edge these share a rank and sit side by side
            c ~~~ b ~~~ r ~~~ f ~~~ s
        end
    
        t -- "one request<br/>ticket + 5 questions" --> req
        req -- "one response: 5 answers<br/>decisions + probabilities" --> route{"<b>filter, combine, and route</b><br/>in your code"}
        route blue_bug@-- "bug_report" --> eng["read severity + repro steps<br/>escalate or backlog"]
        route orange_bill@-- "billing" --> bill["refund requested<br/>send to billing"]
        route purple_feat@-- "feature_request" --> feat["log it<br/>sent to devs"]
        %% Branch colours (styles.css): node classes and green_/blue_/purple_/orange_ edge ids.
        class eng neonBlue
        class bill neonOrange
        class feat neonPurple
        %% Branch edges flow (styles.css pauses this under prefers-reduced-motion).
        blue_bug@{ animate: true }
        orange_bill@{ animate: true }
        purple_feat@{ animate: true }
    
    ```
    
    ### Ask every question in one request
    
    Send the ticket with every question your code might need: the category, plus questions that only matter for some categories.
    
    Try it in the Playground →
    
    > [!NOTE]
    > 
    > Speculative questions: `bug_severity` and `has_reproducible_steps` only matter if the ticket is a bug report. `refund_requested` only matters for billing. We include all upfront because additional questions usually have little effect on response time. If the ticket turns out to be a feature request, the bug severity result will be irrelevant, in which case your code path simply ignores it.
    
    ### Route in your code
    
    Your code decides what is relevant based on the classification result:
    
    ```python
    category = response.answers["category"]
    bug_severity = response.answers["bug_severity"]
    bug_repro = response.answers["has_reproducible_steps"]
    refund = response.answers["refund_requested"]
    frustration = response.answers["frustration"]
    
    if category.choice == "bug_report":
        if bug_severity.score > 1.5 and bug_repro.noul > 0.6:
            escalate_to_engineering(ticket_id, severity="high")
        else:
            add_to_bug_backlog(ticket_id)
    
    elif category.choice == "billing":
        if refund.noul > 0.7:
            route_to_billing_with_flag(ticket_id, refund_likely=True)
        else:
            route_to_billing(ticket_id)
    
    elif category.choice == "feature_request":
        log_feature_request(ticket_id)
    
    # Frustration is useful regardless of category
    if frustration.score > 1.5:
        flag_for_priority_response(ticket_id)
    
    ```
    
    Everything needed for the full decision tree comes from one call. Speculative questions are ignored when irrelevant and save a round trip when they are not.

    # Screen with a Noul first
    URL: https://docs.typesafe.ai/patterns/noul-screen.md
    
    > ## Documentation Index
    > 
    > Fetch the complete documentation index at: https://docs.typesafe.ai/llms.txt
    > Use this file to discover all available pages before exploring further.
    
    # Screen with a Noul first
    
    > Ask one yes/no question first, and run the expensive step only when the answer is a clear yes.
    
    Not every input needs your expensive step. Ask one Noul question first, with a small state such as the input on its own, and run the expensive step only when the answer is a clear yes. A clear no gets cheaper handling, and an answer it can't settle gets a rule of its own, so every input ends up handled.
    
    ## When to screen first
    
    Jev answers all the questions in a request in parallel and reads the state once, so you pay for the state once. If the later questions would use the same state, don't split them off: send them all in one request and let your code ignore the answers that don't apply, we call this pattern speculative fan-out. Asking first is worth the extra request when the later step costs something the first question doesn't:
    
    - A bigger state. The next step needs the customer record, the full thread, or an attachment that code has to fetch first.
    - A slower model. The next step is an LLM call.
    - A person. The next step needs someone to look at the item.
    
    ## Example: triaging a shared inbox
    
    Say you're building a shared-inbox tool. Everything arrives in one stream: customers asking about orders, newsletters, payment receipts, thank-you notes, and the occasional "just so you know". Full triage means fetching the sender's account and order history, then asking several questions about the message. A Noul question that sees only the message, as it arrived, can decide which messages get full triage.
    
    ### Ask whether the sender expects a reply
    
    We ask one thing the message alone can settle: is the sender waiting for a reply? Instead of saying "not waiting", the `false` criterion lists the kinds of message with nothing to answer, including a note from a person that needs no reply.
    
    Try it in the Playground →
    
    Tom's message reports a problem but asks for nothing: the desk is already built, and the message doesn't say whether Tom wants to hear back. The answer is neither a clear yes nor a clear no:
    
    ```json
    {
      "model": "jev-1.14.0",
      "answers": {
        "expects_reply": {
          "type": "noul",
          "noul": 0.44
        }
      },
      "usage": {
        "input_tokens": 414,
        "output_tokens": 21
      }
    }
    
    ```
    
    Jev's answers to the same question for five different messages:
    
    | Message | `expects_reply` |
    | --- | --- |
    | "I ordered a standing desk two weeks ago and the tracking hasn't updated... I'm moving on the 30th and need it before then." | 0.98 |
    | "Just so you know, the desk arrived with one of the cross-bar screws missing. I had a spare so it's built now." | 0.44 |
    | "Thanks, the desk arrived yesterday and it's great." | 0.10 |
    | "20% off every desk and chair until Sunday. Unsubscribe | View in browser" | 0.02 |
    | "Your payment of $129.00 was successful... replies to this address are not monitored." | 0.02 |
    
    ### Handle yes, no and unsure
    
    Compare the Noul with two thresholds: above 0.7 counts as yes, and below 0.3 counts as no. Both are good starting points. An answer between them means the message doesn't settle the question, so give it its own outcome instead of rounding it to yes or no.
    
    ```python
    YES_ABOVE = 0.7
    NO_BELOW = 0.3
    
    def handle(message_id, screen_response):
        expects_reply = screen_response.answers["expects_reply"].noul
    
        if expects_reply < NO_BELOW:
            # Newsletters, receipts, notifications. Nothing to answer.
            file_away(message_id)
    
        elif expects_reply > YES_ABOVE:
            # A person is waiting. Fetch what triage needs and run the full request.
            customer = fetch_customer(message_id)
            triage(message_id, customer)
    
        else:
            # Something to look at, but maybe nothing to answer. One glance settles it.
            queue_for_quick_look(message_id)
    
    ```
    
    Of the five messages above, one leads to a triage request: the standing desk that hasn't arrived. The thank-you note and the two automated messages are filed away, and the missing-screw note goes to a person for a quick look.
    
    ### Triage only the messages that need a reply
    
    Fetch the customer record only for messages with a clear yes. The triage request sends the record with the message and asks questions that each check one thing: `repeat_contact` reads `customer.previous_contacts`, and `urgency` counts from `message.received`. A real triage stage would ask more questions than this.
    
    Try it in the Playground →
    
    Jev's response:
    
    ```json
    {
      "model": "jev-1.14.0",
      "answers": {
        "request": {
          "type": "choice",
          "choice": "order_status",
          "confidence": 1.0,
          "probabilities": {
            "order_status": 1.0,
            "return_or_refund": 0.0,
            "product_question": 0.0,
            "complaint": 0.0
          }
        },
        "urgency": {
          "type": "score",
          "score": 1.99,
          "confidence": 0.98,
          "legend": {
            "0": "No deadline is mentioned",
            "1": "The sender wants an answer soon but gives no date",
            "2": "The sender names a date or event within a week"
          },
          "probabilities": {
            "0": 0.0,
            "1": 0.01,
            "2": 0.99
          }
        },
        "repeat_contact": {
          "type": "noul",
          "noul": 0.99
        }
      },
      "usage": {
        "input_tokens": 803,
        "output_tokens": 84
      }
    }
    
    ```
    
    The `repeat_contact` answer comes from the record: with no previous contacts on file, the same message got 0.05.
    
    From here, your routing code acts on the answers. Dana's urgent, repeated order-status request could go to the front of the queue.
    
    ## Other ways to screen
    
    - Check a cheap step first. Run the cheap step, ask a Noul whether its output is right, and send only the outputs that fail that check to the expensive model.
    - Several screens. A content pipeline might check first for "written in English" and then for "about our product". Each check removes inputs before the next, more expensive step.

    # Companion Noul
    URL: https://docs.typesafe.ai/patterns/companion-noul.md
    
    > ## Documentation Index
    > 
    > Fetch the complete documentation index at: https://docs.typesafe.ai/llms.txt
    > Use this file to discover all available pages before exploring further.
    
    # Companion Noul
    
    > Pair a Choice with a Noul that asks whether any option fits, so your code can tell when none does.
    
    A Choice question always picks an option, even when none of them applies. Ask which of three things an input is about, and an input about none of them still gets an answer, possibly with a high probability. The model is answering the question it was asked, so it picks whichever of the three options is closest.
    
    To fix this, add a second question to the same request: a Noul question that asks whether any of the options fits at all. Your code uses the answer to the Choice only when the Noul is a clear yes.
    
    ```mermaid
    %%{init: {"fontFamily": "Inter, sans-serif", "flowchart": {"rankSpacing": 35, "wrappingWidth": 300, "subGraphTitleMargin": {"top": 12, "bottom": 36}}}}%%
    flowchart LR
        message["support message<br/>+ product list"]
    
        subgraph req["Jev evaluates questions<br/>in parallel"]
            direction TB
            product["<b>Choice:</b> which product?"]
            any["<b>Noul:</b> is message about<br/>one of our products?"]
            %% Invisible links stack the questions; they are answered in parallel.
            product ~~~ any
        end
    
        message -- "one request<br/>message + 2 questions" --> req
        req -- "one response<br/>2 answers" --> check{"<b>Noul above 0.7?</b><br/>your code"}
        check green_yes@-- "yes, and the Choice<br/>is above 0.7" --> team["product team queue"]
        check blue_mid@-- "between 0.3 and 0.7,<br/>or the Choice is unsure" --> agent["general support agent"]
        check purple_no@-- "below 0.3: ignore the Choice" --> general["general inbox"]
        %% Branch colours (styles.css): node classes and green_/blue_/purple_ edge ids.
        class team neonGreen
        class agent neonBlue
        class general neonPurple
        %% Branch edges flow (styles.css pauses this under prefers-reduced-motion).
        green_yes@{ animate: true }
        blue_mid@{ animate: true }
        purple_no@{ animate: true }
    
    ```
    
    ## Example: routing messages to product teams
    
    Say you sell three products, and you send each support message to the relevant product team. Messages about anything else, such as a lamp from another shop or a note from a recruiter, go to a general inbox instead.
    
    ### Ask which product, and whether any fits
    
    Both questions refer to the product list by its key in the state, `products`. Jev sees the Choice question's option names, so names such as `desk_pro` say what each product is. The `false` criterion on the Noul question lists what counts as a no: another product, a service, or something you don't sell.
    
    Try it in the Playground →
    
    Jev's response:
    
    ```json
    {
      "model": "jev-1.14.0",
      "answers": {
        "product": {
          "type": "choice",
          "choice": "desk_pro",
          "confidence": 0.94,
          "probabilities": {
            "desk_pro": 0.96,
            "chair_lite": 0.01,
            "monitor_arm": 0.03
          }
        },
        "about_our_product": {
          "type": "noul",
          "noul": 0.02
        }
      },
      "usage": {
        "input_tokens": 549,
        "output_tokens": 63
      }
    }
    
    ```
    
    The Choice picks `desk_pro` at 0.96, with a confidence of 0.94. Nothing in that answer tells you the message isn't about your desk. Of the three options, a desk lamp is closest to a desk. The companion Noul reads 0.02, which says the message isn't about any of your products. Here are Jev's answers for four different messages:
    
    | Message | Choice | Top probability | Noul |
    | --- | --- | --- | --- |
    | "The motor on my standing desk has started making a grinding noise... the 140 cm one" | `desk_pro` | 1.00 | 0.98 |
    | "The chair arrived but the monitor arm didn't. Can you check where the arm is?" | `monitor_arm` | 1.00 | 0.99 |
    | "My desk lamp stopped working after two weeks..." | `desk_pro` | 0.96 | 0.02 |
    | "I'm a recruiter working with several furniture retailers and wondered if your head of operations is open to a quick call" | `desk_pro` | 0.81 | 0.02 |
    
    ### Trust the Choice only when a product fits
    
    Read the Noul first. On a clear no, ignore the Choice and send the message to the general inbox. A clear yes says the message is about one of your products, but not which one, so also check the probability of the product the Choice picked. If both are high, send the message straight to that product team. Otherwise, a general support agent decides, with the Choice's pick passed along as a suggestion.
    
    ```python
    YES = 0.7
    NO = 0.3
    PRODUCT_SURE = 0.7
    
    def route(message_id, response):
        about_ours = response.answers["about_our_product"].noul
        product = response.answers["product"]
        product_probability = product.probabilities[product.choice]
    
        if about_ours < NO:
            # Nothing fits. The Choice's answer is noise; don't read it.
            send_to_general_inbox(message_id)
    
        elif about_ours > YES and product_probability > PRODUCT_SURE:
            # The Choice is answering a question that applies, and it clearly picked one product. Use it.
            send_to_product_team(message_id, product.choice)
    
        else:
            # Unsettled, or about our products but not clearly which one:
            # a person decides, with the Choice's top option as a hint.
            send_to_general_agent(message_id, suggested_product=product.choice)
    
    ```
    
    ## Why an `other` option falls short
    
    Adding `other: 'Something else'` to the Choice question looks like less work, and it used to be the usual advice. But `other` competes with the product options for probability. A message that is partly about a product and partly about something else splits its probability between `other` and that product, and neither number tells your code what to do. With a companion Noul, the Choice question only picks among the products, and a separate question with concrete `true` and `false` criteria decides whether any product fits. In our tests, that usually works better.
    
    > [!NOTE]
    > 
    > Box, which is a question type for finding where something is in an image, has the same problem: it always returns a location in an image. Pair it with a Noul question such as "Is there a coffee mug in `photo`?" so your code knows whether the box marks a mug at all.
    
    ## Other ways to use a companion Noul
    
    - One Noul question per option. When a message can be about more than one product, a Choice has to split its probability between them. Ask one Noul question per product instead, and read each one on its own. Then the case where nothing fits needs no extra question, because every Noul comes back low.
    - As a screen. Ask a Noul question first, and run the expensive step, which may require a Choice or Score, only when the answer is a clear yes. See screen with a Noul first.
    - Candidates from code. The options don't have to be a fixed list. Your code can pull possible values out of the text and use them as the options in the Choice question, and the companion Noul question asks whether the right value is among them. The value extraction cookbook builds candidates in code this way, but it uses a `none` option instead of a companion Noul.

    URL: https://docs.typesafe.ai/patterns/confidence-routing.md

    > Fetch the complete documentation index at: https://docs.typesafe.ai/llms.txt

    # Routing by confidence
    
    > Use confidence as a second axis. The score tells you what; confidence tells you whether to act on it.
    
    A Score answer gives you a position on the scale, `score`, and a confidence from 0 to 1 that says how certain the answer is. Check the confidence first: send an answer whose probability is spread across the scale to a person, and route the rest on the score.
    
    ## Example: triaging bug reports
    
    Let's imagine you are building a bug tracker that triages incoming reports. A cosmetic issue can wait in the backlog, a broken feature goes into the current sprint, and anything that stops users completing a core task goes straight to the on-call engineer. A report that doesn't make its severity clear should go to a person before anyone messages the engineer.
    
    ```mermaid
    %%{init: {"fontFamily": "Inter, sans-serif", "flowchart": {"rankSpacing": 35, "wrappingWidth": 300, "subGraphTitleMargin": {"top": 12, "bottom": 36}}}}%%
    flowchart LR
        report["bug report"]
    
        subgraph req["Jev evaluates<br/>the question"]
            severity["<b>Score:</b> severity"]
        end
    
        report -- "one request<br/>report + severity<br/>question" --> req
        req -- "one response<br/>severity score +<br/>confidence" --> check{"<b>confidence<br/>at least 0.5?</b><br/>your code"}
        check blue_triage@-- "no" --> triage["a person triages<br/>the report"]
        check -- "yes" --> level{"<b>how severe?</b><br/>severity.score"}
        level green_backlog@-- "below 1.5" --> backlog["add to the backlog"]
        level green_sprint@-- "1.5 to<br/>under 2.5" --> sprint["add to this sprint"]
        level green_page@-- "2.5 or more" --> page["message the on-call<br/>engineer"]
        %% Branch colours (styles.css): node classes and green_/blue_/purple_/orange_ edge ids.
        class backlog,sprint,page neonGreen
        class triage neonBlue
        %% Branch edges flow (styles.css pauses this under prefers-reduced-motion).
        blue_triage@{ animate: true }
        green_backlog@{ animate: true }
        green_sprint@{ animate: true }
        green_page@{ animate: true }
    
    ```
    
    ### Score how severe the report is
    
    Send the report with one Score question. Its five levels run from a cosmetic issue to a critical one.
    
    Try it in the Playground →
    
    Jev's answer doesn't say whether the update lost the notes or the user deleted them:
    
    ```json
    {
      "model": "jev-1.14.0",
      "answers": {
        "severity": {
          "type": "score",
          "score": 3.19,
          "confidence": 0.34,
          "legend": {
            "0": "Cosmetic: wording, layout, or styling only",
            "1": "Minor: something misbehaves, but users can still do what they wanted",
            "2": "Major with a workaround: a feature is broken, but there is another way to get the job done",
            "3": "Major with no workaround: users cannot complete a core task",
            "4": "Critical: data loss, a security hole, or the product is down for everyone"
          },
          "probabilities": {
            "0": 0.01,
            "1": 0.14,
            "2": 0.07,
            "3": 0.19,
            "4": 0.59
          }
        }
      },
      "usage": {
        "input_tokens": 435,
        "output_tokens": 17
      }
    }
    
    ```
    
    A score of 3.19 on its own would message the on-call engineer. The probabilities tell a different story: most of the probability is on "critical", in case the update lost the notes, but 0.14 is on "minor", in case the user deleted them. The probability spread brings the confidence down to 0.34.
    
    ### Send unsettled scores to a person, route the rest
    
    Check confidence before reading the score, and route on the score only when the check passes.
    
    ```python
    severity = response.answers["severity"]
    
    if severity.confidence < 0.5:
        # The probability is spread across the scale. A person reads the report first.
        send_to_triage(report_id)
    
    elif severity.score < 1.5:
        add_to_backlog(report_id)
    
    elif severity.score < 2.5:
        add_to_sprint(report_id)
    
    else:
        message_on_call(report_id)
    
    ```
    
    The "Notes gone?" report goes to triage, where a person can ask the reporter whether the notes were deleted. Reports with a clear severity route straight through, as these recorded `jev-1.14.0` answers show:
    
    | Report | `score` | `confidence` | Outcome |
    | --- | --- | --- | --- |
    | Typo on the settings page | 0.0 | 1.0 | backlog |
    | PDF export fails over 50 pages; splitting the document works | 2.0 | 1.0 | this sprint |
    | Checkout returns a 500 error for every customer | 3.36 | 0.7 | message on-call |
    | Notes gone after the update, or maybe deleted | 3.19 | 0.34 | triage |
    
    ## When two levels split the answer
    
    For a Score, if two levels have the highest and equal probabilities, the score is much higher if those two levels are next to each other than if they are not. The further they are apart, the lower the score.
    A Score's confidence counts probability on a neighboring level as only a small spread. That can be an issue if you set a threshold between those two levels: an answer split between them can pass a confidence check and land on the wrong side of the threshold. The Score explorer shows how the distance between levels changes confidence.
    
    When a decision depends on which side of a level boundary the answer falls, add up the probabilities of the levels on the side that matters:
    
    ```python
    blocked = severity.probabilities[3] + severity.probabilities[4]
    
    if blocked >= 0.3:
        # A real chance users are blocked. Message someone rather than wait for the sprint.
        message_on_call(report_id)
    
    ```
    
    Routing by probability builds a whole router on probabilities like this, with a separate threshold for each action.

    URL: https://docs.typesafe.ai/patterns/probability-routing.md

    # Routing by probability
    
    > Give riskier actions a higher probability threshold. The answer says what to do, and its probability says whether to do it.
    
    Every Jev answer comes with probabilities. For each action your code can take, decide how high the probability must be before you take it. Riskier actions get higher thresholds, and an answer below the threshold gets its own outcome, such as asking the user to clarify, instead of counting as a yes. The actions can be anything your code can call: a function in your app, an LLM, or a person.
    
    ## Example: acting on voice banking commands
    
    Say you're building a voice banking interface where users manage their account by speaking. Before acting on a command, you want to be reasonably sure what the user asked for, and very sure for the riskier actions.
    
    ```mermaid
    %%{init: {"fontFamily": "Inter, sans-serif", "flowchart": {"rankSpacing": 35, "wrappingWidth": 300, "subGraphTitleMargin": {"top": 12, "bottom": 36}}}}%%
    flowchart LR
        command["voice banking command"]
    
        subgraph req["Jev evaluates<br/>the question"]
            intent["<b>Choice:</b> intent"]
        end
    
        command -- "one request<br/>command + intent<br/>question" --> req
        req -- "one response<br/>intent answer +<br/>probabilities" --> check{"<b>probability high enough?</b><br/>your code"}
        check red_low@-- "below 0.7<br/>or other intent" --> human["send to a support agent"]
        check orange_balance@-- "check_balance<br/>at least 0.7" --> balance["show the balance"]
        check yellow_confirm@-- "approve_transfer<br/>0.7 to 0.9" --> confirm["clarify the request"]
        check green_approve@-- "approve_transfer<br/>above 0.9" --> approve["show transfer details<br/>and require confirmation"]
        %% Branch colours (styles.css): a confidence gradient, red -> orange -> yellow -> green.
        class human neonRed
        class balance neonOrange
        class confirm neonYellow
        class approve neonGreen
        %% Branch edges flow (styles.css pauses this under prefers-reduced-motion).
        red_low@{ animate: true }
        orange_balance@{ animate: true }
        yellow_confirm@{ animate: true }
        green_approve@{ animate: true }
    
    ```
    
    ### Ask what the user wants to do
    
    Send the user's command with one Choice question. The `other` option catches commands this system doesn't handle. It keeps the example short, but a companion Noul usually works better as a catch-all.
    
    Try it in the Playground →
    
    Jev's response:
    
    ```json
    {
      "model": "jev-1.14.0",
      "answers": {
        "intent": {
          "type": "choice",
          "choice": "check_balance",
          "confidence": 1.0,
          "probabilities": {
            "check_balance": 1.0,
            "approve_transfer": 0.0,
            "other": 0.0
          }
        }
      },
      "usage": {
        "input_tokens": 343,
        "output_tokens": 41
      }
    }
    
    ```
    
    ### Set a threshold for each action
    
    Compare the probability of the chosen option, `probabilities[choice]`, against the threshold. That number is how likely it is that this option is what the user asked for.
    
    ```python
    action = response.answers["intent"]
    likelihood = action.probabilities[action.choice]
    
    # Below 0.7 on any action, the command didn't settle the intent. Route to a human.
    if likelihood < 0.7:
        route_to_support_agent(account_id)
    
    elif action.choice == "check_balance":
        # Low stakes. 0.7 is sufficient.
        show_balance(account_id)
    
    elif action.choice == "approve_transfer":
        if likelihood > 0.9:
            # Identifying the intent starts confirmation; it does not approve a transfer.
            show_transfer_for_confirmation(account_id)
        else:
            # Clarify what the user wants before opening the transfer workflow.
            ask_user_to_clarify("Would you like to review the pending transfer?")
    
    else:
        route_to_support_agent(account_id)
    
    ```
    
    The thresholds only choose which workflow runs; none of them moves money. A clear transfer request opens a confirmation screen with the amount and recipient, and the transfer runs only after the user confirms them. A less certain one asks the user what they meant first.
    
    The confirmation step matters because a hesitant command can still have a clear intent. With `jev-1.14.0`, "Um, the transfer thing... yeah, go ahead I guess." got 0.99 for `approve_transfer`. That answer says which action the user wants, but not that the user has checked the transfer details.
    
    > [!NOTE]
    > 
    > Why not `confidence`? For a Choice question with a fixed number of options, `confidence` is calculated from the top probability, so a threshold on it adds nothing, and the probability is easier to read as risk. If it matters how the other options compare, check their probabilities too. Confidence is more useful for a Score, as in Routing by confidence. Also take a look at When to act on confidence.

    # Composite scoring
    URL: https://docs.typesafe.ai/patterns/composite-scoring.md

    # Composite scoring
    
    > Break a complex judgment into atomic scores, combine with weights you control in code.
    
    Oftentimes we want to rank a set of items based on several criteria at once. Composite scoring is an easy way to think about this: break the judgment into independent dimensions, score each one separately, and combine them with weights you control in code.
    
    ## Example: screening resumes
    
    Let's imagine you are processing resumes for engineering roles. You want to rank the candidates based on several criteria, and ultimately select the top X candidates for further review.
    
    ```mermaid
    %%{init: {"fontFamily": "Inter, sans-serif", "flowchart": {"rankSpacing": 35, "wrappingWidth": 300, "subGraphTitleMargin": {"top": 12, "bottom": 36}}}}%%
    flowchart LR
        resume["candidate resume"]
    
        subgraph req["Jev evaluates questions<br/>in parallel"]
            direction TB
            py["<b>Score:</b> Python depth"]
            lead["<b>Score:</b> team leadership"]
            arch["<b>Score:</b> system design"]
            general["<b>Score:</b> generalist"]
            %% Invisible links stack the questions; they are answered in parallel.
            py ~~~ lead ~~~ arch ~~~ general
        end
    
        resume -- "one request<br/>resume + 4 questions" --> req
        req -- "one response<br/>4 score answers" --> normalize["<b>normalize scores to 0–1</b><br/>divide each by 4 in your code"]
        normalize ic_weights@--> ic["<b>senior IC weights</b><br/>40% Python + 10% leadership<br/>40% design + 10% generalist"]
        normalize em_weights@--> em["<b>engineering manager weights</b><br/>15% Python + 40% leadership<br/>20% design + 25% generalist"]
        ic --> rank["rank candidates<br/>for each role"]
        em --> rank
        %% The two weighting paths flow (styles.css pauses this under prefers-reduced-motion).
        ic_weights@{ animate: true }
        em_weights@{ animate: true }
    
    ```
    
    ### Score each dimension separately
    
    Send the resume with one Score question per dimension. Each question asks for a single judgment, so each score can be weighted on its own later.
    
    Try it in the Playground →
    
    ### Combine the scores with weights
    
    Each dimension is normalized to 0–1 and weighted. The weights give you an easy way to adjust the relative importance of each dimension, without losing any of the nuance of the individual scores.
    
    ```python
    py      = response.answers["python_depth"].score / 4
    lead    = response.answers["team_leadership"].score / 4
    arch    = response.answers["system_design"].score / 4
    general = response.answers["generalist"].score / 4
    
    # Senior IC
    ic_score = (0.40 * py) + (0.10 * lead) + (0.40 * arch) + (0.10 * general)
    
    # Engineering Manager
    em_score = (0.15 * py) + (0.40 * lead) + (0.20 * arch) + (0.25 * general)
    
    ```
    
    This gives you the ability to rank the candidates based on the composite score. But more importantly, it gives you visibility into how exactly the final score is being calculated. If the highest ranking candidates are not matching your expectations, you can adjust the weights to find the right balance.

There’s also a simpler fit for structured prompts: Pydantic’s public `DecisionRequest`/`.decide()` API preserves candidate records and rubric objects directly, while the higher-level `Agent` annotations mainly expose string descriptions.

## Assistant

Those pages clarify the architecture considerably. **I recommend structured speculative fan-out through Pydantic’s `DecisionRequest` API, initially served by native Kev.** Retrieve candidate companies first, then submit the article once with every candidate’s questions together.

I reviewed the supplied documentation, model/server implementations, and released Pydantic adapters and tests across four research workstreams, including 45 search results.

**The important distinction is between one request and shared computation.** A typed output containing many companies guarantees neither a single article encoding nor constant inference cost. That depends on the model and its serving implementation.

**How the TypeSafe patterns apply**

The [advanced primitives](https://docs.typesafe.ai/primitives/advanced) support structured objects inside instructions and criteria. We should therefore supply actual company records and explicit rubrics, rather than burying these in long prose prompts.

The [patterns](https://docs.typesafe.ai/patterns) suggest this design:

| Pattern | Application to CCFinance |
|---|---|
| Speculative fan-out | Ask every candidate’s identity and coverage questions together; interpret answers afterward in Python. |
| Companion Noul | Check that a reference actually denotes the candidate issuer before accepting its coverage classification. |
| Probability routing | Apply documented acceptance, rejection and review thresholds to the returned distributions. |
| Confidence routing | Identify unsettled judgments, while keeping provider-specific confidence semantics explicit. |
| Screen first | Reserve for a genuinely more expensive subsequent operation, such as fetching additional evidence. |
| Composite scoring | Add only if researchers need several distinct dimensions. Preserve those dimensions and publish the weighting rule. |

In particular, the screening documentation recommends keeping questions together when they use the same evidence. We should avoid an identity request followed by a coverage request for each company. [Screening guidance](https://docs.typesafe.ai/patterns/noul-screen).

**I would use two narrow judgments per candidate.** This revises my preliminary suggestion of folding everything into one categorical judgment:

1. **Identity — Noul:** Does an organization reference in this article denote this particular issuer?
2. **Coverage — Choice:** Assuming the reference denotes that issuer, is its editorial role incidental, substantive secondary coverage, or central coverage?

Both go into the same request. The coverage question states its premise explicitly; it cannot consume the identity question’s answer during inference.

This follows the companion-Noul pattern and avoids forcing an irrelevant article into a substantive category. Several companies can independently be central. We never ask one Choice question to select a single company from the candidate list. [Companion Noul](https://docs.typesafe.ai/patterns/companion-noul).

**The simplest suitable Pydantic interface**

Pydantic AI’s public, lower-level `.decide()` interface is a better fit here than dynamically generating an `Agent` output model. Its native question types preserve structured candidate records and criteria directly. The high-level annotations currently expose mainly string descriptions. I verified this against release **v2.68.0**. [Decision API](https://pydantic.dev/docs/ai/api/models/decision/), [released System One transport](https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic-ai/blob/v2.68.0/pydantic_ai_slim/pydantic_ai/models/system_one.py).

The essential request construction would be:

```python
from pydantic_ai.models.decision import (
    ChoiceQuestion,
    DecisionRequest,
    NoulCriteria,
    NoulQuestion,
)
from pydantic_ai.models.system_one import SystemOneModel
from pydantic_ai.providers.system_one import SystemOneProvider

model = SystemOneModel(
    "kev-latest",
    provider=SystemOneProvider(base_url="http://127.0.0.1:8008"),
)

coverage_criteria = {
    "incidental": {
        "definition": "The issuer is mentioned without developed reporting about it.",
        "examples": ["A passing comparison", "A disclosure or boilerplate mention"],
    },
    "substantive": {
        "definition": "The article develops meaningful issuer-specific information.",
        "excludes": ["The issuer is a principal or jointly principal subject"],
    },
    "central": {
        "definition": "The issuer is a principal or jointly principal subject.",
        "includes": ["An acquisition article centrally covering both counterparties"],
    },
}

questions: dict[str, NoulQuestion | ChoiceQuestion] = {}

for candidate in candidates:
    key = candidate["issuer_id"]

    questions[f"{key}.identity"] = NoulQuestion(
        instructions={
            "question": "Does an organization reference in the article denote this issuer?",
            "candidate": candidate,
            "identity_policy": identity_policy,
        },
        criteria=NoulCriteria(
            true={"definition": "A reference denotes the candidate issuer itself."},
            false={
                "definition": "The issuer is absent or the apparent match denotes something else."
            },
        ),
    )
    questions[f"{key}.coverage"] = ChoiceQuestion(
        instructions={
            "question": (
                "Assuming the references denote this issuer, "
                "what editorial role does it have?"
            ),
            "candidate": candidate,
        },
        criteria=coverage_criteria,
    )

response = await model.decide(
    DecisionRequest(state=article, questions=questions),
    model_settings={"timeout": 60},
)
```

This is **one request containing `2 × candidate_count` questions**. The loop constructs questions; it does not perform inference.

The server checkpoint must be pinned independently: `kev-latest` is an accepted API alias, not a reproducibility guarantee.

The article state should contain its title, body and publication date. Each candidate should contain a permanent issuer ID, article-date name, relevant aliases and concise distinguishing facts. Eligibility dates, identifier mappings and parent/subsidiary policy belong in deterministic code. Opaque question keys alone do not communicate company identity to the model.

**What the “primary subject” score would mean**

For each candidate, retain:

- `identity_probability`: the Noul answer.
- `coverage_probabilities`: the complete incidental/substantive/central distribution.
- `primary_subject_score`: the central-category probability, interpreted only when issuer identity is accepted.
- An explicit accepted, rejected, unresolved or failed status.

That primary score describes the model’s support for the authored central-subject category. It is **not yet an empirically calibrated probability of annotation correctness**.

Do not multiply independently inferred identity and coverage probabilities and present the result as calibrated joint correctness. Preserve both judgments, gate coverage in Python and validate the thresholds on human-reviewed examples.

If researchers later want a graded *intensity* measure, an ordinal Score can provide that separately. An expected rubric position divided by its maximum is an intensity index, not a probability. Likewise, composite scoring should expose its component judgments and weights. [Score semantics](https://docs.typesafe.ai/primitives/score), [composite scoring](https://docs.typesafe.ai/patterns/composite-scoring).

**Which model/runtime actually shares the article computation**

| Model/runtime | Actual execution | Recommendation |
|---|---|---|
| **Native Kev-0.8B** | Computes the article prefix once, then evaluates independent question branches from cached state. | First baseline and serving smoke test. |
| **Native Kev-4B** | Same shared-prefix approach, with bounded branch batches. | Quality challenger, subject to measured VRAM acceptance. |
| **Kev through current SGLang** | Repeats the full article prefill for each question; explicitly disables Radix caching, chunked prefill and CUDA graphs. | Does not provide the sharing we want. |
| **Native GLiDE-0.8B** | Recomputes the full state per question, using GPU micro-batches. | Worth comparing: its small size could still produce good throughput. |
| **Clef-Flash 9B** | Genuine joint-schema execution with one backbone prefill. | Official BF16 weights exceed 16 GiB before runtime overhead. |

These are implementation findings, rather than assumptions from the API shape. [Native Kev implementation](https://github.com/jaredpalmer/kev/blob/2074cc44256200bb37540103fa4572901faa10f3/kev/model.py), [SGLang Kev documentation](https://docs.sglang.io/cookbook/autoregressive/Kev/kev), [GLiDE model card](https://huggingface.co/fastino/GLiDE-0.8B), [Clef-Flash weight index](https://huggingface.co/Cloudflare/clef-flash/blob/main/model.safetensors.index.json).

GLiDE’s full-attention layers are bidirectional and its implementation disables caching. Applying ordinary causal prefix reuse would change its computation. Its dedicated decision head also means that serving it as an ordinary chat checkpoint is insufficient.

**The 16 GiB configuration**

I verified your GPU as an **RTX 5060 Ti with 16,311 MiB total VRAM**. I have not launched these native servers or measured their inference peaks during this review.

I would start with **Kev-0.8B in BF16**, then admit Kev-4B only after a measured memory test. BF16 avoids introducing low-bit probability drift before we have a reliable baseline. The verified native Kev implementation supports BF16; I did not establish a production-ready FP8 path.

For the initial native Kev pilot:

```bash
KEV_BACKEND=torch
KEV_DTYPE=bf16
KEV_PREFIX_CACHE=1
KEV_PREFIX_MAX_TOKENS=8192
KEV_CUDA_GRAPHS=0
KEV_TRUNCATE_STATES=0
```

Here, `KEV_PREFIX_CACHE=1` means **one cached article**, and `KEV_PREFIX_MAX_TOKENS` limits cached state tokens. Neither sets the request admission limit. We must separately require each article-plus-question branch, including framing, to fit the initial 8,192-token budget.

Use one article in flight initially. Reject or defer overlong articles explicitly. Native fused kernels can be evaluated afterward, using the implementation’s pinned `flash-linear-attention` version and checking output parity. [Native server configuration](https://github.com/jaredpalmer/kev/blob/2074cc44256200bb37540103fa4572901faa10f3/kev/serve.py).

Kev-4B has approximately 8 GB of BF16 weights; its card reports approximately 14.3 GB resident on other hardware. That makes it plausible here, but does not establish our worst-case peak with long articles and question batches. [Kev-4B card](https://huggingface.co/jaredpalmer/kev-4b).

**Several compatibility traps need explicit checks**

- **Structured prompts render differently.** Native Kev recursively renders structured fields into labelled text. GLiDE handles structured Choice descriptions through JSON serialization, but some structured Noul/Score descriptions become Python representations. Preserve exact requests, ordering and rendered prompts. [Kev parser](https://github.com/jaredpalmer/kev/blob/2074cc44256200bb37540103fa4572901faa10f3/kev/api.py), [GLiDE renderer](https://huggingface.co/fastino/GLiDE-0.8B/blob/main/glide/prompt.py).
- **GLiDE’s Score semantics differ.** Its `score` is the most likely level, with the mean in `expected_level`; Pydantic’s System One adapter expects the mean in `score`. Noul plus Choice avoids that particular mismatch. [Pydantic validation](https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic-ai/blob/v2.68.0/pydantic_ai_slim/pydantic_ai/models/decision.py#L350).
- **Confidence is provider-specific.** GLiDE uses the gap between its two largest Choice probabilities; Kev uses a different normalization. Use full distributions and explicit probability policies instead of transferring confidence cutoffs.
- **API names do not establish protocol equivalence.** OpenAI Decisions and System One are distinct transports. Pydantic provides separate adapters; `pydantic_graph.decision` is ordinary workflow branching. [OpenAI Decisions](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/decisions), [Pydantic System One](https://pydantic.dev/docs/ai/models/system-one/).
- **Licences differ.** Kev is Apache-2.0; GLiDE uses the Fastino Community licence with commercial restrictions. [GLiDE licence](https://huggingface.co/fastino/GLiDE-0.8B/blob/main/LICENSE).

**The pilot should resolve accuracy and actual execution efficiency**

Use a small, deliberately varied human-reviewed set: namesakes, historical names, subsidiaries, advertisements, incidental comparisons, substantive secondary coverage, joint subjects and negative articles. Keep the separate missed-company retrieval audit you selected.

Compare native Kev-0.8B, native Kev-4B if it fits, and native GLiDE-0.8B. Measure:

- Identity precision/recall and coverage classification separately.
- Probability calibration and threshold behaviour.
- Candidate-count scaling at 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 and 32 candidates.
- Short and long articles, cold and warm cache behaviour.
- Articles/second, latency, peak VRAM, failures and actual article-prefill reuse.
- Singleton versus fan-out answer differences.

    ---
    
    # Architecture layout
    
    ## Workflow
    
    1. Establish the requested scope and outcome: evaluate the current layout,
       design a layout, or implement an authorized change. Read nearby README and
       ARCHITECTURE files. Identify existing owners and consumers before proposing
       a new abstraction; reuse an existing module or library when it satisfies the
       contract. File size alone is not a reason to split or create a package.
    2. Examine the relevant boundaries using evidence:
       - **Ownership and cohesion:** Can a contributor find the owner, and do things
         that change together live together? Keep each unit's responsibility clear.
       - **Dependencies and encapsulation:** Trace relevant imports and public
         interfaces. Keep intended dependency direction clear and cycles forbidden;
         avoid reaching into another module's internals without a reason.
       - **Coupling:** Identify changes that force unrelated owners to change.
         Share a contract only when consumers actually need the same behavior; a
         little local duplication may be preferable to coupling distinct contracts.
       - **Discoverability:** Make CLI commands, transformations, schemas, tests,
         fixtures and documents easy to find from their owning area.
    3. Choose the smallest useful boundary: a function, module, package or separate
       workspace project. A package or project should reflect an actual dependency,
       distribution, build or ownership need. Organize by layer, capability or a
       combination according to the work; do not impose a universal directory tree.
    4. For pipeline work, preserve the established `raw`, `processed` and `research`
       stage ownership. Organize capabilities within those layers as they arise.
       Distinguish Python imports from DVC artifact dependencies: the latter connect
       producers and consumers without requiring cross-layer Python imports. Apply
       Tach rules to durable module boundaries and DVC to artifact dependencies.
    5. For a move or split, trace the affected consumers before changing paths:
       imports and public APIs, CLI registration, package configuration, tests and
       fixtures, Tach, DVC and Semflow dependencies, and documentation links as
       applicable. Preserve behavior and scientific contracts unless the user asks
       for a change; report any intended behavior change separately. Do not treat
       missing static references as proof that dynamic or external consumers do not

    6. Use the repository's existing gates rather than adding tests that merely
       assert a directory tree or private call sequence. For tests and fixtures,

       working and `just check` before handoff; report checks that could not run.

    ---
    name: python-testing
    description: Use when writing, changing, reviewing or organizing Python tests, pytest fixtures or Hypothesis strategies in CCFinance.
    ---
    
    # Python testing
    
    ## Workflow
    
    1. Inspect the code contract, nearby tests, `conftest.py`, shared fixtures and
       strategies, the package's test README, and pytest configuration. Reuse an
       existing test or generator when it covers the behavior; extend it only for a
       distinct, meaningful risk. Do not add tests for trivial or reversible changes
       just to increase counts, or tests that restate implementation details.
    2. Prefer Hypothesis for input variation when a general property is meaningful.
       Prefer a small explicit example for a single known boundary, regression or
       command smoke check. Decide the expected outcome independently of the code
       under test. Use tiny representative data, bounded generators and the smallest
       appropriate test boundary. Assert public behavior, including error contracts.
    3. Place a test beside its source owner under the mirrored `tests/` layout. Reuse
       existing factories and strategies first. Keep a helper local until several
       tests need it; put cross-module strategies in `tests/_strategies.py` and
       shared pytest fixtures in the nearest common `conftest.py`. Place a fixture
       at broader scope only when its state is safe to share. Measure costly setup
       before broadening scope; avoid creating generic fixture frameworks.
    4. Arrange inputs and prerequisites, act on the behavior, and assert observable
       results (AAA). Cleanup belongs in a fixture finalizer or context manager.
       Label each phase with an `# Arrange`, `# Act` or `# Assert` comment, as in
       the example below. Favor DAMP: clear names and visible expected values can
       justify a little repetition.
    5. Give each new or modified test exactly one scope marker from the table below;
       add `slow` or `external` only when applicable. Mark a class or module only
       when every inherited test has the same scope. Never stack or override scope
       markers, including inherited marks. Before using markers, register the six
       names in the owning pytest configuration; unknown names fail under
       `--strict-markers`. This skill defines the policy; it does not mean the
       current unmarked suite already enforces it. Migrate existing tests deliberately
       if adding a collection-time enforcement hook.
    6. During development, run the smallest relevant test or selection and check
       its output. Before handoff run the repository's required full checks, including
       the complete non-Testmon suite. Run any affected slow or external tests when
       their prerequisites and authorization are available; report what was not run
       and why. A targeted pass is not evidence that the full suite passed.
    
    ## Markers
    
    Use only these six custom markers. Built-in pytest mechanisms such as
    `parametrize`, `skipif` and `xfail` remain available for their intended purposes.
    Scope describes the boundary the assertions exercise, not the number of files,
    the use of Hypothesis, or the choice of a reference oracle.
    
    | Marker | Rule |
    | --- | --- |
    | `unit` | Exactly one scope: an isolated operation or small self-contained behavior. |
    | `component` | Exactly one scope: one coherent subsystem or component through its public behavior. |
    | `integration` | Exactly one scope: interactions across components or a real dependency boundary. |
    | `e2e` | Exactly one scope: a complete user-visible workflow through the public CLI or API. A CLI help check alone is not end-to-end. |
    | `slow` | Optional execution label: the complete test, including setup, teardown and generated examples, consistently exceeds two seconds on the normal local environment. Confirm with repeated pytest duration reports; a single noisy measurement is not enough. |
    | `external` | Optional execution label: the test accesses a live network service or external account. Use even if it is usually fast; require explicit opt-in and appropriate credentials. A local temporary file, subprocess or fake alone does not qualify. |
    
    `slow` and `external` are independent and may accompany any one scope. Do not
    invent custom markers for regression, reference, property, smoke, tools or
    implementation techniques; communicate those in descriptive test names and
    assertions. Run fast local iteration with `-m "not slow and not external"`
    after the markers are registered. Full checks must not silently omit slow tests;
    external tests need a separate explicit lane and must not mutate live services
    without authorization.
    
    ## Hypothesis examples and fixtures
    
    Hypothesis strategies generate values; pytest fixtures manage resources. If
    Hypothesis is absent, add it to the locked workspace development dependencies
    when introducing the first test that uses it. Search
    for reusable strategies or an appropriate first-party Hypothesis extra before
    adding one. Compose built-in strategies, use `@composite` for dependent values,
    and generate valid inputs directly rather than filtering most examples. Keep
    sizes bounded and counterexamples understandable. Preserve an important known
    failure using `@example` or an explicit regression; do not duplicate a property
    with a long list of examples that establish the same behavior.
    
    A function-scoped pytest fixture runs once per test function, not once per
    `@given` example. For per-example mutable resources, create and clean them inside
    the test, for example with `TemporaryDirectory()`. Reuse immutable shared data
    only when safe. Do not suppress health checks or disable deadlines globally to
    make a test pass; investigate the cause and document a narrowly justified
    exception. Choose explicit settings or a shared profile only when warranted by
    measured cost. Preserve failing examples and replay information as appropriate.
    
    This self-contained example illustrates a small property, AAA and the scope
    marker; it uses the standard-library URL parser rather than a CCFinance stage:
    
    ```python
    from string import ascii_lowercase, digits
    from urllib.parse import urlsplit
    
    import pytest
    from hypothesis import example, given, strategies as st
    
    
    @pytest.mark.unit
    @example(host="news")
    @given(host=st.text(alphabet=ascii_lowercase + digits, min_size=1, max_size=20))
    def test_url_hostname_normalizes_ascii_case(host: str) -> None:
        # Arrange: build a URL with an uppercase hostname.
        url = f"https://{host.upper()}.example/article"
    
        # Act: extract the hostname.
        hostname = urlsplit(url).hostname
    
        # Assert: the hostname is lowercase.
        assert hostname == f"{host}.example"
    ```
    
    Use a real local Parquet or filesystem boundary for a small integration test
    when that interaction matters; use a stub or fake for costly or nondeterministic
    remote services. A fake cannot establish that the real service works. Keep
    randomized tests independent of execution order; for numerical or sampling
    claims define tolerances and uncertainty rather than requiring arbitrary
    bit-for-bit agreement across environments.
    
    Consult the Hypothesis [tutorial](https://hypothesis.readthedocs.io/en/latest/tutorial/),
    [how-to guides](https://hypothesis.readthedocs.io/en/latest/how-to/),
    [strategies and API reference](https://hypothesis.readthedocs.io/en/latest/reference/)
    and [extras](https://hypothesis.readthedocs.io/en/latest/extras.html) when
    choosing or debugging a strategy.

    133:This dataset is structurally different because its unit of observation is a **firm pair in a given year**, rather than a news article.

    # Define dataset requirements
    
    ## Goal
    
    Specify a public, reproducible financial news dataset for firm-level text,
    co-mention networks and market research.
    
    ## Requirements
    
    - **Coverage:** Report distinct usable articles per company-year, including zero
      counts for a declared universe, and firms meeting selectable annual thresholds
      over consecutive years. Compare with 47 raw articles per year over 2018–2022
      for the 100-firm Pricing Perspective frame; report raw and usable counts separately.
    - **Articles:** Provide stable IDs, source and publisher, URL, title, article text,
      language, publication and capture times with precision, quality flags, and
      traceable capture provenance where available.
    - **Companies:** Preserve all article–company links, dated issuer identifiers,
      supporting evidence, ambiguity and substantive relevance. Distinguish mentions
      from company-focused coverage and retain unresolved identities.
    - **Sources:** Maintain versioned publisher selection criteria and distinguish
      original reporting, syndicated material and press releases where possible.
      Deduplicate stories without discarding source records or company links.
    - **Research validity:** Evaluate extraction, deduplication, dates, company links
      and relevance against human-adjudicated samples. Report precision, recall,
      uncertainty and coverage gaps across years, publishers and firms.
    - **Reproducibility:** Publish a versioned schema, data dictionary, lineage,
      checksums, methods, coverage reports and examples for firm-year panels and
      co-mention networks. Document article-text access and redistribution conditions.
    - **Extensions:** Treat company-specific sentiment and events, article topics and
      novelty as separately versioned, evaluated enrichments.
    
    Numerical coverage and quality targets remain provisional until the staging audit.
    Publication dates before CC-News began do not establish when text was observable.
    See the [Pricing Perspective comparison](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.23447v3#Sx1)
    for the baseline and its limitations.
    
    ## Acceptance
    
    - [ ] Review these requirements against staging evidence and intended studies.
    - [ ] Set evidence-based coverage and quality targets for a first release.

    # Publisher-filter sampling methods
    
    ## Population and outcome
    
    The experiment estimates English source records retained by the historical
    115-domain allowlist, including subdomains. Each configured commit and native
    Parquet glob defines a finite source frame. Fine News uses its English files;
    Infini News uses its inline `eng_Latn` label; FineWeb-HQ uses `en`; RefinedWeb
    declares its release English. These source-specific definitions are recorded,
    not independently validated language labels.
    
    The outcome is publisher retention. Dates, tickers, financial relevance and
    article quality are not requirements in this pilot. Physical rows, rather than
    distinct URLs or stories, are counted. Training weights in Fine News do not
    change this record-count estimand. The original compressed DCLM source is
    deferred, and its partial Parquet conversion cannot represent the full source.
    
    ## Selection
    
    Enumerate every eligible file and its stored size at the pinned commit. Make
    four independent draws with replacement: choose a file uniformly from the
    frame, read its footer, then choose one of its row groups uniformly. Only
    selected files require footers. Sort inventories and use a separate deterministic
    seed per source. Persist every selected path, group, row bounds and probability.
    
    For a frame of M files, with G_i groups in selected file i, the probability
    of that physical group on one draw is q = 1 / (M × G_i). This is a draw
    probability, not the probability of appearing at least once in the sample.
    Repeated draws remain in the estimator. Identical groups are acquired once and
    their counts reused, without duplicating retained sample articles.
    
    Selection is fixed before reading outcomes. Do not replace expensive or failing
    draws, select the smallest files, stop after enough matches or interpret a
    convenience partition as a representative source. A costly preparation can be
    deferred; changing the design requires a separately recorded experiment.
    
    ## Acquisition
    
    Read only the selected group's half-open `file_row_number` interval and the
    explicit source projection. DuckDB 1.5.6 pushes those bounds to its Parquet
    reader. A local HTTP test compares transferred body bytes with a full projected
    scan. Ordinary `SYSTEM` or reservoir sampling is not the I/O boundary.
    
    The source must answer a small range request with HTTP 206 and matching source
    size. There is no whole-file fallback. Group sizes and necessary column chunks
    come from the footer; media and embeddings are excluded. Useful native metadata
    and file/row provenance remain in the retained output. A selected group is
    materialized once to reconcile input, English and retained counts.
    
    Listed file bytes describe stored source objects. Projected compressed chunk
    bytes describe selected columns before HTTP overhead, footer reads, prefetching
    or retries. Retained output bytes are measured locally. Actual network bytes
    are not measured and remain null. A single-group file may offer little saving.
    
    ## Estimation and uncertainty
    
    For draw d, count English records n_d and publisher-matched English records
    y_d. Let X_d = y_d / q_d and Z_d = n_d / q_d. The Hansen–Hurwitz estimates are:
    
    ```text
    Publisher records: Y_hat = mean(X_d)
    English records:   N_hat = mean(Z_d)
    Publisher yield:   p_hat = Y_hat / N_hat
    Var(Y_hat):       sum((X_d - Y_hat)^2) / (m × (m - 1))
    Var(p_hat):       sum((X_d - p_hat × Z_d)^2) / (m × (m - 1) × N_hat^2)
    ```
    
    Totals and their design-variance estimates are unbiased for independent
    replacement draws. Yield is a ratio estimate with approximate linearized
    variance, not an exactly unbiased estimator. Unequal group counts make an
    unweighted pooled sample yield inappropriate for population inference.
    
    Approximate 95% intervals use the Student t critical value with m - 1 degrees
    of freedom, with totals bounded below by zero and yield bounded to [0, 1].
    Four draws provide only three degrees of freedom. Rare or skewed group totals
    can make these intervals unreliable; label them exploratory. Zero matches,
    insufficient draws or degenerate variation leave the relevant uncertainty null,
    with an insufficient-evidence status. Zero English rows also leave yield null.
    
    Statsmodels `DescrStatsW` receives the probability-expanded draw values with
    unit frequency weights. Its mean, standard error and t interval provide the
    same total estimator; the yield uses the linearized residuals above. These are
    estimates over independent group draws, rather than over individual source rows.
    `Summary` and `SimpleTable` render the estimates in LaTeX. The full summary
    retains methods notes, while individual tables can be included with paper captions.
    
    The implementation tests weights against exact expectations over small finite
    frames, validates repeated draws and count reconciliation, and keeps physical
    sample counts separate from statistical draw totals. Sampling uncertainty does
    not include source omissions, language errors or publisher-registry validity.
    
    ## Further inference
    
    This pilot cannot establish unique research articles, cross-source incremental
    yield or companies meeting article thresholds over consecutive publication
    years. Source time composition differs, and crawl time is not publication time.
    Treat capture partitions as source provenance rather than an annual coverage
    estimate. Plan a larger, potentially stratified probability sample and a desired
    precision before a publication-grade comparison. Do not use outcome-dependent
    stopping without a suitable sequential design.
    
    ## References
    
    - [DuckDB Parquet metadata](https://duckdb.org/docs/1.5/data/parquet/metadata)
      describes group counts and compressed column sizes.
    - [DuckDB sampling](https://duckdb.org/docs/1.5/sql/query_syntax/samples)
      describes execution-vector sampling and reservoir behavior.
    - [Hugging Face Parquet conversion](https://huggingface.co/docs/dataset-viewer/parquet)
      describes partial conversions and their scope.
    - [Knottnerus and van Duin, Appendix A](https://www.scb.se/contentassets/ca21efb41fee47d293bbee5bf7be7fb3/variances-in-repeated-weighting-with-an-application-to-the-dutch-labour-force-survey.pdf#page=17)
      gives the Hansen–Hurwitz total and variance formulas.
    - [Statsmodels LaTeX summaries](https://www.statsmodels.org/stable/generated/statsmodels.iolib.summary.Summary.as_latex.html)
      describes summary export and recommends individual table export when columns differ.
