    ## Company decisions
    
    The selected rubric asks three binary questions per resolved company, using its
    canonical name and tickers: whether the article mentions it, provides meaningful
    company-specific information beyond a mention, and treats it as a main subject.
    Several companies may be primary. The manifest records the exact question
    templates and article-kind criteria. The current runtime is Kev-4B in BF16.
    Production uses the separate `kev-4b-low-memory.json` profile. It retains the
    same model and 8,192-token admission while reducing GPU graph buffers. A fixed
    16-request parity check preserved all tested 0.5 and 0.95 threshold decisions;
    the original corrected pilot retains its original runtime profile.
    
    `identity_score`, `substantive_score` and `raw_primary_score` preserve independent
    model outputs. `coverage_score` is their substantive/primary maximum: a ranking
    rule rather than a calibrated union probability. Contradictory marginals retain
    consistency flags. `primary_score` is available only after identity meets the
    configured cutoff. A provisional accepted pair requires confident identity and
    coverage without a strong coverage contradiction. Article kind does not gate it.
    Saved outputs support later threshold comparisons without rerunning inference.
    
    ## Native inference and checkpoints
    
    [Native Kev](../../../infra/inference/README.md) runs in a separate pinned GPU
    runtime. Pydantic's System One client shares each article across company questions
    in one request. Exact repeated company descriptors share questions while retaining
    all namespace-specific links. Large candidate sets use bounded requests.
    Article kind is an annotation, rather than an automatic editorial-content gate.
    
    The runtime profile records model revisions, checkpoint hashes, precision,
    kernels and context admission. Oversized documents are explicitly deferred;
    silent text truncation is disabled. Prediction manifests preserve the scorer and
    runtime contract. A changed scientific contract requires a new output directory.
    Operational deadlines, transport timeouts and concurrency can change on resume.
    Pass `--source data/raw/fine-news` to override archived absolute source locations.
    
    ```bash
    just dvc repro score_company_labels
    ```
    
    Production stores compressed source-record Parquet chunks and a small SQLite
    resume ledger in `data/processed/experiments/article-labels/corpus/`. It preserves
    source metadata, candidate provenance and raw model outputs. Successful identical
    requests can be reused; transient server failures are retried on resume. Context
    failures, unresolved identities and pending records stay separate from negatives.
    `progress.json` reports counts and `storage.json` gives a conditional disk estimate.
    
    The first production attempt stopped after 1,598 records because temporary JSON
    payloads left sparse SQLite pages after export. That attempt and its implementation
    are preserved under `corpus-pre-storage-fix/` and the scorer archive. Production
    checkpoints now replace exported request payloads with compact lookup records in
    one transaction; the disk estimate still accounts for allocated pages.
    
    An incomplete, storage-limited or deadline-limited run exits unsuccessfully after
    saving checkpoints. DVC therefore does not proceed automatically to its report.

    $ cat data/research/experiments/article-labels/cpu-audit/report.md
    # CPU filter audit
    
    The completed CPU stage reproduces literal candidate extraction and conserves
    source records. Its output is too permissive to use as company relevance labels.
    Generic aliases, unrelated publisher tags, page furniture and a confirmed
    date-aware identity/name defect require separate treatment.
    
    ## Review basis
    
    The fixed benchmark contains 1,000 of 12,241,870 retained source records, ordered
    by `sha256('42:' || article_id), article_id`. The 100-row retained audit is a
    second deterministic hash sample within that cohort. Its first 25 records were
    reviewed in that hash order. The separate 100-row no-hit sample uses the same
    audit seed across all no-company-candidate exclusions; its first 20 were reviewed.
    The seed is `ccfinance-cpu-audit-2026-11-16-v1`.
    
    Original text hashes were verified before review. No model predictions were read.
    These are qualitative AI source observations, not independently adjudicated
    human gold. No population precision, recall or confidence interval is claimed.
    The unit is a source record; identical articles can occur more than once.
    
    The rubric distinguishes a primary issuer in the title/lead and business facts,
    a secondary issuer with a financial role, incidental or footer mentions, and a
    surface match referring to ordinary language or another entity. Among the 25
    retained records, observations were: 2 primary, 2 business-secondary, 3 incidental
    or footer-only, and 18 with no genuine candidate entity identified. All 93 stored
    name spans examined matched the original NFKC/casefold text at their recorded
    offsets. Correct literal offsets do not establish correct entity association.
    
    ## Evidence in the fixed 1,000
    
    There are 3,137 article/issuer-namespace candidate pairs. The following counts
    refer to aliases present in stored spans, counted once per article or pair.
    Spans are capped, so these are observed evidence counts rather than all matches.
    
    | Alias | Articles | Candidate pairs |
    | --- | ---: | ---: |
    | people | 331 | 331 |
    | price | 241 | 476 |
    | new | 216 | 216 |
    | news | 209 | 209 |
    | target | 102 | 102 |
    
    Of 1,000 articles, 226 have every candidate supported exclusively by these five
    surfaces, with all counted name matches stored and no counted signals. Another
    30 show only these surfaces but have capped evidence. The remaining 744 have
    another stored alias or signal, which does not guarantee identity or relevance.
    At the pair level these classes contain 1,189, 143 and 1,805 records respectively.
    This diagnostic set is not exhaustive: `fossil`, `premier`, `popular`, `time`
    and other ambiguous surfaces also occur. Duplicate economic issuers across the
    top1000 and GH namespaces explain, for example, the additional `price` pairs.
    
    Full-corpus diagnostics independently show the leading first stored aliases:
    `people` for PERMCO 11901 in 4,100,590 articles; `price` for Costco in 2,905,743 GH
    and 2,849,044 top1000 articles; `new` for Navient in 2,354,510; and `news` for
    News Corp in 2,267,666. These overlapping counts must not be added as unique
    articles. The frozen registry contains the corresponding aliases, including
    Navient's `New Corp`/`New` and Costco's historical `PRICE`.
    
    ## Confirmed defects and semantic failures
    
    1. **Date-aware identity/name contamination.** The article
       `89567ed1cd7c15ffcf445271425e85d21fa9aabd457db74883938cb7248a868e`,
       dated 2021-01-14, is at `2021-01/eng_Latn/part-000001.parquet`, physical row
       20489. Its American Airlines comparison is matched as `top1000:20010`, with
       ticker `AAL`, verified CIK `0000006201`, and alias `american airlines`, but its
       display name is **Alpha Metallurgical Resources, Inc.** The registry contains
       an older candidate-only AMR/Alpha link for 2002–2006 and the verified American
       Airlines link for 2021. Legacy `company/universe.py` lines 41–71 pool names and
       aliases across all registry years and select the alphabetically first legal
       name. `company/tagging.py` lines 140–142 attach it to year-specific records.
       All five occurrences of this candidate in the 1,000-row cohort have the same
       Alpha-name/AAL-identity inconsistency. A classifier prompted with that name
       can evaluate the wrong company even when lexical matching is correct.
    2. **Generic and capitalized surfaces are not resolved entities.** The petroleum
       reserve article `96e3934d...` is retained solely through `Office of Fossil
       Energy` → Fossil Group. The Petraeus article `370a66e2...` matches the dateline
       `Nov 15` → NOV Inc. `Queensland Premier` and sentence-initial `People` produce
       other capitalized false associations. Legacy `tagging.py` lines 324–326 and
       347–348 count any name match lacking `lowercase_single_token` as cased;
       multiword aliases can receive that count without uppercase characters.
    3. **Publisher keyword collisions.** Article `51c152f9...`, source
       `2023-12/eng_Latn/part-000000.parquet`, physical row 35818, is about the AAP
       politician Sanjay Singh and India's Enforcement Directorate. Its original
       tags include `AAP` and `ED`; these become Advance Auto Parts and Consolidated
       Edison candidates. Legacy `tagging.py` lines 386–403 interpret standalone
       uppercase tags as tickers. The uncertainty flags correctly call these signals
       unverified; a publisher-tag count must not be treated as a precision guarantee.
    4. **Document boundaries matter.** Article `7a6e8366...` concerns Canary Gold;
       Comcast/NASDAQ:CMCSA appears only in a Trending Articles link. Article
       `3d7f10c2...` includes social-platform footer names and `NOW WATCH`, while
       `7bf224cc...` begins with an unrelated story teaser. Nonempty raw text alone
       does not remove these sources of false association.
    
    ## No-hit observations
    
    The 20 reviewed no-hit records did not establish a DFA implementation miss.
    They exposed catalog scope limits that must be reported separately from recall:
    the Philip Morris International story is from 2026, beyond the 2002–2025
    membership roster, and GameStop is not eligible in article year 2021 in that
    roster. Other stories concern foreign/private companies, politics or sport.
    Several Law360 and Seeking Alpha records contain clipped bodies, trial prompts
    or substantial boilerplate. These are quality observations, not validated
    automatic exclusion rules.
    
    ## Recommended next decisions
    
    - Preserve this frozen cohort and broad candidate stage as baseline evidence.
      Do not publish candidate presence as company relevance or as model gold.
    - Resolve display names and permitted aliases against the article-year verified
      CIK/issuer membership. Quarantine candidate-only crosswalks from verified
      identities; retain the original link evidence and version any corrected run.
    - Give aliases explicit provenance, historical validity and ambiguity status.
      Generic legal roots and placeholder-like aliases need contextual adjudication.
      Capitalization and a hand-written list of forbidden words are insufficient.
    - Distinguish financial security tags from general publisher keywords using
      documented field semantics. Treat unverified bare uppercase tags as candidate
      retrieval evidence.
    - Separate article body from recommendations, navigation and subscription text
      before assessing substantive relevance. First validate a small set of such
      rules against preserved source examples.
    - Compare the 1,000 model outputs with this blinded rubric and then independently
      adjudicate disputed cases. Measure accepted precision and excluded recall
      separately, including roster/year coverage and exact-duplicate dependence.
    
    The JSON artifacts hold complete IDs, source coordinates, hashes, observations
    and counts. `manifest.json` records the frozen benchmark and selection hashes;
    `methods.sql` records the aggregate and sample queries. Original reviewed texts
    are retained as audit evidence alongside their SHA256 values.

    _ARTICLES = """
    CREATE TEMP TABLE articles AS
    WITH joined AS (
        SELECT t.row_key AS article_id, a.id AS source_article_id,
            t.source_path, t.source_row, a.metadata.title AS title,
            a.metadata.url AS url, a.metadata.publish_date AS publish_date,
            t.year AS publish_year, t.top1000_coverage,
            sha256(a.text) AS text_sha256, length(a.text) AS text_chars,
            a.text IS NOT NULL AND length(trim(a.text)) > 0 AS usable_text,
            lower(rtrim(trim(coalesce(nullif(trim(a.metadata.url_hostname), ''),
                regexp_extract(a.metadata.url, '(?i)^https?://([^/:?#]+)', 1))), '.'))
                AS hostname,
            len(t.top1000_candidates) AS top1000_candidate_count,
            len(t.gh_candidates) AS gh_candidate_count,
            list_concat(t.top1000_candidates, t.gh_candidates) AS candidates
        FROM read_parquet($source, file_row_number=true, hive_partitioning=false) a
        JOIN read_parquet($tags, hive_partitioning=false) t
            ON a.file_row_number = t.source_row
    ), policy AS (
        SELECT *, top1000_candidate_count + gh_candidate_count AS candidate_count,
            coalesce('sha256:' || text_sha256, 'source:' || article_id) AS document_id,
            EXISTS (
                SELECT 1 FROM read_csv($domains, header=true) d
                WHERE hostname = lower(rtrim(trim(d.domain), '.'))
                   OR ends_with(hostname, '.' || lower(rtrim(trim(d.domain), '.')))
            ) AS publisher_allowed
        FROM joined
    )
    SELECT * EXCLUDE (usable_text, publisher_allowed),
        publisher_allowed AND usable_text AND candidate_count > 0 AS retained,
        CASE WHEN NOT publisher_allowed THEN 'publisher_not_allowed'
             WHEN text_chars IS NULL THEN 'missing_text'
             WHEN NOT usable_text THEN 'empty_text'
             WHEN candidate_count = 0 THEN 'no_company_candidate'
             ELSE NULL END AS exclusion_reason,
        list_filter([
            CASE WHEN NOT publisher_allowed THEN 'publisher_not_allowed' END,
            CASE WHEN text_chars IS NULL THEN 'missing_text'
                 WHEN NOT usable_text THEN 'empty_text' END,

    class Tagger:
        """Compile once per worker; ``tag`` preserves raw source row identity."""
    
        def __init__(self, membership: Path, registry: Path, gh: Path):
            universe, top_metadata = load_universe(membership, registry)
            self.top_records: dict[int, dict[str, dict]] = defaultdict(dict)
            self.top_tickers: dict[int, dict[str, set[str]]] = defaultdict(
                lambda: defaultdict(set)
            )
            with membership.open(newline="", encoding="utf-8") as stream:
                for row in csv.DictReader(stream):
                    year, permco = int(row["effective_year"]), str(row["permco"])
                    issuer = f"top1000:{permco}"
                    detail = self.top_records[year].setdefault(
                        issuer,
                        {
                            "name": None,
                            "tickers": set(),
                            "ciks": set(),
                            "link_statuses": set(),
                            "issuer_keys": set(),
                        },
                    )
                    for key, column in (
                        ("ciks", "cik"),
                        ("link_statuses", "link_status"),
                        ("issuer_keys", "issuer_key"),
                    ):
                        if row.get(column):
                            detail[key].add(row[column])
                    ticker = (row.get("ticker") or "").strip().upper()
                    if ticker:
                        detail["tickers"].add(ticker)
                        self.top_tickers[year][ticker].add(issuer)
            for year, rows in universe.items():
                for row in rows:
                    self.top_records[year][f"top1000:{row['permco']}"]["name"] = row["name"]
            top_transformed = transform_universe(universe, POLICIES["extended_cased"])
            self.top_owners = {
                year: {
                    alias: tuple(f"top1000:{i}" for i in ids)
                    for alias, ids in _aliases(rows).items()
                }
                for year, rows in top_transformed.items()
            }
            self.gh_records: dict[str, dict] = {}
            self.gh_tickers: dict[str, set[str]] = defaultdict(set)
            gh_defs: dict[str, dict] = {}
            gh_missing = []
            gh_missing_cik = 0
            with gh.open(newline="", encoding="utf-8") as stream:
                for row in csv.DictReader(stream):
                    cik = (row.get("cik") or "").strip()
                    if not cik:
                        gh_missing_cik += 1
                        continue
                    # SEC CIKs have one canonical 10-digit form within this namespace.
                    cik = str(int(cik)).zfill(10)
                    issuer = f"gh:{cik}"
                    name = (row.get("company_legal_name") or "").strip()
                    ticker = (row.get("ticker") or "").strip().upper()
                    detail = self.gh_records.setdefault(
                        issuer, {"name": None, "tickers": set()}
                    )
                    if name:
                        if detail["name"] is None:
                            detail["name"] = name
                        definition = gh_defs.setdefault(
                            cik, {"permco": cik, "name": name, "aliases": []}
                        )
                        definition["aliases"] = sorted(
                            set(definition["aliases"])
                            | {name}
                            | set(_strings(row.get("other_names")))
                        )
                    else:
                        gh_missing.append(cik)
                    if ticker:
                        detail["tickers"].add(ticker)
                        self.gh_tickers[ticker].add(issuer)
            gh_transformed = transform_universe(
                {0: list(gh_defs.values())}, POLICIES["extended_cased"]
            )[0]
            self.gh_owners = {
                alias: tuple(f"gh:{i}" for i in ids)
                for alias, ids in _aliases(gh_transformed).items()
            }
            all_aliases = sorted(
                set(self.gh_owners).union(*(set(x) for x in self.top_owners.values()))
            )
            # One engine for all years and both catalogs. Scan raw overlapping hits;
            # Matcher._matches cannot be used because it would select overlaps before
            # actual-year and per-universe ownership filtering.
            self.matcher = Matcher(
                {0: [{"permco": "union", "name": "", "aliases": all_aliases}]}, "rust_dfa"
            )
            self.metadata = {
                "version": 1,
                "backend": "rust_dfa",
                "automata": 1,
                "alias_policy": "extended_cased_with_uncased_candidates_retained",
                "offset_space": _OFFSET,
                "name_view": (
                    "NFKC + casefold; explicit exchange/cashtag annotations "
                    "masked with equal-length spaces"
                ),
                "overlap_policy": (
                    "leftmost-longest independently per eligible universe, "
                    "before case flags"
                ),
                "top1000": top_metadata,
                "gh": {
                    "sha256": sha256_file(gh),
                    "issuer_count": len(self.gh_records),
                    "missing_names": sorted(set(gh_missing)),
                    "missing_cik_rows": gh_missing_cik,
                    "membership": "fixed catalog across all years, including missing year",
                    "tickers_historically_certified": False,
                    "issuers": {
                        key: {"name": value["name"], "tickers": sorted(value["tickers"])}
                        for key, value in sorted(self.gh_records.items())
                    },
                },
                "alias_count": len(all_aliases),
                "probabilities": False,
                "note": (
                    "Candidates are mentions/signals, not substantive-association "
                    "decisions. No inferred PERMCO-CIK crosswalk."
                ),
            }
            self.coverage = {
                year: ("partial" if len(rows) > len(universe.get(year, [])) else "complete")
                for year, rows in self.top_records.items()
            }

    """Bounded, deterministic company candidates from names and publisher signals.
    
    This is candidate extraction, not an association classifier or probability model.
    Offsets are Python character indices in NFKC + casefold text, with explicit
    security annotations replaced by equal-length spaces in the name matching view.
    The single Rust DFA is shared by both universes; eligibility precedes overlap
    selection, and each universe retains its own legal-root ownership policy.
    """
    
    from __future__ import annotations
    
    import csv
    import json
    import re
    import unicodedata

    _OFFSET = "normalized_nfkc_casefold"
    _BARE_TAG = re.compile(r"[A-Z][A-Z0-9.\-]{1,9}")
    _SYMBOL = re.compile(r"[:=]\s*\$?([A-Z0-9][A-Z0-9.\-/]{0,14})\b", re.I)
    
    
    def _strings(value: str | None) -> list[str]:
        parsed = json.loads(value or "[]")
        if not isinstance(parsed, list):
            raise ValueError("catalog alias field must be a JSON list")
        return [x.strip() for x in parsed if isinstance(x, str) and x.strip()]
    
    
    def _aliases(rows: list[dict]) -> dict[str, tuple[str, ...]]:
        owners: dict[str, set[str]] = defaultdict(set)
        for row in rows:
            for value in [row["name"], *row.get("aliases", [])]:
                alias = normalize(value.strip())
                if len(alias) >= 3:
                    owners[alias].add(row["permco"])
        return {alias: tuple(sorted(ids)) for alias, ids in owners.items()}
    
    
    def _view(value: str) -> tuple[str, str | list[bool], list[dict]]:
        """Separate explicit metadata while leaving ordinary company prose intact."""
        nfkc = unicodedata.normalize("NFKC", value)
        folded = nfkc.casefold()
        # Inspect case only at matches on the usual one-to-one casefold path.
        # Expanding folds (sharp S etc.) retain the exact coordinate behavior.
        expands = len(nfkc) != len(folded)
        cased = (
            [char.isupper() or char.istitle() for char in nfkc for _ in char.casefold()]
            if expands
            else nfkc
        )
        offsets = None
        signals = []
        occupied = []
        for pattern, source in ((EXCHANGE, "exchange_symbol"), (CASHTAG, "cashtag")):
            for match in pattern.finditer(nfkc):
                if any(
                    start <= match.start() and match.end() <= end for start, end in occupied
                ):
                    continue
                ticker = (
                    _SYMBOL.search(match.group()).group(1)
                    if source == "exchange_symbol"
                    else match.group()[1:]
                ).upper()
                if expands:
                    if offsets is None:
                        offsets = [0]
                        for char in nfkc:
                            offsets.append(offsets[-1] + len(char.casefold()))
                    start, end = offsets[match.start()], offsets[match.end()]
                else:
                    start, end = match.span()
                signals.append(
                    {"start": start, "end": end, "ticker": ticker, "source": source}
                )
                occupied.append(match.span())
        if not signals:
            return folded, cased, []
        signals.sort(key=lambda x: (x["start"], x["end"]))
        pieces, previous = [], 0
        for signal in signals:
            start, end = signal["start"], signal["end"]
            if start >= previous:
                pieces.append(folded[previous:start])
            if end > previous:
                pieces.append(" " * (end - max(previous, start)))
                previous = end
        pieces.append(folded[previous:])
        return "".join(pieces), cased, signals
    
    
    def _has_case(value: str | list[bool], start: int, end: int) -> bool:
        if isinstance(value, str):
            return any(char.isupper() or char.istitle() for char in value[start:end])
        return any(value[start:end])

            for owners in (self.top_owners.get(year, {}), self.gh_owners):

                            add(issuer, field, span, flags)
    
            signals("title", title_signals)

    """Preserve the historical Fine News publisher acquisition command."""
    
    import os
    from pathlib import Path
    from tempfile import TemporaryDirectory
    from typing import Annotated
    
    import duckdb
    import typer
    from pydantic import BaseModel, ConfigDict
    
    from pipeline.stages.raw.publishers import PUBLISHER_MATCH, SOURCES, write_parquet
    
    
    class FineNewsConfig(BaseModel):
        """Versioned inputs and output for the Fine News selection."""
    
        model_config = ConfigDict(extra="forbid")
    
        source: str
        domains: Path
        output: Path
    
    
    def filter_fine_news(
        config: Annotated[
            Path, typer.Option(help="Historical acquisition configuration.")
        ] = Path("data/inputs/fine-news/acquisition.json"),
    ) -> None:
        """Select English publisher shards from a pinned Fine News revision."""
        settings = FineNewsConfig.model_validate_json(config.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
        target = settings.output / "articles.parquet"
        if target.exists():
            raise FileExistsError(f"Output exists: {target}")
        target.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
        with TemporaryDirectory(dir=target.parent) as staging, duckdb.connect() as con:
            if settings.source.startswith("hf://"):
                con.execute("INSTALL httpfs; LOAD httpfs")
            temporary = Path(staging) / "articles.parquet"
            write_parquet(
                con,
                f"""WITH articles AS (
                    SELECT {SOURCES["fine_news"].projection} FROM read_parquet($source)
                ) SELECT text, id, metadata FROM articles WHERE {PUBLISHER_MATCH}""",  # noqa: S608 - authored projection and predicate.
                {"source": settings.source, "domains": str(settings.domains)},
                temporary,
            )
            os.link(temporary, target)
        typer.echo(f"Wrote: {settings.source} -> {target}")

## Assistant

The 12.24 million are **candidate articles for company tagging**. Each retained source record met three conditions:

1. Its hostname matched the existing list of 115 publisher domains or a subdomain. The input was already selected from Fine News’s English `eng_Latn` partitions.
2. Its article text was present and non-empty.
3. The CPU matcher found **at least one possible company candidate** in the title, body or publisher tags. [Retention rule](/home/marcussky/Git/CCFinance/src/python/apps/pipeline/src/pipeline/stages/processed/experiments/article_labels.py:155)

For the third condition, the matcher looked for company names and aliases, explicit ticker forms such as `NASDAQ:AAPL` or `$AAPL`, and certain uppercase publisher tags that could be tickers. It matched against an article-year US top-1,000 company roster and a separate fixed company catalogue. These are **retrieval signals**: a match did not have to be in a headline, refer to the intended company, or establish that the company was the article’s main subject. [Matcher implementation](/home/marcussky/Git/fine-news-financial-publishers/src/python/apps/fine_news_cli/src/fine_news_cli/company/tagging.py:272)

Of the 14,807,287 source records, **12,241,870 were retained** and **2,565,417 were excluded because no company candidate was found**. The retained records contain 38,053,717 candidate associations; some represent the same issuer in both catalogues. They are source records, not necessarily distinct syndicated stories. [CPU metrics](/home/marcussky/Git/CCFinance/data/research/experiments/article-labels/cpu/metrics.json)

The filter is **very permissive**. In the 1,000-record pilot, 226 records had fully observed candidates supported *only* by the generic words `people`, `price`, `new`, `news` or `target`. Footer content and ambiguous publisher tags also produced candidates. The [CPU audit](/home/marcussky/Git/CCFinance/data/research/experiments/article-labels/cpu-audit/report.md) documents examples.

So the 12.24 million should not be interpreted as company-relevant financial articles. They are the broad set we sent forward for potential adjudication. Likewise, the earlier **~15 billion input-token estimate applies to this broad candidate set**; a carefully validated, more selective CPU filter could reduce it. The excluded set also needs a recall audit before assuming it contains no relevant company articles.

Yes. As a **provisional model-based estimate**, Kev suggests roughly **4 million of the 12.24 million retained records** mention at least one retrieved company. That is an estimate of Kev’s classifications, not yet an estimate of the true number of mentions.

In the corpus-wide 1,000-record pilot:

- **331 articles** had at least one company with a mention score of **0.5 or higher**. Extrapolated, that is **33.1%**, or about **4.05 million records**.
- **592 articles** had no score reaching 0.5 and all their candidates were scored.
- **77 articles** had no score reaching 0.5 but had at least one unresolved candidate or were too long to score. They cannot yet be called negatives.

The threshold matters a lot: requiring a score of **0.95** leaves **80 of 1,000 articles**, equivalent to roughly **980,000 records**. Neither threshold has been calibrated against human labels, and a score of 0.95 does not establish 95% accuracy. The underlying [pilot decisions](/home/marcussky/Git/CCFinance/data/processed/experiments/article-labels/benchmark-corrected-1000/decisions.jsonl) preserve the scores.

As a cross-check, **23,807 of the 93,582 records** processed in the larger run—about **25%**—had a score of at least 0.5. That run followed source order, so it is less suitable for extrapolation across the corpus than the pilot.

A *mention* can still be incidental or appear in a footer. For the stricter provisional rule combining identity and substantive or primary coverage, only **21 of the 1,000 pilot articles** had an accepted candidate. Before relying on either estimate, the useful next step is a human review of a small random sample stratified by Kev score, including unresolved records and some CPU-filter exclusions. That would let us estimate false positives and missed companies.

    # Accepted pilot source review
    
    All 24 accepted namespace pairs in 21 original articles identify the displayed company and contain developed company-specific information. Each company is defensibly one of the article's main subjects, including the two companies in the rail roundup. No accepted pair appears to be a generic-word collision, footer-only mention or attribution-only link in this qualitative review.
    
    This is an AI-assisted **post-selection** check: acceptance was known, model score values were not loaded, and the original text checksums were verified for all 21 articles. These observations are not human gold, a population precision estimate, a 95% precision finding or a recall assessment. The 24 namespace pairs represent 22 distinct article/CIK combinations; Micron and Tractor Supply each appear in both Top1000 and GH namespaces.
    
    Company relevance does not establish suitability for the default editorial dataset:
    
    - **19 articles / 20 pairs** contain identifiable editorial reporting or investment analysis, often syndicated. Twelve of those articles also contain publisher or subscription promotions; the company evidence is developed in the article body.
    - **One article / two pairs** is an explicit Tractor Supply issuer press release syndicated from Business Wire. Its notes offering is primary company coverage, but it belongs in the separate release view under the current intended policy.
    - **One article / two pairs** is a developed Zacks rail roundup with “For Immediate Release,” media-contact and marketing material. The company roles are clear; its editorial-versus-promotional format needs policy review. No exclusion was applied.
    
    The examples expose source-quality limits: Micron is a summary/truncated excerpt; several analyses reference missing figures or tables; Delta contains internally inconsistent revenue/cash-burn wording, and FirstCash appears to omit revenue scale units. The Tesla item's relative weekday wording needs date review. Chipotle and Oracle publication dates precede their crawl partitions, so partition dates must not substitute for publication dates. These are observations about the retained text, not externally verified factual corrections.
    
    Only 15 of the 24 accepted links carry the verified-title-and-body discovery tier. The other nine include developed Nektar, BILL, Delta, Walmart, Chipotle, Micron and United Bankshares coverage, plus the GH Tractor Supply link. This selected subset cannot estimate a stricter filter's population recall, but it shows why stored lexical tiers must not be treated as relevance truth.
    
    The accepted links look sensible for a provisional company-relevance filter. A full run should preserve the separate source-format and quality fields and keep human validation pending. This review did not change any scoring threshold, exclusion rule, source record or sealed audit label.

## Assistant

Your arithmetic is right. The key constraint is that we **cannot identify the approximately 4 million predicted mentions for free**: at the moment, that number comes from applying Kev to a sample of the much broader 12.24-million-record candidate set.

At the current listed price of **$0.01 per million input tokens**, and using Kev’s measured token counts as a planning proxy:

| Workload | Approximate input tokens | Estimated model charge |
|---|---:|---:|
| Score all 12.24M candidates | 15.3 billion | **$153** |
| Score 4M articles, if already identified | 5.0 billion | **$50** |
| Score the 1.93M stronger CPU candidates | 2.66 billion | **$26.60** |

The last row uses the stronger tier’s **own pilot average of about 1,376 tokens per article**, rather than the overall 1,249. All three figures need confirmation with the selected hosted model’s tokenizer and actual billing. They exclude credit-purchase fees and any applicable taxes.

[Span-02](https://openrouter.ai/respan/span-02) and [Perplexity Decider Flash](https://openrouter.ai/perplexity/pplx-decider-flash-v1.2) are listed at $0.01/M input and $0/M output. Hosted [Kev 4B](https://openrouter.ai/jaredpalmer/kev-4b) is currently listed at **$0.042/M**, so repeating the full run with hosted Kev would be roughly **$642** at the same token count.

I would use a **measured cascade**, with the CPU tier controlling *priority* until we can measure what it misses:

1. **Improve and evaluate the CPU shortlist.** We already have 1.93M records with a verified article-year company identity and name evidence in both title and body. In the 1,000-record pilot, those 160 sampled articles contained **108 of the 331** Kev-positive mentions and **14 of the 21** articles with an accepted substantive/primary candidate. That is a useful concentration, but it also means a strict cutoff would miss **223 of the 331 provisional mentions** and seven of the 21 accepted articles. Those are model results, not human-validated recall figures.

2. **Run a small, capped hosted comparison first.** Test Span-02 and Decider Flash on the same preserved sample, with human review of a stratified selection of positives, negatives, ambiguous aliases and CPU-excluded articles. Measure each model’s actual billed input tokens, throughput, precision and recall. A longer advertised context window is useful for transcripts, but does not establish that a model handles them accurately.

3. **Spend most of the budget on the best-performing queue.** For an all-in target below $25, I’d initially reserve roughly **$1 for model comparison, $20 for the high-yield queue and $1–2 for a random audit of lower-priority records**, leaving room for fees. At the pilot’s stronger-tier token average and $0.01/M, $20 would cover roughly **1.45 million articles**. The rest remain explicitly pending, with their selection tier recorded; they are not silently labelled negative.

4. **Only then consider a cheaper screening pass.** To screen *all* 12.24M records for $25 at $0.01/M, the complete request would need to average at most **204 tokens per article**—before fees and with nothing left for full-text scoring. Title-and-lead or mention-window screening could help, but it needs a recall study against full text before we use it to exclude records. It may miss companies introduced later in an article.

For each full-text request, I’d send the article **once**, with questions for all retrieved companies: identity, substantive coverage and primary-subject score, plus a small article-level classification such as reporting, opinion, issuer release or promotional content. Publisher, date, URL, candidate evidence, source hashes and processing provenance already exist locally and do not need to be re-extracted by the model. Additional decision questions still consume input tokens, so we should measure their incremental cost and quality.

Network volume is material but not necessarily the main bottleneck. The pilot averaged about **4,044 body characters**, suggesting roughly **50 GB of article text** to send the whole retained set once, before request JSON, responses and retries. Over 24 hours that is about **0.6 MB/s average upload**; however, one request per article requires about **142 successful requests per second**. Provider throughput, concurrency, rate limits and response handling therefore need an actual load test.

For the hard budget, I’d pin the model and provider, disable expensive fallback, enforce a per-key spend limit, and use a local admission budget that reserves for in-flight requests. OpenRouter documents [per-key limits and in-flight accounting](https://openrouter.ai/docs/api/reference/limits); its [pricing page](https://openrouter.ai/pricing) also notes credit-purchase fees and possible taxes. The cap should sit below the user’s all-in limit, rather than assuming a $100 token budget costs exactly $100.

My recommendation is to treat **$25 as a high-yield first release plus an audit**, not a promise of four million verified articles. A budget below $100 could cover substantially more of the corpus, but even that needs either a validated cheaper screen or a selective queue at current prices.

    - `hf repos duplicate FROM_ID` — Duplicate a repo on the Hub (model, dataset, or Space). `[--type [model|dataset|space] --private --public --protected --exist-ok --flavor [cpu-basic|cpu-upgrade|zero-a10g|t4-small|t4-medium|l4x1|l4x4|l40sx1|l40sx4|l40sx8|a10g-small|a10g-large|a10g-largex2|a10g-largex4|a100-large|a100x4|a100x8] --storage [small|medium|large] --sleep-time INTEGER --secrets TEXT --secrets-file TEXT --env TEXT --env-file TEXT --volume TEXT --format [auto|human|agent|json|quiet]]`
    - `hf repos list` — List all repos (models, datasets, spaces, buckets) with storage info. `[--namespace TEXT --type [model|dataset|space|bucket] --search TEXT --limit INTEGER --explore --format [auto|human|agent|json|quiet]]`
    - `hf repos move FROM_ID TO_ID` — Move a repository from a namespace to another namespace. `[--type [model|dataset|space] --format [auto|human|agent|json|quiet]]`
    - `hf repos settings REPO_ID` — Update the settings of a repository. `[--gated [auto|manual|false] --private --public --protected --type [model|dataset|space] --format [auto|human|agent|json|quiet]]`
    - `hf repos tag create REPO_ID TAG` — Create a tag for a repo. `[--message TEXT --revision TEXT --type [model|dataset|space] --format [auto|human|agent|json|quiet]]`
    - `hf repos tag delete REPO_ID TAG` — Delete a tag for a repo. `[--yes --type [model|dataset|space] --format [auto|human|agent|json|quiet]]`
    - `hf repos tag list REPO_ID` — List tags for a repo. `[--type [model|dataset|space] --format [auto|human|agent|json|quiet]]`
    
    ### `hf sandbox` — Run and manage experimental sandboxes on Hugging Face Jobs.
    
    - `hf sandbox cp SRC DST` — Copy a file between the local machine and a sandbox (docker-style). `[--namespace TEXT --format [auto|human|agent|json|quiet]]`
    - `hf sandbox create` — Create a sandbox: a dedicated VM by default, or a cheap shared one with `--pool`. `[--pool TEXT --flavor [cpu-basic|cpu-upgrade|cpu-performance|cpu-xl|t4-small|t4-medium|l4x1|l4x4|l40sx1|l40sx4|l40sx8|a10g-small|a10g-large|a10g-largex2|a10g-largex4|a100-large|a100x4|a100x8|h200|h200x2|h200x4|h200x8|rtx-pro-6000|rtx-pro-6000x2|rtx-pro-6000x4|rtx-pro-6000x8] --idle-timeout TEXT --env TEXT --secrets TEXT --env-file TEXT --secrets-file TEXT --volume TEXT --namespace TEXT --forward-hf-token --format [auto|human|agent|json|quiet]]`
    - `hf sandbox exec SANDBOX_ID COMMAND` — Run a command in a sandbox, streaming output. Exits with the command's exit code. `[--workdir TEXT --env TEXT --env-file TEXT --timeout FLOAT --namespace TEXT]`
    - `hf sandbox kill` — Terminate a sandbox, a whole shared host, or everything (--all). `[--all --yes --namespace TEXT --format [auto|human|agent|json|quiet]]`
    - `hf sandbox pool create` — Warm a pool: boot one host VM now, tagged so it can be found later by its pool id. `[--flavor [cpu-basic|cpu-upgrade|cpu-performance|cpu-xl|t4-small|t4-medium|l4x1|l4x4|l40sx1|l40sx4|l40sx8|a10g-small|a10g-large|a10g-largex2|a10g-largex4|a100-large|a100x4|a100x8|h200|h200x2|h200x4|h200x8|rtx-pro-6000|rtx-pro-6000x2|rtx-pro-6000x4|rtx-pro-6000x8] --per-host INTEGER RANGE --max-hosts INTEGER RANGE --idle-timeout TEXT --namespace TEXT --format [auto|human|agent|json|quiet]]`
    - `hf sandbox pool delete POOL_ID` — Terminate every host VM of a pool (and therefore all its sandboxes). `[--yes --namespace TEXT --format [auto|human|agent|json|quiet]]`
    - `hf sandbox pool ls` — List running sandbox pools (grouped from their host VMs). `[--namespace TEXT --format [auto|human|agent|json|quiet]]`
    - `hf sandbox process kill SANDBOX_ID PID` — Stop a background process running in a sandbox. `[--namespace TEXT --format [auto|human|agent|json|quiet]]`
    - `hf sandbox process ls SANDBOX_ID` — List the background processes running in a sandbox (started with `hf sandbox spawn`). `[--namespace TEXT --format [auto|human|agent|json|quiet]]`
    - `hf sandbox spawn SANDBOX_ID COMMAND` — Start a long-running command in the background and return its pid (don't wait). `[--workdir TEXT --env TEXT --env-file TEXT --namespace TEXT]`
    
    ### `hf skills` — Manage skills for AI assistants.
    
    - `hf skills add` — Install a Hugging Face skill for an AI assistant. `[--claude --global --dest PATH --force --format [auto|human|agent|json|quiet]]`
    - `hf skills list` — List available skills from the Hugging Face marketplace. `[--format [auto|human|agent|json|quiet]]`
    - `hf skills preview` — Print the generated `hf-cli` SKILL.md to stdout. `[--format [auto|human|agent|json|quiet]]`
    - `hf skills update` — Update installed Hugging Face marketplace skills. `[--claude --global --dest PATH --format [auto|human|agent|json|quiet]]`
    
    ### `hf spaces` — Interact with spaces on the Hub.
    
    - `hf spaces card SPACE_ID` — Get the Space card (README) for a Space on the Hub. `[--metadata --text --format [auto|human|agent|json|quiet]]`
    - `hf spaces dev-mode SPACE_ID` — Enable or disable dev mode on a Space. `[--stop --format [auto|human|agent|json|quiet]]`
    - `hf spaces hardware` — List available hardware options for Spaces. `[--format [auto|human|agent|json|quiet]]`
    - `hf spaces hot-reload SPACE_ID` — Hot-reload any Python file of a Space without a full rebuild + restart. `[--local-file PATH --skip-checks --skip-summary --format [auto|human|agent|json|quiet]]`
    - `hf spaces info SPACE_ID` — Get info about a space on the Hub. `[--revision TEXT --expand TEXT --format [auto|human|agent|json|quiet]]`
    - `hf spaces list` — List spaces on the Hub, or files in a space repo. `[--search TEXT --author TEXT --filter TEXT --sort [created_at|last_modified|likes|trending_score] --limit INTEGER --expand TEXT --human-readable --tree --recursive --revision TEXT --format [auto|human|agent|json|quiet]]`
    - `hf spaces logs SPACE_ID` — Fetch the run or build logs of a Space. `[--build --follow --tail INTEGER --format [auto|human|agent|json|quiet]]`
    - `hf spaces pause SPACE_ID` — Pause a Space. `[--format [auto|human|agent|json|quiet]]`
    - `hf spaces restart SPACE_ID` — Restart a Space. `[--factory-reboot --format [auto|human|agent|json|quiet]]`
    - `hf spaces search QUERY` — Search spaces on the Hub using semantic search. `[--filter TEXT --sdk TEXT --include-non-running --description --limit INTEGER --format [auto|human|agent|json|quiet]]`
    - `hf spaces secrets add SPACE_ID` — Add or update secrets for a Space. `[--secrets TEXT --secrets-file TEXT --format [auto|human|agent|json|quiet]]`
    - `hf spaces secrets delete SPACE_ID KEY` — Remove a secret from a Space. `[--yes --format [auto|human|agent|json|quiet]]`
    - `hf spaces secrets list SPACE_ID` — List secrets for a Space. Secret values are write-only and not returned. `[--format [auto|human|agent|json|quiet]]`
    - `hf spaces settings SPACE_ID` — Update the settings of a Space. `[--sleep-time INTEGER --hardware [cpu-basic|cpu-upgrade|zero-a10g|t4-small|t4-medium|l4x1|l4x4|l40sx1|l40sx4|l40sx8|a10g-small|a10g-large|a10g-largex2|a10g-largex4|a100-large|a100x4|a100x8] --format [auto|human|agent|json|quiet]]`
    - `hf spaces ssh SPACE_ID` — SSH into a Space's Dev Mode container. `[--identity-file PATH --dry-run --auto --format [auto|human|agent|json|quiet]]`
    - `hf spaces templates` — List the available Space templates. `[--format [auto|human|agent|json|quiet]]`
    - `hf spaces variables add SPACE_ID` — Add or update environment variables for a Space. `[--env TEXT --env-file TEXT --format [auto|human|agent|json|quiet]]`
    - `hf spaces variables delete SPACE_ID KEY` — Remove an environment variable from a Space. `[--yes --format [auto|human|agent|json|quiet]]`
    - `hf spaces variables list SPACE_ID` — List environment variables for a Space. `[--format [auto|human|agent|json|quiet]]`
    - `hf spaces volumes delete SPACE_ID` — Remove all volumes from a Space. `[--yes --format [auto|human|agent|json|quiet]]`
    - `hf spaces volumes list SPACE_ID` — List volumes mounted in a Space. `[--format [auto|human|agent|json|quiet]]`
    - `hf spaces volumes set SPACE_ID` — Set (replace) volumes for a Space. `[--volume TEXT --format [auto|human|agent|json|quiet]]`
    - `hf spaces wait SPACE_ID` — Wait for a Space to finish building/starting. `[--timeout TEXT --format [auto|human|agent|json|quiet]]`
    
    ### `hf webhooks` — Manage webhooks on the Hub.
    
    - `hf webhooks create --watch TEXT` — Create a new webhook. `[--url TEXT --job-id TEXT --domain [repo|discussions] --secret TEXT --format [auto|human|agent|json|quiet]]`
    - `hf webhooks delete WEBHOOK_ID` — Delete a webhook permanently. `[--yes --format [auto|human|agent|json|quiet]]`
    - `hf webhooks disable WEBHOOK_ID` — Disable an active webhook. `[--format [auto|human|agent|json|quiet]]`
    - `hf webhooks enable WEBHOOK_ID` — Enable a disabled webhook. `[--format [auto|human|agent|json|quiet]]`
    - `hf webhooks info WEBHOOK_ID` — Show full details for a single webhook. `[--format [auto|human|agent|json|quiet]]`
    - `hf webhooks list` — List all webhooks for the current user. `[--format [auto|human|agent|json|quiet]]`
    - `hf webhooks update WEBHOOK_ID` — Update an existing webhook. Only provided options are changed. `[--url TEXT --watch TEXT --domain [repo|discussions] --secret TEXT --format [auto|human|agent|json|quiet]]`
    
    ## Common options
    
    - `--format` — Output format: `--format json` (or `--json`) or `--format table` (default).
    - `-q / --quiet` — Quiet output (one ID per line).
    - `--revision` — Git revision id which can be a branch name, a tag, or a commit hash.
    - `--token` — Use a User Access Token. Prefer setting `HF_TOKEN` env var instead of passing `--token`.
    - `--type` — The type of repository (model, dataset, or space).
    
    ## Mounting repos as local filesystems
    
    To mount Hub repositories or buckets as local filesystems — no download, no copy, no waiting — use `hf-mount`. Files are fetched on demand. GitHub: https://github.com/huggingface/hf-mount
    
    Install: `brew install hf-mount`, or download a binary from https://github.com/huggingface/hf-mount/releases
    
    Some command examples:
    - `hf-mount start repo openai-community/gpt2 /tmp/gpt2` — mount a repo (read-only)
    - `hf-mount start --hf-token $HF_TOKEN bucket myuser/my-bucket /tmp/data` — mount a bucket (read-write)
    - `hf-mount status` / `hf-mount stop /tmp/data` — list or unmount
    
    ## Tips
    
    - Use `hf <command> --help` for full options, descriptions, usage, and real-world examples
    - Authenticate with `HF_TOKEN` env var (recommended) or with `--token`
    - Update the CLI with `hf update` (uses the correct command for the detected install method)

    ## Independent QC
    
    ```sh
    just python::run eval qc --backend dictionary --backend spacy --backend gliner \
      --device cuda:0 --batch-size 32 --limit 10 --output .tmp/company-eval-qc-smoke
    ```
    
    QC uses the same verified sanitized title/body. The dictionary, spaCy transformer
    NER and native GLiNER produce independent suggestions with character offsets,
    candidate PERMCOs and disagreements for review. GPU inference uses one process
    and overlapping bounded text windows; the GLiNER revision and model versions are
    recorded. Failed partial inference is not published as an empty prediction.
    QC suggestions never gate the decision models or become gold automatically.
    
    `eval link` reuses frozen spaCy and GLiNER v2.1 mention spans and replaces their
    exact-alias candidates with a shared pretrained contextual linker. It uses
    [`knowledgator/gliner-linker-large-v1.0`](https://huggingface.co/knowledgator/gliner-linker-large-v1.0)
    directly through GLiNER; the GLinker framework is not a dependency. The checkpoint
    and software versions are recorded in the output summary. The model's native
    span representation and label-scoring head classify the original spans. Entity
    label embeddings are computed once, and every named registry issuer is scored
    for each mention. No exact-name, fuzzy-name or NER-derived candidate shortlist
    is used. Canonical names and aliases are embedded separately, following the
    documented default name-label format. Each issuer receives its highest native
    alias logit; aliases shared across issuers remain competing identities. Names
    exceeding encoder limits are explicitly clipped and counted. Registry
    descriptions are retained for audit but excluded from inference: the current
    metadata includes unreviewed matches and disambiguation-page text, and combining
    names, alias lists and long descriptions degraded the pilot. Article context is
    bounded around the original mention without discarding any part of that mention.
    
    ```sh
    just python::run eval link --prepared .tmp/company-eval-text-v4 \
      --qc .tmp/company-eval-qc-v4 --output .tmp/company-eval-linked-v2
    just python::run eval score-signals --prepared .tmp/company-eval-text-v4 \
      --decisions .tmp/company-decisions-single-v3 --qc .tmp/company-eval-linked-v2
    ```
    
    Linking uses the model's default 0.5 threshold, without fitting it to publisher
    signals. At most one company is accepted per mention. Ties, below-threshold
    scores, unalignable spans and excessive contexts are explicit unresolved states.
    Year eligibility is checked after scoring: an ineligible winner is not replaced
    by the next eligible company. Noneligible named registry issuers serve as
    distractors, but the registry does not represent every outside company. The
    threshold is not a trained open-world NIL classifier. Registry aliases are not
    all reviewed or historically valid; modern names can postdate articles. These
    limitations remain material for academic use. This is an exploratory pilot:
    changing the label representation after inspecting initial errors means a
    fresh, independently reviewed holdout is needed for confirmatory results.
    
    The linked output keeps source file hashes, raw spans, previous alias candidates,
    top model candidates, scores and link states. It has the same article format as
    QC, so `score-signals` can compare before and after linking on the identical
    common reference subset. The resolver never receives publisher reference
    signals. Its output still represents company mentions, not primary-company
    labels.
    
    The alias-aware pilot relinked all 1,135 clean articles. On the same 224
    signal-bearing articles (311 observed article/issuer pairs), descriptive overlap
    F1 changed from 0.631 to 0.352 for spaCy, and from 0.666 to 0.373 for GLiNER
    v2.1. Observed-signal recall was 0.842 for both linked systems; many additional
    predictions lacked observed publisher signals. The incomplete reference cannot
    establish that every such prediction is false. These results do not support
    promoting the default 0.5 acceptance threshold to an automatic enrichment policy.
    The new command remains explicit; the frozen baseline is retained. Reports,
    model provenance and link audits are in `.tmp/company-eval-linked-v2/`.
    `--limit 0` processes all clean inputs; choose a fresh output directory.
    
    `fine-news eval score-signals` reports overlap with the observed publisher ticker
    signals—including uniquely resolved standalone uppercase ticker tags—on
    signal-bearing articles for which every decision model and both NER
    OS page cache.
    
    The independent source sample has 30,000 rows: 9,910 clean, 20,090 quarantined.
    Of the clean rows, 8,267 fall in the fully supported 2016–2025 model catalog;
    1,643 remain outside supported timing coverage. The historical catalog audit

## Assistant

Yes—I think **GLiNER2.5 is worth testing locally**. It could replace much of the expensive broad decision-model pass with a smaller model that extracts company mentions and useful article metadata together. The important question is whether it can do that **accurately enough, and fast enough on our corpus**; we have not measured either yet.

The names refer to different things:

| Item | What it is | Relevance to us |
|---|---|---|
| [`gliner2-base-v1`](https://huggingface.co/fastino/gliner2-base-v1) | The older **span-architecture** model, 205M parameters | A useful baseline for comparison. |
| [`gliner2.5-small-v1`](https://huggingface.co/fastino/gliner2.5-small-v1) | The newer **boundary-architecture** model, 74M parameters | The first speed-focused local candidate I would test. |
| [`gliner2.5-base-v1`](https://huggingface.co/fastino/gliner2.5-base-v1) | The newer boundary architecture, 194M parameters | The stronger English multitask candidate to compare against small. |
| [GLiNER2 v2.1.0](https://github.com/fastino-ai/GLiNER2/releases/tag/v2.1.0) | A **library release**, not a model | It adds inference improvements and support for optimized attention; it did not itself change the model weights. |

**Span versus boundary** describes how the model finds the start and end of an item in the text:

- The older span model considers candidate text spans up to a fixed maximum width and scores them against labels such as `company`.
- The newer boundary model predicts likely **start and end positions**, pairs promising boundaries, and scores those candidates. It can represent a span of any length that fits in its encoded window.

The boundary approach avoids the older fixed-width span grid. That makes the *extraction head* more economical for longer inputs; it does not mean the entire transformer will necessarily scale linearly or that long articles will be cheap on our GPU. [Fastino’s architecture explanation](https://fastino.ai/blog/gliner2-5-span-free-information-extraction) describes the distinction.

The interesting part for CCFinance is that GLiNER2.5 can use **one schema for several tasks on the same encoded text**. For example, we could ask it to return:

- **Company and person mentions**, with character offsets and extraction scores.
- **Mention attributes**, such as whether a company mention appears primary, secondary or incidental.
- **Article-level labels**, such as reporting, opinion, press release or promotional content.
- **Financial entities or events**, such as monetary amounts, dates, earnings announcements or acquisitions.
- **Relations**, such as one extracted company acquiring another.

The “primary/secondary/incidental” labels would be an experiment we define—not an accuracy guarantee. They apply to **individual extracted spans**; we would still need to combine repeated mentions and decide whether a company is a primary subject of the whole article. GLiNER2.5 supports span attributes, classifications, relations and structured records in a combined schema. [Model documentation](https://huggingface.co/fastino/gliner2.5-small-v1)

A schema could look like this:

```python
from gliner2 import AttributeGroup, AutoExtractor

model = AutoExtractor.from_pretrained("fastino/gliner2.5-small-v1")

schema = (
    model.create_schema()
    .entities({
        "company": "Named companies or business organizations",
        "person": "Named people",
        "money": "Monetary amounts",
    })
    .entity_attributes({
        "article_role": AttributeGroup(
            ["primary", "secondary", "incidental"],
            applies_to=["company"],
            qualify_labels=True,
        )
    })
    .classification(
        "article_type",
        ["reporting", "opinion", "press release", "promotional", "other"],
    )
)

result = model.extract(
    article_text,
    schema,
    include_spans=True,
    include_confidence=True,
)
```

That uses the documented API shape; the particular financial labels above are **untested**. We should retain the raw spans and scores and validate them before treating them as research labels. The [v2.1.0 examples](https://github.com/fastino-ai/GLiNER2/blob/v2.1.0/README.md) show entity attributes and combined schemas.

There are two limits that matter for our dataset. First, extracting “Apple” as an organization does **not** establish which issuer it is: we still need to link the span to an article-year CIK/PERMCO, handle ambiguous names, and preserve unresolved cases. We should also audit companies GLiNER finds that our existing catalogue missed, rather than only intersecting its output with Aho–Corasick candidates.

Second, “one pass” applies **per encoded window**. The small checkpoint specifies `max_len=4096`, and its normal extraction method can truncate. Its long-document helpers use overlapping chunks; a span or relation whose necessary endpoints never appear in the same chunk can be missed. That matters for our long transcripts and for article-level primary-subject judgments. [Long-document limitations](https://huggingface.co/fastino/gliner2.5-small-v1)

For our machine, the 74M checkpoint’s stated FP32 weights are approximately **296 MB**, and local CPU and CUDA inference are supported. The RTX 5060 Ti currently has about **4.2 GiB free** while the Kev server occupies GPU memory; weights alone would fit, but batch activations and long windows must be measured. The v2.1 library also offers optional **DisentangledFlash** attention for DeBERTa on supported NVIDIA GPUs, which is a more relevant optimization here than SGLang’s generative-model serving machinery. [Release notes](https://github.com/fastino-ai/GLiNER2/releases/tag/v2.1.0)

I would compare **2.5 small and 2.5 base** on the preserved 1,000-article pilot, then benchmark a larger representative sample for articles per second, memory and chunking. Quality review should cover entity spans, issuer linking, primary-subject labels, generic aliases and CPU-filter exclusions. Our staging repo did test an older, different `urchade/gliner_large-v2.1` checkpoint, but its linking results against incomplete publisher signals were mixed and do not validate these newer models. [Prior experiment](/home/marcussky/Git/fine-news-financial-publishers/src/python/apps/fine_news_cli/docs/company-decisions.md:111)

For scale, processing all 12.24M retained records in 24 hours requires roughly **142 articles/second end to end**, including chunking and writing results. GLiNER may be much faster than the local Kev run, but I would not assume it reaches that rate until we measure it. I haven’t run a GLiNER2.5 benchmark yet; `gliner2` and PyTorch are not installed in this repo’s locked Python environment.

    ---
    name: python-testing
    description: Use when writing, changing, reviewing or organizing Python tests, pytest fixtures or Hypothesis strategies in CCFinance.
    ---
    
    # Python testing
    
    ## Workflow
    
    1. Inspect the code contract, nearby tests, `conftest.py`, shared fixtures and
       strategies, the package's test README, and pytest configuration. Reuse an
       existing test or generator when it covers the behavior; extend it only for a
       distinct, meaningful risk. Do not add tests for trivial or reversible changes
       just to increase counts, or tests that restate implementation details.
    2. Prefer Hypothesis for input variation when a general property is meaningful.
       Prefer a small explicit example for a single known boundary, regression or
       command smoke check. Decide the expected outcome independently of the code
       under test. Use tiny representative data, bounded generators and the smallest
       appropriate test boundary. Assert public behavior, including error contracts.
    3. Place a test beside its source owner under the mirrored `tests/` layout. Reuse
       existing factories and strategies first. Keep a helper local until several
       tests need it; put cross-module strategies in `tests/_strategies.py` and
       shared pytest fixtures in the nearest common `conftest.py`. Place a fixture
       at broader scope only when its state is safe to share. Measure costly setup
       before broadening scope; avoid creating generic fixture frameworks.
    4. Arrange inputs and prerequisites, act on the behavior, and assert observable
       results (AAA). Cleanup belongs in a fixture finalizer or context manager.
       Label each phase with an `# Arrange`, `# Act` or `# Assert` comment, as in
       the example below. Favor DAMP: clear names and visible expected values can
       justify a little repetition.
    5. Give each new or modified test exactly one scope marker from the table below;
       add `slow` or `external` only when applicable. Mark a class or module only
       when every inherited test has the same scope. Never stack or override scope
       markers, including inherited marks. Before using markers, register the six
       names in the owning pytest configuration; unknown names fail under
       `--strict-markers`. This skill defines the policy; it does not mean the
       current unmarked suite already enforces it. Migrate existing tests deliberately
       if adding a collection-time enforcement hook.
    6. During development, run the smallest relevant test or selection and check
       its output. Before handoff run the repository's required full checks, including
       the complete non-Testmon suite. Run any affected slow or external tests when
       their prerequisites and authorization are available; report what was not run
       and why. A targeted pass is not evidence that the full suite passed.
    
    ## Markers
    
    Use only these six custom markers. Built-in pytest mechanisms such as
    `parametrize`, `skipif` and `xfail` remain available for their intended purposes.
    Scope describes the boundary the assertions exercise, not the number of files,
    the use of Hypothesis, or the choice of a reference oracle.
    
    | Marker | Rule |
    | --- | --- |
    | `unit` | Exactly one scope: an isolated operation or small self-contained behavior. |
    | `component` | Exactly one scope: one coherent subsystem or component through its public behavior. |
    | `integration` | Exactly one scope: interactions across components or a real dependency boundary. |
    | `e2e` | Exactly one scope: a complete user-visible workflow through the public CLI or API. A CLI help check alone is not end-to-end. |
    | `slow` | Optional execution label: the complete test, including setup, teardown and generated examples, consistently exceeds two seconds on the normal local environment. Confirm with repeated pytest duration reports; a single noisy measurement is not enough. |
    | `external` | Optional execution label: the test accesses a live network service or external account. Use even if it is usually fast; require explicit opt-in and appropriate credentials. A local temporary file, subprocess or fake alone does not qualify. |
    
    `slow` and `external` are independent and may accompany any one scope. Do not
    invent custom markers for regression, reference, property, smoke, tools or
    implementation techniques; communicate those in descriptive test names and
    assertions. Run fast local iteration with `-m "not slow and not external"`
    after the markers are registered. Full checks must not silently omit slow tests;
    external tests need a separate explicit lane and must not mutate live services
    without authorization.
    
    ## Hypothesis examples and fixtures
    
    Hypothesis strategies generate values; pytest fixtures manage resources. If
    Hypothesis is absent, add it to the locked workspace development dependencies
    when introducing the first test that uses it. Search
    for reusable strategies or an appropriate first-party Hypothesis extra before
    adding one. Compose built-in strategies, use `@composite` for dependent values,
    and generate valid inputs directly rather than filtering most examples. Keep
    sizes bounded and counterexamples understandable. Preserve an important known
    failure using `@example` or an explicit regression; do not duplicate a property
    with a long list of examples that establish the same behavior.
    
    A function-scoped pytest fixture runs once per test function, not once per
    `@given` example. For per-example mutable resources, create and clean them inside
    the test, for example with `TemporaryDirectory()`. Reuse immutable shared data
    only when safe. Do not suppress health checks or disable deadlines globally to
    make a test pass; investigate the cause and document a narrowly justified
    exception. Choose explicit settings or a shared profile only when warranted by
    measured cost. Preserve failing examples and replay information as appropriate.
    
    This self-contained example illustrates a small property, AAA and the scope
    marker; it uses the standard-library URL parser rather than a CCFinance stage:
    
    ```python
    from string import ascii_lowercase, digits
    from urllib.parse import urlsplit
    
    import pytest
    from hypothesis import example, given, strategies as st
    
    
    @pytest.mark.unit
    @example(host="news")
    @given(host=st.text(alphabet=ascii_lowercase + digits, min_size=1, max_size=20))
    def test_url_hostname_normalizes_ascii_case(host: str) -> None:
        # Arrange: build a URL with an uppercase hostname.
        url = f"https://{host.upper()}.example/article"
    
        # Act: extract the hostname.
        hostname = urlsplit(url).hostname
    
        # Assert: the hostname is lowercase.
        assert hostname == f"{host}.example"
    ```
    
    Use a real local Parquet or filesystem boundary for a small integration test
    when that interaction matters; use a stub or fake for costly or nondeterministic
    remote services. A fake cannot establish that the real service works. Keep
    randomized tests independent of execution order; for numerical or sampling
    claims define tolerances and uncertainty rather than requiring arbitrary
    bit-for-bit agreement across environments.
    
    Consult the Hypothesis [tutorial](https://hypothesis.readthedocs.io/en/latest/tutorial/),
    [how-to guides](https://hypothesis.readthedocs.io/en/latest/how-to/),
    [strategies and API reference](https://hypothesis.readthedocs.io/en/latest/reference/)
    and [extras](https://hypothesis.readthedocs.io/en/latest/extras.html) when
    choosing or debugging a strategy.

    name: architecture-layout
    description: Use when evaluating or designing where CCFinance code, data stages, tests, documents or infrastructure belong, including module boundaries and repository restructures.
    ---
    
    # Architecture layout
    
    ## Workflow
    
    1. Establish the requested scope and outcome: evaluate the current layout,
       design a layout, or implement an authorized change. Read nearby README and
       ARCHITECTURE files. Identify existing owners and consumers before proposing
       a new abstraction; reuse an existing module or library when it satisfies the
       contract. File size alone is not a reason to split or create a package.
    2. Examine the relevant boundaries using evidence:
       - **Ownership and cohesion:** Can a contributor find the owner, and do things
         that change together live together? Keep each unit's responsibility clear.
       - **Dependencies and encapsulation:** Trace relevant imports and public
         interfaces. Keep intended dependency direction clear and cycles forbidden;
         avoid reaching into another module's internals without a reason.
       - **Coupling:** Identify changes that force unrelated owners to change.
         Share a contract only when consumers actually need the same behavior; a
         little local duplication may be preferable to coupling distinct contracts.
       - **Discoverability:** Make CLI commands, transformations, schemas, tests,
         fixtures and documents easy to find from their owning area.
    3. Choose the smallest useful boundary: a function, module, package or separate
       workspace project. A package or project should reflect an actual dependency,
       distribution, build or ownership need. Organize by layer, capability or a
       combination according to the work; do not impose a universal directory tree.
    4. For pipeline work, preserve the established `raw`, `processed` and `research`
       stage ownership. Organize capabilities within those layers as they arise.
       Distinguish Python imports from DVC artifact dependencies: the latter connect
       producers and consumers without requiring cross-layer Python imports. Apply
       Tach rules to durable module boundaries and DVC to artifact dependencies.
    5. For a move or split, trace the affected consumers before changing paths:
       imports and public APIs, CLI registration, package configuration, tests and
       fixtures, Tach, DVC and Semflow dependencies, and documentation links as
       applicable. Preserve behavior and scientific contracts unless the user asks
       for a change; report any intended behavior change separately. Do not treat
       missing static references as proof that dynamic or external consumers do not
       exist.
    6. Use the repository's existing gates rather than adding tests that merely
       assert a directory tree or private call sequence. For tests and fixtures,
       follow [Python testing](../python-testing/SKILL.md). Run focused checks while
       working and `just check` before handoff; report checks that could not run.
    
    ## Results
    
    For an evaluation, report concrete findings with locations, effects and ranked
    recommendations. For a design, show the proposed ownership and dependency
    boundaries, explain meaningful tradeoffs and how they are enforced. For an
    implementation, summarize what moved, whether behavior changed and the evidence
    from verification. Keep the review proportional to the requested change.
    
    For example, if both article cleaning and company linking need the same
    publication-date parser, first inspect its existing owner and date semantics.
    Share it only if both consumers require the same contract; keep separate rules
    when their treatment of missing or ambiguous dates differs.

    ## Company decisions
    
    The selected rubric asks three binary questions per resolved company, using its
    canonical name and tickers: whether the article mentions it, provides meaningful
    company-specific information beyond a mention, and treats it as a main subject.
    Several companies may be primary. The manifest records the exact question
    templates and article-kind criteria. The current runtime is Kev-4B in BF16.
    Production uses the separate `kev-4b-low-memory.json` profile. It retains the
    same model and 8,192-token admission while reducing GPU graph buffers. A fixed
    16-request parity check preserved all tested 0.5 and 0.95 threshold decisions;
    the original corrected pilot retains its original runtime profile.
    
    `identity_score`, `substantive_score` and `raw_primary_score` preserve independent
    model outputs. `coverage_score` is their substantive/primary maximum: a ranking
    rule rather than a calibrated union probability. Contradictory marginals retain
    consistency flags. `primary_score` is available only after identity meets the
    configured cutoff. A provisional accepted pair requires confident identity and
    coverage without a strong coverage contradiction. Article kind does not gate it.
    Saved outputs support later threshold comparisons without rerunning inference.
    
    ## Native inference and checkpoints
    
    [Native Kev](../../../infra/inference/README.md) runs in a separate pinned GPU
    runtime. Pydantic's System One client shares each article across company questions
    in one request. Exact repeated company descriptors share questions while retaining
    all namespace-specific links. Large candidate sets use bounded requests.
    Article kind is an annotation, rather than an automatic editorial-content gate.
    
    The runtime profile records model revisions, checkpoint hashes, precision,
    kernels and context admission. Oversized documents are explicitly deferred;
    silent text truncation is disabled. Prediction manifests preserve the scorer and
    runtime contract. A changed scientific contract requires a new output directory.
    Operational deadlines, transport timeouts and concurrency can change on resume.
    Pass `--source data/raw/fine-news` to override archived absolute source locations.

    source metadata, candidate provenance and raw model outputs. Successful identical
