    # Local company-extraction benchmark
    
    The 74M-parameter GLiNER2.5 small checkpoint exceeded the computational target
    on the source-verified 10,000-record sample. Three repetitions averaged
    **162.8 records/second**, projecting **20.9 hours of extraction** for the
    12,241,870 retained records. This is a runtime projection, not a completed
    population-labeling run or a validated accuracy result.
    
    ## Selected configuration
    
    | Setting | Value |
    | --- | --- |
    | GPU | NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5060 Ti, 16 GiB class, CUDA capability 12.0 |
    | Driver | 595.71.05 |
    | Runtime | Pinned CUDA 13 container, PyTorch 2.14.1, GLiNER2 2.1.0 |
    | Checkpoint | `fastino/gliner2.5-small-v1`, pinned revision in `manifest.json` |
    | Precision | FP16; all 334 parameter tensors verified on `cuda:0` |
    | Encoder | DisentangledFlash 1.1.0 |
    | Extraction heads | Compiled separately from the prepared encoder |
    | Role scoring | Batched across the exact spans selected by GLiNER's decoder |
    | GPU batch | 128 windows |
    | Article buffer | 8,192 records; four preprocessing workers |
    | Windows | 384 GLiNER word tokens, 64-token overlap |
    | Peak PyTorch reserved CUDA memory | 7.50 GiB; driver allocations are separate |
    
    | Repetition | Records | Timed seconds | Records/second |
    | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
    | 1 | 10,000 | 61.088 | 163.699 |
    | 2 | 10,000 | 61.614 | 162.301 |
    | 3 | 10,000 | 61.530 | 162.523 |
    
    The aggregate rate divides 30,000 completed records by the sum of timed
    durations. The required rate is 138.89/second for 12 million records, or
    141.69/second for the current retained population. The observed range is
    repeat variation on one sample, not a population confidence interval.
    
    Timing includes tokenization, worker preprocessing, inference, role scoring,
    window merging, source-offset checks and compressed prediction output. Sample
    loading, model loading and warmup are recorded separately in each run's JSON.
    Sparse source reconstruction, model downloads, downstream issuer linking and
    semantic validation are outside this timed workload.
    
    ## Sampling and provenance
    
    The 10,000 retained source rows were selected by SHA-256 priority using seed 43.
    Every original article body was checked against its stored SHA-256 digest.
    `sample/selection.parquet`, its adjacent manifests and `metrics.json` preserve
    membership and checksums. The existing 1,000-record Kev pilot uses seed 42 and
    is preserved separately. Source article bodies are not copied into this artifact.
    
    Early screening used a second deterministic 500-record subset. Later paired
    optimization used the first 2,000 source-ordered rows of the 10,000-record
    sample; that prefix has shorter articles on average. Absolute screening rates
    therefore must not be substituted for the full-sample rate.
    
    The pinned image, model revisions, weight digests and code digests are in
    `manifest.json`. Run configurations, timings, predictions, logs, compatibility
    probes and source snapshots are retained with the artifact. `throughput.csv`
    indexes 37 timed configurations. Historical launchers are archived under
    `code/historical-launchers/`; current commands are documented in the
    [inference guide](../../../../../infra/inference/README.md).
    
    ## Optimization evidence
    
    These configurations used the same 2,000-record prefix and 64-window GPU batch:
    
    | Configuration | Records/second |
    | --- | ---: |
    | FP16, compiled encoder and heads, buffered input, no workers | 78.1 |
    | Same, four preprocessing workers | 94.7 |
    | FP16, DisentangledFlash, four workers | 109.6 |
    | FP16, DisentangledFlash and compiled heads, four workers | 144.7 |
    | BF16, DisentangledFlash and compiled heads, four workers | 142.8 |
    | Dynamic FP8 encoder projections, compiled standard encoder | 108.1 |
    | Dynamic NVFP4 encoder projections, compiled standard encoder | 81.0 |
    
    The FP8 and NVFP4 CUDA probes both passed. Their model trials retained BF16
    embeddings, heads and other operations; they were not fully low-precision
    models. Those paths changed outputs more and were slower than the hybrid
    FP16 path in this experiment. This does not establish a general ranking of
    precision formats or all possible kernel implementations.
    
    On the complete sample, the buffered FP16 hybrid initially reached
    117.8/second. Batching the role-head work raised the measured rate to
    162.3–163.7/second while retaining the original 384-token windows. Wider
    512- and 768-token windows reached 129.1 and 132.0/second without batched
    role scoring; neither was selected. Their context and outputs differ.
    
    ## Structural and numerical checks
    
    All three final runs passed finite-confidence, label and source-span checks.
    Each run retained 15 explicit synthetic-suffix corrections. The first and third
    runs produced identical prediction contents across all 10,000 records.
    
    Three local compatibility patches are preserved: CUDA-safe indexing of CPU
    attribute logits, removal of synthetic terminal punctuation from source spans,
    and an optional hook for batched role scoring. Fresh package installation and
    CPU/CUDA regression checks passed with the patches applied.
    
    Against the saved unbatched full-sample run, all 179,257 company spans and all
    10,000 article-type labels matched. There were 346 role-label changes, or
    0.19% of spans, with maximum top-role confidence difference 0.00367. In the
    separate FP32 parity check, all 1,714 spans, roles and article types matched;
    maximum top-role confidence difference was 0.00000483. These checks support
    numerical consistency, not semantic accuracy.
    
    ## Label quality and interpretation
    
    The model has not been validated as a replacement for Kev or as research labels.
    Diagnostic examples include the place “Manila” and the person “Rodrigo Duterte”
    classified as companies. These selected examples are AI observations, not an
    estimated error rate. Company names still need dated issuer linking, and scores
    need evaluation against a human-reviewed reference set.
    
    For the optimized 1,000-record pilot, 109 articles had at least one unresolved
    Kev candidate and were excluded from the descriptive comparison below. Among
    the remaining 891 articles, exact NFKC/casefold matching of extracted names to
    supported candidate aliases gave:
    
    | | Exact candidate alias found | No exact candidate alias |
    | --- | ---: | ---: |
    | Kev mention score at least 0.5 | 256 | 43 |
    | Kev mention score below 0.5 | 43 | 549 |
    
    Kev is not ground truth. Exact alias matching can miss valid variants or retain
    ambiguous words, and GLiNER also extracts companies outside the candidate
    universe. The pilot comparison therefore establishes neither precision nor
    recall. Its raw counts are preserved in the optimized pilot's JSON report.
    
    Roles describe extracted mentions within windows. For long articles, GLiNER
    selects the highest-confidence window's article-type label. Neither output is
    a calibrated whole-article probability that a linked company is the primary
    subject. Computational feasibility is established for the measured workload;
    semantic validation and production pipeline integration remain separate work.

## User

SO what is the optimal fast attention method, quant-level, batch size etc for this?

## Assistant

The **fastest configuration we validated** was:

| Component | Setting |
|---|---|
| Model | GLiNER2.5 Small, **74M parameters** |
| Attention | **DisentangledFlash 1.1.0**, automatic packed/unpadded execution |
| Precision | **FP16**, without low-bit quantization |
| Compilation | `torch.compile` on **extraction heads only** |
| Attribute scoring | **Batched GPU scoring** using our optional patch |
| GPU batch size | **128 windows** |
| Input buffer | **8,192 articles** |
| Preprocessing | **4 workers** |
| Long articles | **384-word windows**, overlapping by **64 words** |

This achieved **162.8 articles/sec** across three full-sample runs, with **7.5 GiB peak PyTorch-reserved GPU memory**.

BF16 performed similarly on the smaller comparison. FP8 and NVFP4 were slower in the tested implementations and changed predictions more. The biggest gains came from **buffered preprocessing, optimized attention, and batching role scoring**.

I’d use this FP16 configuration as our baseline. It establishes throughput feasibility; the company and primary-subject labels still need semantic validation.

    ## Common options
    
    - `--format` — Output format: `--format json` (or `--json`) or `--format table` (default).
    - `-q / --quiet` — Quiet output (one ID per line).
    - `--revision` — Git revision id which can be a branch name, a tag, or a commit hash.
    - `--token` — Use a User Access Token. Prefer setting `HF_TOKEN` env var instead of passing `--token`.
    - `--type` — The type of repository (model, dataset, or space).
    
    ## Mounting repos as local filesystems
    
    To mount Hub repositories or buckets as local filesystems — no download, no copy, no waiting — use `hf-mount`. Files are fetched on demand. GitHub: https://github.com/huggingface/hf-mount
    
    Install: `brew install hf-mount`, or download a binary from https://github.com/huggingface/hf-mount/releases
    
    Some command examples:
    - `hf-mount start repo openai-community/gpt2 /tmp/gpt2` — mount a repo (read-only)
    - `hf-mount start --hf-token $HF_TOKEN bucket myuser/my-bucket /tmp/data` — mount a bucket (read-write)
    - `hf-mount status` / `hf-mount stop /tmp/data` — list or unmount
    
    ## Tips
    
    - Use `hf <command> --help` for full options, descriptions, usage, and real-world examples
    - Authenticate with `HF_TOKEN` env var (recommended) or with `--token`
    - Update the CLI with `hf update` (uses the correct command for the detected install method)

    In **Appendix A, Table 5** of <Link url="https://arxiv.org/html/2410.23447v3#Sx1" title="Systematic Covariance Envelopes from Wasserstein Geometry"/>, the authors compare their Nasdaq-hosted financial-news dataset against **four other financial-news datasets**.
    
    | Dataset | Reference | Coverage |
    |---|---|---|
    | **RavenPack Equity – Dow Jones Edition** | Ge et al. (2023) | Large proprietary archive; 2004–2015 in the cited study |
    | **Thomson Reuters News Analytics (TRNA)** | Scherbina & Schlusche (2013) | Approximately 5.5 million stories, 1996–2012 |
    | **Raw Reuters financial-news corpus (Ding et al. corpus)** | Schwenkler & Zheng (2020) | 106,521 full-text articles, 2006–2013 |
    | **RESET Financial Text Intelligent Analysis Platform + Juyuan** | Ge et al. (2026) | 1,138,247 relevant Chinese financial-news articles, 2006–2021 |
    
    <Cite refs={["turn302746view1"]}/>
    
    ### How they compare
    
    The authors evaluate these datasets along six dimensions: geographical/language coverage, availability of full article text, entity annotations, scale, accessibility/reproducibility, and researcher control over text processing.
    
    Their own dataset is the **Nasdaq-hosted public per-symbol news archive**, which provides full article bodies and permits independent embedding and text processing. Its main limitation is narrower, coverage-conditioned sampling compared with proprietary archives.
    
    ### One additional dataset worth noting
    
    Appendix A also discusses the **Hoberg–Phillips ETNIC-All product-market similarity dataset** (Hoberg & Phillips, 2016; 2025). This is not one of the four news-corpus comparisons in Table 5, but it is used as an empirical benchmark.
    
    ETNIC measures firm similarity from 10-K business descriptions using doc2vec embeddings. The authors compare it with their news-embedding Wasserstein distances for 81 firms. <Cite refs={["turn302746view2"]}/>
    
    **Source:** <Link url="https://arxiv.org/html/2410.23447v3" title="Paper HTML, Appendix A, Table 5"/>. Note that this is version 3, revised November 5, 2026.

    ### **You** · Mon 16 Nov, 11:11
    
    What metadata do these datasets contain?
    
    ---
    
    ### **ChatGPT** · Mon 16 Nov, 11:11
    
    <small><strong>Reasoning / progress:</strong><br>
    I’ll distinguish metadata documented for each dataset from fields that may be available only in particular versions or licensing arrangements.</small>
    
    The datasets differ substantially in the **article-level metadata** they provide, particularly company identifiers, timestamps, sentiment scores, event classifications, and entity mentions.
    
    The key distinction is that **RavenPack and Thomson Reuters News Analytics provide structured, vendor-generated metadata**, whereas the raw Reuters and Nasdaq datasets offer greater control over the article text but fewer precomputed annotations.
    
    ## 1. Metadata comparison
    
    The paper's Appendix A, Table 5, confirms which datasets have entity annotations and full text, but it does **not** provide exhaustive field-level schemas. The comparison below therefore distinguishes documented features from metadata that depends on the particular dataset version or processing pipeline. <Cite ref="turn287435view0"/>
    
    | Dataset | Article metadata | Entity metadata | Analytical metadata | Full text |
    |---|---|---|---|---|
    | **RavenPack Equity – Dow Jones** | Timestamp, story ID, source | Company ID, ticker/ISIN mappings | Sentiment, relevance, event category, novelty | No, in standard analytics files |
    | **Thomson Reuters News Analytics (TRNA)** | Timestamp, story ID, source | Company identifiers, firm mentions | Sentiment, relevance, novelty, volume measures | Requires companion archive |
    | **Raw Reuters (Ding et al.)** | Article text and associated records; exact fields vary | Automatically extracted company mentions | Derived co-mentions and network relationships | Yes |
    | **RESET + Juyuan** | Financial news records; exact schema not established | Chinese listed-company mentions | Text-derived firm relationships | Partial, licence-dependent |
    | **Nasdaq archive (authors' dataset)** | Article date, URL/identifier, ticker association | Source-level ticker association | Researcher-generated embeddings and distances | Yes |
    
    These are not all equivalent types of metadata: the sentiment and event scores in commercial analytics products are typically vendor-produced, while the embeddings and network measurements in the research datasets are created by researchers.
    
    ## 2. Detailed metadata by dataset
    
    ### RavenPack Equity – Dow Jones Edition
    
    RavenPack is especially rich in **company-level and event-level metadata**. Documented fields in RavenPack analytics products include:
    
    - **Identification:** story ID, timestamp, company name, company identifier, ticker, ISIN, source.
    - **Entity relevance:** how strongly a story concerns a particular company.
    - **Sentiment:** event sentiment and composite sentiment scores.
    - **Event classification:** event category or taxonomy, such as earnings or corporate developments.
    - **Novelty:** whether similar information has appeared previously.
    - **Other analytics:** story-event counts and related measures.
    
    An academic description of RavenPack News Analytics 3.0 reports 39 fields for the Global Equities edition. The exact schema depends on the product version. <Cite refs={["turn983798search14","turn983798search0"]}/>
    
    ### Thomson Reuters News Analytics (TRNA)
    
    TRNA is also highly structured. Historical documentation describes more than 80 metadata fields, including:
    
    - **Identification:** item ID, timestamp, Reuters instrument code (RIC), source, feed.
    - **Entity information:** companies mentioned, number of companies, first-mention position.
    - **Sentiment:** positive, negative and neutral probabilities.
    - **Relevance:** a numerical company-specific relevance score.
    - **Novelty:** counts and links to similar previous stories across several lookback windows.
    - **Topics:** subject categories, broker actions and market commentary classifications.
    - **Volume and structure:** news intensity, word counts, sentence counts, story type.
    
    Importantly, TRNA can generate **different relevance and sentiment metadata for different companies mentioned in the same article**. <Cite refs={["turn657501search1","turn657501search39","turn657501search37"]}/>
    
    ### Raw Reuters financial-news corpus
    
    The appendix confirms that this corpus contains full article text and was processed using automated named-entity recognition (NER).
    
    This makes it possible to derive company mentions, co-mentions, sentence-level relationships and news networks.
    
    However, the appendix does **not** establish a complete original-record schema for timestamps, article IDs, publisher fields or entity identifiers. Those should be checked against the historical corpus documentation rather than assumed to be available as standardized columns. <Cite ref="turn287435view1"/>
    
    ### RESET + Juyuan
    
    The documented relevant features are Chinese financial-news text and company mentions, used to infer financial relationships among China A-share firms.
    
    The exact company-annotation pipeline, field names and availability of full-text exports are not established in the appendix. In particular, I would not assume that it supplies standardized sentiment, relevance or event-category fields without inspecting the licensed product documentation. <Cite ref="turn287435view1"/>
    
    ### Nasdaq news archive
    
    For the authors' own dataset, the paper confirms:
    
    - Article identifiers used for deduplication.
    - Article dates for window filtering.
    - URLs used for deterministic sampling.
    - Full article bodies.
    - Source-level ticker associations, rather than manually validated article-level entity annotations.
    - Firm names and sector labels obtained from separate Nasdaq summary metadata.
    
    The authors subsequently calculate document embeddings and firm-pair distances. Those are **derived research variables**, not metadata supplied by Nasdaq. <Cite ref="turn287435view2"/>
    
    ## 3. Additional comparison: Hoberg–Phillips ETNIC-All
    
    This dataset is structurally different because its unit of observation is a **firm pair in a given year**, rather than a news article.
    
    Its principal information is firm identification, year and an embeddings-based product-market similarity score. ETNIC-All includes similarity measures for all firm pairs, not just close competitors. <Cite ref="turn657501search0"/>
    
    ## Which dataset is most useful?
    
    For research requiring **timestamped, company-specific news with ready-made sentiment and event metadata**, RavenPack and TRNA are the strongest of these options.
    
    For research requiring **raw text, custom entity extraction or independently generated embeddings**, the raw Reuters corpus and the Nasdaq archive are more suitable, subject to accessibility and coverage limitations.
    
    One particularly important distinction for constructing firm networks is whether a dataset identifies **every company mentioned in an article**, rather than merely associating the article with one primary ticker. The former is much more useful for building reliable co-mention networks, while the latter may require a separate NER pipeline.

    ## 2. Thomson Reuters News Analytics: Topic codes
    
    Reuters uses a predefined set of codes, but unlike RavenPack's event hierarchy, the taxonomy mixes several kinds of classification.
    
    Here are examples documented in the Reuters taxonomy and historical TRNA materials:
    
    | Code | Classification | Meaning |
    |---|---|---|
    | `MRG` | Mergers & acquisitions | Takeovers, mergers, acquisitions |
    | `RES` | Results | Corporate financial results |
    | `RESF` | Results forecast | Forecast financial results |
    | `DIV` | Dividends | Dividend announcements and forecasts |
    | `IPO` | Initial public offerings | New public stock offerings |
    | `ISU` | New issues | New debt or equity issuance |
    | `RCH` | Research | Research-related coverage |
    | `JOB` | Labour/personnel | Employment and labour issues |
    | `AAA` | Credit/debt ratings | Creditworthiness assessments |
    | `CEN` | Central banks | Central-bank activity |
    | `ECI` | Economic indicators | Economic data releases |
    | `GDP` | Economic output | GDP and GNP data |
    | `INT` | Interest rates/policy | Central-bank rate policy |
    | `ESG` | ESG | Environmental, social and governance issues |
    | `TECH` | Technology | Broad technology subject |
    | `SOFW` | Software | Technology subcategory |
    
    <Cite refs={["turn572709search21","turn572709search23","turn572709search0"]}/>
    
    A few important characteristics:
    
    - **Multi-label:** One news article can have several topic codes.
    - **Hierarchical:** Some codes have parent–child relationships, such as `TECH` and `SOFW`.
    - **Not exclusively events:** Codes can represent industries, asset classes, geographic regions or economic subjects.

    ---
    name: Search
    description: "Deep research powered by Exa. Use for lead generation, literature reviews, deep dives, competitive analysis, or any query where one search falls short, including phrases like 'research this', 'find everything about', 'find me all', or 'deep dive on'."
    ---
    
    # Exa Search And Research
    
    Use Exa to search the web and fetch source pages when the user needs current web information, research support, source discovery, or source-grounded synthesis. Understand the query, plan the searches, validate results, and deliver a compact answer with useful links.
    
    This skill uses the bundled Exa app tools:
    - `web_search_exa` for web search
    - `web_fetch_exa` for reading known URLs
    
    ## Prerequisites: Exa App Connection
    
    The bundled Exa app must be connected before this skill can use Exa tools.
    
    If `web_search_exa` or `web_fetch_exa` is unavailable:
    1. Ask the user to connect or re-authenticate the Exa app from the plugin/app install flow.
    2. Tell them to start a new Codex thread if the tools still do not appear after connecting.
    3. Do not fall back to generic web search, ask the user to re-try connecting to the Exa App.
    
    On auth, connection, or rate-limit errors, surface the Exa app connection fix clearly.
    
    ## Date Calculation (Do This First)
    
    If the query involves time ("last week", "recent", "past 6 months"), calculate exact dates from today's date in your environment context. Write out the calculation explicitly before doing anything else. Never eyeball dates or reuse dates from examples.
    
    ## Step 1: Assess the Query
    
    Read the user's query and determine two things:
    
    **How complex is this?**
    - **Extremely Simple** (e.g. reading the contents of 1-2 pages): Handle it yourself. Read `references/searching.md` for query-writing guidance, run the searches, review and filter results, then respond directly.
    - **Moderate** (when a fast or low-effort search is requested): Run a small set of targeted searches and fetch only the most useful pages.
    - **Advanced** (clear topic, clear filters, a few parallel searches): Break the task into distinct search angles, search each angle, then compile.
    - **Complex** (cross-referencing across entity types, multi-hop chains, exhaustive coverage, semantic filtering): Use a multi-pass workflow where later searches depend on earlier findings.
    
    **Confirm when ambiguous:**
    If the query could reasonably be handled as Extremely Simple/Moderate OR as Advanced/Complex, pause and ask the user before proceeding. Present:
    1. Your interpretation of the query
    2. The two (or more) plausible complexity levels
    3. What each level would look like in practice (e.g., "I can do a quick 1-2 search lookup, or I can do a deeper multi-angle sweep")
    4. Let the user choose
    
    Examples of ambiguous queries:
    - "What are the best LLM fine-tuning frameworks?" — could be a quick opinionated list (Moderate) or an exhaustive evaluated comparison (Complex)
    - "Find competitors to Acme Corp" — could be a quick search for known competitors (Moderate) or a deep sweep across funding databases, press, and niche directories (Complex)
    - "What's the latest on WebGPU?" — could be one news search (Extremely Simple) or a multi-angle survey of specs, browser support, community adoption, and benchmarks (Advanced)
    
    Do NOT ask for confirmation when:
    - The query is clearly extremely simple (fact lookups, single-entity questions)
    - The query is clearly complex (explicit multi-constraint, "find everything", "exhaustive", "comprehensive")
    - The user has already specified depth ("do a deep dive", "quick answer")
    
    Note: if the user explicitly asks for something (e.g. "100" of something), continue to work until you've achieved it.
    
    **What work needs to happen?** Identify which of these apply (most queries use 3-5):
    
    1. **Seed from user input**: The user provided a list of entities to start from (company names, tickers, paper titles). Each seed becomes a parallel workstream.
    2. **Define what qualifies**: What makes a result a valid "row"? Translate the user's criteria into concrete checks.
    3. **Define what to capture**: What fields ("columns") does each result need? Build the schema before searching.
    4. **Search broadly**: Generate diverse queries and run them to find candidates.
    5. **Extract structured data**: Pull specific fields from raw search results into the schema.
    6. **Filter**: Apply hard constraints (dates, geography, thresholds) and soft judgments (quality, relevance, semantic checks).
    7. **Merge and deduplicate**: Combine results from multiple searches. Same URL = drop duplicate. Same entity from different sources = merge fields, keep best data.
    8. **Score and rank**: For "best of" (e.g. "what's the best ___?") queries, define the scoring criteria explicitly, then rank.
    9. **Synthesize narrative**: For research queries, organize findings by theme and write prose with citations.
    
    ## Step 2: Run Search Workstreams
    
    ### What workstreams do
    
    Search workstreams keep the investigation organized. Each workstream should:
    - Read the reference file(s) you point it to
    - Run the specific searches you assign
    - Return compact, structured output
    
    Use Codex subagents only when the user explicitly asks for parallel agent work or when the active Codex instructions allow delegation. Otherwise, run the workstreams yourself with direct Exa calls.
    
    For each workstream, define:
    1. Which reference file(s) to read for instructions (always include the absolute path)
    2. What specific searches to run or what specific work to do
    3. What output format to return
    
    **Template:**
    ```
    Read the file at [this skill's directory]/references/searching.md for instructions on how to query Exa effectively.
    
    Then do the following:
    [specific task description]
    [specific queries to run, if you are prescribing them]
    [validation criteria -- what makes a result qualify, so irrelevant results are filtered before returning]
    
    Return: [output format -- e.g. "compact JSON with name, url, snippet per result" or "markdown table with columns X, Y, Z"].
    
    Track `sources_reviewed: N` where N = sum of `numResults` across every `web_search_exa` call (including retries). For example, calls with numResults 10, 10, 5 -> `sources_reviewed: 25`.
    ```
    
    ### Which reference files to use
    
    Always use `references/searching.md`. It contains Exa query guidance and an index of domain-specific pattern files to select from based on the task.
    
    Use whichever of these also apply:
    
    | File | Use this when... |
    |---|---|
    | `references/extraction.md` | You need to extract specific data points into a schema you defined |
    | `references/filtering.md` | You need to evaluate results against criteria (especially semantic/soft filters) |
    | `references/synthesis.md` | You are producing a prose synthesis rather than structured data |
    | `references/source-quality.md` | You need to assess source credibility, especially for "best of", ranking, or expert-finding queries |
    
    ### How to split work
    
    Decompose the primary task/question into **sub-questions** to cover different search territories.
    
    For example, "best open-source LLM fine-tuning frameworks for production use" can be decomposed into multiple parallel sub-questions:
    1. "What open-source LLM fine-tuning frameworks do production engineers recommend, and what do they say about using them in real deployments?"
    2. "What open-source LLM fine-tuning tools have launched or gained traction in the last 6 months that aren't yet widely known?"
    3. "What are the most common complaints, failure modes, and reasons teams migrated away from specific open-source LLM fine-tuning frameworks in production?"
    
    Depending on your "**How complex is this?**" analysis: Some need 2-3; some need many. Some need several different angles, creative thought patterns, adversarial perspectives. It depends on what the user is asking for and how deep they want you to go.
    
    Keep each sub-question direct and specific.
    
    ### Workstream sizing
    
    - Aim for 3-5 searches per workstream.
    - Keep independent workstreams separate in your notes so their results are easy to merge.
    - For per-seed work (enriching a list of 20 companies), batch 3-5 seeds per workstream.
    
    ### Token isolation
    
    Avoid dumping raw search output into the final answer. Process results and return only distilled output with links.
    
    ### When things go wrong
    
    - **A workstream returns empty**: Rephrase queries with different angles, not synonyms. If still empty, the topic may have limited web coverage -- report that.
    - **A workstream returns off-topic results**: Queries were too vague. Retry with longer, more specific queries.
    
    ## Step 3: Compile Results
    
    After search workstreams return:
    
    **Deduplicate:**
    1. Collect all results into a single list
    2. Remove exact URL duplicates
    3. Same entity from different sources: merge fields, keep the most complete/recent data
    4. Track: "Deduplicated X results down to Y unique entries"
    
    **Validate coverage:**
    - Are there obvious gaps? (missing time periods, missing geographic regions, missing entity types)
    - For each gap found, run targeted follow-up searches.
    - For "find everything" queries, check if results from different workstreams overlap heavily (good sign) or are completely disjoint (may indicate missed angles)
    
    **Format the output:**
    
    For deeper research, open with: "I used Exa to review {X} sources across {Y} search workstreams. Here's what was found:" (X = sum of `sources_reviewed` across all workstreams and passes plus any direct searches you ran; Y = total workstreams. Pluralize naturally.)
    
    Then: Format output beautifully, filling up no more than one screen when possible. Include hyperlinked text where relevant. Below it, you may also include things (in a short, easy-to-read format) that:
    - ("Result") directly answer the original user request (in few words; make every word count)
    - ("Process") include anything worth noting about your process and what you consider to be high-signal in this domain vs. what you filtered out.
    - ("Patterns") any patterns identified that are non-obvious, require n-th order thinking, and are not included or alluded to in the rest of the output but might be interesting to the user.
    - ("Notes") based on everything you know about the user and their work beyond this task, mention anything notable/useful you found that is not included or alluded to in the rest of the output.
    
    If it's impossible to fit the full output in a single screen, write a file in the most relevant/useful file format (.csv, .md) to `./exa-results/<topic>-<YYYY-MM-DD>` and include a pointer to the full file below the 1-screen output.
    
    **General output rules:**
    - No emojis unless the user requested them
    - Include in-line 1-word or multi-word hyperlinks throughout outputs where hyperlinking is a value-add.
    - Prefer tables over lists (fall back to lists only when fields are non-uniform or values are too long to fit cleanly)
    
    ## Multi-Pass Queries
    
    Some queries require multiple sequential passes where later passes depend on earlier results. Common patterns:
    
    **Entity chaining** (multi-hop): Pass 1 finds entities (companies), Pass 2 finds related entities per result (people at those companies), Pass 3 enriches those (their public statements). Each pass is a round of focused workstreams.
    
    **Exploratory then targeted**: Pass 1 scouts the landscape broadly, Pass 2 searches deeply in the most promising directions found in Pass 1.
    
    **Criteria discovery**: When "best" isn't predefined, Pass 1 surveys what practitioners actually value, Pass 2 searches for candidates matching those criteria.
    
    Between passes, compile and deduplicate before dispatching the next round.
    
    ## Evaluating Source Quality
    
    Source quality matters most for "best of", ranking, expert-finding, and best-practices queries, but is useful context for almost any research task.
    
    **At the workstream level:** Use `references/source-quality.md` so source quality is tagged in the output. This lets you weight results during compilation.
    
    **At the orchestrator level**, when compiling search results:
    
    1. **Convergence across high-signal sources**: Convergence alone isn't meaningful (3 low-quality sources agreeing is just shared noise). What matters is when multiple independent, high-signal sources (practitioners, people with skin in the game) converge on the same finding.
    2. **Practitioner vs commentator**: Weight practitioners (people doing the work) higher than commentators (people writing about the work).
    3. **Via negativa**: Before synthesizing, define who to exclude (sources with misaligned incentives, no skin in the game, or unfalsifiable claims). Filtering out noise is more valuable than seeking brilliance.
    4. **Red-team your compiled results**: What perspectives are missing? What biases might be distorting the aggregate? If a gap emerges, run a targeted follow-up.
    5. **Ideas over entities**: For expert-finding and best-practices queries, the primary output is convergent truths, not a ranked list of names. Lead with what the best sources agree on, then cite who said it.
    
    ## Gotchas
    
    - **Over-execution on simple queries**: If the user asks "what year was X founded", don't spin up a broad research process. One search, one answer.
    - **Under-execution on hard queries**: If the query has 4+ constraints, temporal joins, or semantic filtering, a single search will not cut it. Fan out.
    - **Synonym queries**: Running "overrated AI tools" and "overhyped AI tools" as separate queries wastes tokens. These hit the same embedding region. Diversify by angle instead.
    - **Forgetting to deduplicate**: Multiple searches will return overlapping results. Always deduplicate before synthesis.
    - **Treating Exa results as validated**: Exa returns similarity, not yet validated. A result appearing in search output does not mean it meets the user's criteria. You must validate.
    - **Date drift**: Always calculate dates from the current environment date. Never reuse dates from these instructions or from previous queries.

    # CCFinance
    
    CCFinance is a data engineering project for filtering and enriching public
    Common Crawl News (CC-News) copies for research into language in finance.
    
    ## Start
    
    Exordio supplies the Python and LaTeX toolchains, a pinned Nix environment and CI.
    Copier answers record Exordio `v0.1.1-alpha` (the documented `v0.1.0` tag was not
    available in the local source).
    
    ```bash
    bash infra/nix/install-devenv.sh
    devenv shell
    just setup
    just python::run --help
    just python::run stages list
    just check
    ```
    
    Shared agent instructions and Codex configuration are maintained in
    [`.agents/`](.agents/README.md). `just setup` applies them; use
    `just agents::preview` to preview link changes and `just agents::check` to
    verify the generated links.
    
    `just check` validates Justfile syntax and formatting alongside the other
    quality gates. Run `just fmt` to format Justfiles and other source files.
    
    For Python alone, with Python 3.13, uv and just installed:
    
    ```bash
    just python::setup
    just python::check
    ```
    
    ## Data and reproducibility
    
    DVC is initialized at the repository root with analytics disabled. Use:
    
    ```bash
    just dvc status
    just dvc dag
    ```
    
    Semflow tracks the executable Python dependencies of DVC stages. When adding a
    stage, run `just semflow-patch` to review its proposed fingerprints, then
    `just semflow-apply` to materialize them. Commit the generated
    `.semflow/hashes/` files with the DVC definition. After semantic source changes,
    run `just semflow-refresh`; `just semflow-check` detects stale fingerprints.
    The frozen [Fine News acquisition stage](data/inputs/fine-news/README.md) retains
    the published staging snapshot and its historical selection recipe. DVC verifies
    the restored output during reproduction. The
    [source comparison](data/inputs/source-comparison/README.md) prepares small
    probability samples using Parquet metadata before acquiring article payloads.
    Keep data, configuration and environment dependencies explicit in DVC: Semflow's
    static analysis cannot discover string-driven dynamic imports.
    
    See [Python commands](src/python/README.md), [LaTeX commands](src/latex/README.md)
    and [infrastructure](infra/README.md). The scaffold's Apache-2.0 license covers
    code; it does not grant rights to upstream article content.
    # Architecture
    
    CCFinance separates code and research artifacts. Git stores source, configuration,
    locks, provenance definitions and documentation. DVC defines data dependencies
    and tracks materialized source snapshots and experiment outputs.
    
    - `src/python/apps/pipeline` owns the CLI and data stage implementations.
    - `src/python/uv.lock` locks runtime, quality, testing, packaging and DVC tools.
    - `src/latex` owns the manuscript source and bibliography.
    - `data` holds ignored data payloads and versioned DVC pointer files.
    - `infra/nix` and `devenv.lock` own the reproducible system environment.
    
    Tach enforces module boundaries; Ruff and strict Pyrefly check Python source.
    pytest-layout-enforcer checks test file placement during collection and CI.
    Semflow fingerprints the Python code used by DVC stages, allowing DVC to
    invalidate tracked results when executable behavior changes.
    CI executes those checks, tests and builds through the same just recipes as local
    work. Setup may download dependencies; ordinary checks use cached dependencies
    and do not repair authored content. LaTeX uses a versioned Tectonic asset bundle.
    
    The Hugging Face dataset is staging, and the bucket is intended for intermediate
    and experiment artifacts. The frozen raw acquisition stage documents the
    historical selection without fetching its output. Company labels and coverage
    are provisional experiments; release validation and remote artifact transport
    remain future work. The raw comparison stages prepare
    sampling manifests from Hub listings and Parquet footers, then acquire only the
    selected row groups through the shared publisher filter. Research aggregation
    reads those artifacts without importing raw-stage modules. DVC connects these
    steps; pinned source revisions and recorded draw probabilities define the
    experiment's population and sampling design.
    
    The article-labeling experiment adopts checksum-verified CPU company candidates
    and materializes compact source-linked selections without copying article bodies.
    Native Kev runs in a separately pinned GPU environment; the pipeline communicates
    through typed System One requests. Article-company probabilities and filtering
    policies remain separate, with resumable checkpoints and explicit unresolved
    outcomes. The research layer reconciles candidate and model-scored coverage and
    reports runtime estimates without treating AI agreement as human validation.
    Completed pilots remain frozen. Full scoring uses compressed source-record
    chunks, a resumable request ledger and explicit pending counts. Separate runtime
    profiles preserve GPU memory experiments without overwriting completed evidence.
    
    Each data layer groups experimental artifacts beneath `experiments/<name>/`.
    Experimental stage code follows the same grouping under its owning layer.
    `pipeline.experiments.source_comparison` defines shared parameters and artifacts;
    Tach permits raw and research to depend on these contracts without importing one
    another. Raw publisher extraction owns one source-field registry, deriving both
    SQL projections and projected column sizes from it. DVC supplies artifact paths
    explicitly. Research uses statsmodels for survey-estimate summaries and LaTeX
    tables; it preserves the probability-sampling design.
    
    Copier answers record the source and tag for future template updates. Review
    update conflicts and preserve project-specific code and configuration. The
    upstream template is [Exordio](https://github.com/marcusinthesky/exordio).
    # Native decision inference
    
    These scripts run the pinned native Kev server using the CUDA libraries of an
    already cached container image. SGLang is not launched. Native Kev shares the
    article prefix across its independent identity and coverage questions.
    
    From the repository root, prepare the small serving dependencies and then supply
    the existing checkpoint and Hugging Face base-model cache:
    
    ```bash

    just inference::serve /path/to/kev-4b /path/to/huggingface/hub \

    docker logs ccfinance-kev-native
    just inference::status
    ```
    
    The versioned runtime manifest records the model, source, image, precision,
    kernels and admission limit. The entrypoint applies that limit to both the
    article and every complete article-question sequence. Oversized inputs fail
    explicitly; text truncation is disabled. Local package and compilation caches
    live under ignored `.runtime/`.
    
    The third argument selects the versioned runtime profile. Pass the selected 4B
    profile explicitly; omitting it selects the historical 0.8B baseline.
    
    The 4B profile uses BF16 and retains one article prefix. Its adapter and head
    checksums are checked before loading. The serving trial records actual memory
    use separately from the model publisher's memory estimate.

        --revision 1001bb4d826a52d1f399e183466143f4da7b741b \
        --include '*.json' --include '*.safetensors' \

    The base weights require approximately 9.3 GB of storage. Model files and caches

    The completed company-labeling pilot used `kev-4b.json` with three concise

    ## GLiNER extraction benchmark
    
    The separate GLiNER environment measures company spans, per-span roles and
    article type on source-verified samples. Its image is pinned above; the package
    and model revisions are pinned in `gliner-requirements.txt` and
    `gliner-setup.sh`. Setup downloads public model weights and applies a small
    GLiNER 2.1.0 patches: attribute logits are on the CPU when indexed, so their
    index tensor must be on that same device; and synthetic sentence punctuation
    must not be mapped onto the source when a window ends without punctuation.
    The patches do not change the model weights. Corrected window spans retain a
    `synthetic_suffix_removed` flag; other out-of-window spans are marked invalid.
    An additional opt-in patch supports `--batched-attributes`: it collects spans
    using GLiNER's existing decoder, then scores their role attributes together on
    the GPU. The original path remains the default. Floating-point reassociation
    can change nearly tied role labels, so paired parity checks remain necessary.
    
    ```bash
    bash infra/inference/gliner-setup.sh
    just inference::gliner-check
    uv run --project src/python --offline --frozen --all-packages \
        python infra/inference/gliner_sample.py --output .runtime/gliner-benchmark/sample
    bash infra/inference/gliner-run.sh gliner2.5-small-v1 \
        --sample .runtime/gliner-benchmark/sample/articles.jsonl \
        --output .runtime/gliner-benchmark/results/small-fp16-flash \
        --limit 10000 --batch-size 64 --precision fp16 --backend disentangled_flash
    ```
    
    The sample is drawn from retained source rows by a seeded SHA-256 priority; its
    selection and body checksums are recorded. Samples contain article text and
    remain in ignored local storage. The output preserves model predictions and
    identifies invalid offsets explicitly. Timings include extraction, validation
    and compressed output but exclude model loading, warmup and source reads; those
    are reported separately. They do not establish model accuracy.
    
    Long documents are split into overlapping 384-word windows, with 64 words of
    overlap. GLiNER merges entity spans across windows and selects the highest
    confidence window's classification. Roles are per extracted mention and need
    not describe the entire article. These experimental outputs require validation
    and a separate company-identity linking step before use as research labels.
    `quantize=True` in GLiNER means FP16; INT8 is a separate TorchAO trial. GLiNER
    2.1.0 does not allow DisentangledFlash and `torch.compile` simultaneously.
    The experimental `disentangled_flash_heads` backend keeps the prepared encoder
    outside compilation and compiles only the extraction-head modules. Validate
    paired output agreement before adopting it.
    
    For a shorter paired comparison, select a deterministic 500-record subset and
    run each configuration through the same entrypoint. Each run has its own
    container and output directory. Keep initialization and timed extraction
    separate when comparing configurations.
    
    ```bash
    python infra/inference/gliner_screen_sample.py \
        .runtime/gliner-benchmark/sample/articles.jsonl \
        .runtime/gliner-benchmark/screen.jsonl
    bash infra/inference/gliner-run.sh gliner2.5-small-v1 \
        --sample .runtime/gliner-benchmark/screen.jsonl \
        --output .runtime/gliner-benchmark/screen-results/small-fp32 \
        --limit 500 --batch-size 64 --precision fp32
    bash infra/inference/gliner-run.sh gliner2.5-small-v1 \
        --sample .runtime/gliner-benchmark/screen.jsonl \
        --output .runtime/gliner-benchmark/screen-results/small-fp16-flash \
        --limit 500 --batch-size 64 --precision fp16 --backend disentangled_flash
    python infra/inference/gliner_compare.py \
        .runtime/gliner-benchmark/screen-results/small-fp32/predictions.jsonl.gz \
        .runtime/gliner-benchmark/screen-results/small-fp16-flash/predictions.jsonl.gz \
        --output .runtime/gliner-benchmark/screen-results/comparison.json
    ```
    
    Agreement between configurations measures stability, not accuracy. The output
    does not resolve extracted names to issuers or show that a company is a primary
    subject of a complete article.
    
    The GPU batch size and article buffer size are separate. A larger article
    buffer lets GLiNER's DataLoader prepare future window batches while the GPU
    processes the current batch. Use `--buffer-size 2048 --workers 4` to test this
    schedule; the container provides 1 GiB of shared memory for worker transfers.
    The benchmark caps its CUDA allocator at 80% of device memory by default.
    Reports record every parameter device and dtype, CUDA memory, and worker counts.
    FP8 and NVFP4 trials quantize encoder linear projections; embeddings, extraction
    heads and other operations retain their higher precision.
    
    ```bash
    bash infra/inference/gliner-run.sh gliner2.5-small-v1 \
        --script infra/inference/gliner_profile.py \
        --sample .runtime/gliner-benchmark/screen.jsonl \
        --output .runtime/gliner-benchmark/profile-compiled --limit 64
    ```
    
    Profiling attributes CPU calls and CUDA kernels, with instrumentation overhead;
    use separate unprofiled runs for throughput. Precision probes test CUDA kernel
    compatibility independently of model speed and extraction quality.
    
    ## Measured configuration
    
    On 17 November 2026, the 74M-parameter small checkpoint completed three runs of
    the same source-verified 10,000-record sample at 163.7, 162.3 and 162.5 articles
    per second on the RTX 5060 Ti. The aggregate rate was 162.8/second, projecting
    20.9 hours of extraction for 12,241,870 retained records. This excludes source
    reconstruction and downstream issuer linking. Peak PyTorch reserved CUDA memory
    was 7.50 GiB; driver allocations are separate.
    
    The configuration uses FP16, DisentangledFlash, compiled extraction heads,
    batched role scoring, 128-window GPU batches, four preprocessing workers and an
    8,192-article buffer. Windows contain 384 word tokens with 64-token overlap.
    All model parameters were verified on CUDA. Every record passed structural
    checks; the first and third repetitions produced identical predictions.
    
    ```bash
    just inference::gliner-run gliner2.5-small-v1 \
        --sample .runtime/gliner-benchmark/sample/articles.jsonl \
        --output .runtime/gliner-benchmark/custom-run \
        --limit 10000 --batch-size 128 --buffer-size 8192 --workers 4 \
        --precision fp16 --backend disentangled_flash_heads --batched-attributes
    ```
    
    The [benchmark report](../../data/research/experiments/article-labels/gliner-benchmark/report.md)
    and its DVC artifact retain selections, predictions, timings, comparisons,
    compatibility probes and historical experiment launchers. These results establish
    computational feasibility, not label accuracy. Diagnostic examples include
    people and places labeled as companies; the roles also describe windows rather
    than calibrated whole-article subject probabilities. Human validation and dated
    issuer linking remain prerequisites for research use.

    # Define dataset requirements
    
    ## Goal
    
    Specify a public, reproducible financial news dataset for firm-level text,
    co-mention networks and market research.
    
    ## Requirements
    
    - **Coverage:** Report distinct usable articles per company-year, including zero
      counts for a declared universe, and firms meeting selectable annual thresholds
      over consecutive years. Compare with 47 raw articles per year over 2018–2022
      for the 100-firm Pricing Perspective frame; report raw and usable counts separately.
    - **Articles:** Provide stable IDs, source and publisher, URL, title, article text,
      language, publication and capture times with precision, quality flags, and
      traceable capture provenance where available.
    - **Companies:** Preserve all article–company links, dated issuer identifiers,
      supporting evidence, ambiguity and substantive relevance. Distinguish mentions
      from company-focused coverage and retain unresolved identities.
    - **Sources:** Maintain versioned publisher selection criteria and distinguish
      original reporting, syndicated material and press releases where possible.
      Deduplicate stories without discarding source records or company links.
    - **Research validity:** Evaluate extraction, deduplication, dates, company links
      and relevance against human-adjudicated samples. Report precision, recall,
      uncertainty and coverage gaps across years, publishers and firms.
    - **Reproducibility:** Publish a versioned schema, data dictionary, lineage,
      checksums, methods, coverage reports and examples for firm-year panels and
      co-mention networks. Document article-text access and redistribution conditions.
    - **Extensions:** Treat company-specific sentiment and events, article topics and
      novelty as separately versioned, evaluated enrichments.
    
    Numerical coverage and quality targets remain provisional until the staging audit.
    Publication dates before CC-News began do not establish when text was observable.
    See the [Pricing Perspective comparison](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.23447v3#Sx1)
    for the baseline and its limitations.
    
    ## Acceptance
    
    - [ ] Review these requirements against staging evidence and intended studies.
    - [ ] Set evidence-based coverage and quality targets for a first release.

    """The shared extraction contract used by local GLiNER experiments."""
    
    from __future__ import annotations
    
    from typing import TYPE_CHECKING
    
    from gliner2 import AttributeGroup
    
    if TYPE_CHECKING:
        from gliner2.inference.runtime import ExtractorRuntimeMixin
        from gliner2.inference.schema import Schema
    
    
    def build_schema(model: ExtractorRuntimeMixin) -> Schema:
        """Request company spans, per-mention roles, and the article's text type."""
        return (
            model.create_schema()
            .entities({"company": "Names of companies and businesses"})
            .entity_attributes(
                {
                    "article_role": AttributeGroup(
                        ["primary", "secondary", "incidental", "uncertain"],
                        applies_to=["company"],
                        qualify_labels=True,
                    )
                }
            )
            .classification(
                "article_type",
                ["reporting", "opinion", "press release", "promotional", "other"],
            )
        )

    # CCFinance
    
    CCFinance is a data engineering project for filtering and enriching public
    Common Crawl News (CC-News) copies for research into language in finance.
    
    ## Start
    
    Exordio supplies the Python and LaTeX toolchains, a pinned Nix environment and CI.
    Copier answers record Exordio `v0.1.1-alpha` (the documented `v0.1.0` tag was not
    available in the local source).
    
    ```bash
    bash infra/nix/install-devenv.sh
    devenv shell
    just setup
    just python::run --help
    just python::run stages list
    just check
    ```
    
    Shared agent instructions and Codex configuration are maintained in
    [`.agents/`](.agents/README.md). `just setup` applies them; use
    `just agents::preview` to preview link changes and `just agents::check` to
    verify the generated links.
    
    `just check` validates Justfile syntax and formatting alongside the other
    quality gates. Run `just fmt` to format Justfiles and other source files.
    
    For Python alone, with Python 3.13, uv and just installed:
    
    ```bash
    just python::setup
    just python::check
    ```
    
    ## Data and reproducibility
    
    DVC is initialized at the repository root with analytics disabled. Use:
    
    ```bash
    just dvc status
    just dvc dag
    ```
    
    Semflow tracks the executable Python dependencies of DVC stages. When adding a
    stage, run `just semflow-patch` to review its proposed fingerprints, then
    `just semflow-apply` to materialize them. Commit the generated
    `.semflow/hashes/` files with the DVC definition. After semantic source changes,
    run `just semflow-refresh`; `just semflow-check` detects stale fingerprints.
    The frozen [Fine News acquisition stage](data/inputs/fine-news/README.md) retains
    the published staging snapshot and its historical selection recipe. DVC verifies
    the restored output during reproduction. The
    [source comparison](data/inputs/source-comparison/README.md) prepares small
    probability samples using Parquet metadata before acquiring article payloads.
    Keep data, configuration and environment dependencies explicit in DVC: Semflow's
    static analysis cannot discover string-driven dynamic imports.
    
    See [Python commands](src/python/README.md), [LaTeX commands](src/latex/README.md)
    and [infrastructure](infra/README.md). The scaffold's Apache-2.0 license covers
    code; it does not grant rights to upstream article content.
    # Architecture
    
    CCFinance separates code and research artifacts. Git stores source, configuration,
    locks, provenance definitions and documentation. DVC defines data dependencies
    and tracks materialized source snapshots and experiment outputs.
    
    - `src/python/apps/pipeline` owns the CLI and data stage implementations.
    - `src/python/uv.lock` locks runtime, quality, testing, packaging and DVC tools.
    - `src/latex` owns the manuscript source and bibliography.
    - `data` holds ignored data payloads and versioned DVC pointer files.
    - `infra/nix` and `devenv.lock` own the reproducible system environment.
    
    Tach enforces module boundaries; Ruff and strict Pyrefly check Python source.
    pytest-layout-enforcer checks test file placement during collection and CI.
    Semflow fingerprints the Python code used by DVC stages, allowing DVC to
    invalidate tracked results when executable behavior changes.
    CI executes those checks, tests and builds through the same just recipes as local
    work. Setup may download dependencies; ordinary checks use cached dependencies
    and do not repair authored content. LaTeX uses a versioned Tectonic asset bundle.
    
    The Hugging Face dataset is staging, and the bucket is intended for intermediate
    and experiment artifacts. The frozen raw acquisition stage documents the
    historical selection without fetching its output. Company labels and coverage
    are provisional experiments; release validation and remote artifact transport
    remain future work. The raw comparison stages prepare
    sampling manifests from Hub listings and Parquet footers, then acquire only the
    selected row groups through the shared publisher filter. Research aggregation
    reads those artifacts without importing raw-stage modules. DVC connects these
    steps; pinned source revisions and recorded draw probabilities define the
    experiment's population and sampling design.
    
    The article-labeling experiment adopts checksum-verified CPU company candidates
    and materializes compact source-linked selections without copying article bodies.
    Native Kev runs in a separately pinned GPU environment; the pipeline communicates
    through typed System One requests. Article-company probabilities and filtering
    policies remain separate, with resumable checkpoints and explicit unresolved
    outcomes. The research layer reconciles candidate and model-scored coverage and
    reports runtime estimates without treating AI agreement as human validation.
    Completed pilots remain frozen. Full scoring uses compressed source-record
    chunks, a resumable request ledger and explicit pending counts. Separate runtime
    profiles preserve GPU memory experiments without overwriting completed evidence.
    
    Each data layer groups experimental artifacts beneath `experiments/<name>/`.
    Experimental stage code follows the same grouping under its owning layer.
    `pipeline.experiments.source_comparison` defines shared parameters and artifacts;
    Tach permits raw and research to depend on these contracts without importing one
    another. Raw publisher extraction owns one source-field registry, deriving both
    SQL projections and projected column sizes from it. DVC supplies artifact paths
    explicitly. Research uses statsmodels for survey-estimate summaries and LaTeX
    tables; it preserves the probability-sampling design.
    
    Copier answers record the source and tag for future template updates. Review
    update conflicts and preserve project-specific code and configuration. The
    upstream template is [Exordio](https://github.com/marcusinthesky/exordio).

    73:These are not all equivalent types of metadata: the sentiment and event scores in commercial analytics products are typically vendor-produced, while the embeddings and network measurements in the research datasets are created by researchers.
    75:## 2. Detailed metadata by dataset
    77:### RavenPack Equity – Dow Jones Edition
    79:RavenPack is especially rich in **company-level and event-level metadata**. Documented fields in RavenPack analytics products include:
    81:- **Identification:** story ID, timestamp, company name, company identifier, ticker, ISIN, source.
    82:- **Entity relevance:** how strongly a story concerns a particular company.
    83:- **Sentiment:** event sentiment and composite sentiment scores.
    84:- **Event classification:** event category or taxonomy, such as earnings or corporate developments.
    86:- **Other analytics:** story-event counts and related measures.
    90:### Thomson Reuters News Analytics (TRNA)
    94:- **Identification:** item ID, timestamp, Reuters instrument code (RIC), source, feed.
    96:- **Sentiment:** positive, negative and neutral probabilities.
    97:- **Relevance:** a numerical company-specific relevance score.

    106:The appendix confirms that this corpus contains full article text and was processed using automated named-entity recognition (NER).

    112:### RESET + Juyuan

    118:### Nasdaq news archive
    126:- Source-level ticker associations, rather than manually validated article-level entity annotations.
    131:## 3. Additional comparison: Hoberg–Phillips ETNIC-All
    137:## Which dataset is most useful?
    139:For research requiring **timestamped, company-specific news with ready-made sentiment and event metadata**, RavenPack and TRNA are the strongest of these options.

    260:| Free-form event labels | No | No |
    261:| Hierarchical | Yes, explicit event hierarchy | Yes, parent–child topic codes |
    262:| Company-specific event roles | Yes, for applicable events | Not generally encoded in topic codes |
    264:| Granular event distinctions | Strong | More limited |

    274:- RavenPack may distinguish the acquiring company from the acquired company through event categories.

    # Searching with Exa
    
    You have two tools:
    - **`web_search_exa`** -- search by query. Supports `query` and `numResults` params. Use `category:<type>` inline in the query string for category filtering.
    - **`web_fetch_exa`** -- read full content from known URLs. Use after search when snippets are insufficient.
    
    ## How Exa Search Works
    
    Exa uses vector embeddings, not keywords. It finds pages semantically similar to your query. It does not match keywords exactly, directly understand boolean logic (AND/OR/NOT), or validate that results meet your criteria. You are describing a target page, and Exa returns the nearest neighbors in embedding space.
    
    ## Writing Good Queries
    
    **Describe the page you want to find**, not the fact you want to know.
    
    | Looking for | Bad query | Good query |
    |---|---|---|
    | Blog posts about X | "X" | "detailed blog post about X written by a practitioner" |
    | Company doing Y | "Y company" | "category:company startup building Y for enterprise" |
    | Person at company | "person at company" | "category:people senior engineer at Acme" |
    
    Write queries as natural grammatical phrases.
    
    **`numResults` sizing -- match to query precision:**
    
    | Query precision | numResults | Example |
    |---|---|---|
    | Named entity (specific person/company) | 5 | `"WaveForms AI founding story funding details"` |
    | Precise filter (narrow category + constraints) | 10 | `"category:company developer tools API testing Series A"` |
    | Broad discovery (wide category, few constraints) | 15 | `"category:news engineer launches startup 2025 2026"` |
    
    Never use numResults above 25. If you need more coverage, run more queries with different angles at n=10-15 rather than one query at n=50.
    
    **Use category filters** when searching for a specific entity type. Available inline categories: `company`, `research paper`, `news`, `personal site`, `people`. Add `category:<type>` at the start of your query string.
    
    ```
    web_search_exa { "query": "category:research paper sparse attention mechanisms for long context", "numResults": 10 }
    web_search_exa { "query": "category:people VP Engineering AI infrastructure San Francisco", "numResults": 10 }
    web_search_exa { "query": "category:company developer tools for API testing", "numResults": 10 }
    ```
    
    ## Query Diversity
    
    When you need to run multiple queries on the same topic, make sure they target genuinely different angles, not just synonym swaps. "overhyped" vs "overrated" vs "disappointment" are the same angle. A skeptic angle vs a builder angle vs a practitioner angle are genuinely different.
    
    **Word order affects embeddings.** "Python async patterns for web scraping" and "web scraping async patterns in Python" can sometimes return different results. Use this to your advantage when you need coverage -- run 2-3 phrasings in parallel.
    
    ## Encoding Time
    
    If your task involves time ("last week", "recent", "this month"), calculate exact dates FIRST from the current date in your environment context. Then encode dates semantically in the query: "published in March 2026" rather than using date filters. Never eyeball dates.
    
    ## Anti-Patterns
    
    - Boolean operators ("AND", "NOT") are just words to Exa, not operators
    - Quotes don't force exact phrase matching
    - Very short queries (1-2 words) produce scattered, low-quality results
    - Don't use dates from examples -- always calculate from the current date
    
    ## When Searches Return Nothing
    
    If a query returns 0 or only irrelevant results:
    a. Make the query longer and more specific
    b. Try a different angle, not a synonym swap
    c. If multiple angles return nothing, the topic likely has limited web coverage -- report that rather than fabricating results
    
    ## Domain-Specific Patterns
    
    If your task involves any of these domains, read the relevant pattern file(s) for specialized query strategies. Pick whichever files match your task — most tasks use 1-2.
    
    | File (same directory as this file) | Domain |
    |---|---|
    | `patterns-people.md` | People by role, company, location |
    | `patterns-companies.md` | Companies by category, stage, competitors, funding |
    | `patterns-papers.md` | Academic/research papers |
    | `patterns-relationships.md` | Hidden connections (clients, collaborators) |
    | `patterns-code.md` | Code, APIs, docs, errors |
    | `patterns-news.md` | News, recent events, reactions |
    
    ## When `web_fetch_exa` Fails
    
    Fall back to fetching with any other fetch tool you have access to. If that also fails, skip it and work with remaining sources.
    
    ## After Getting Results
    
    Exa returns similarity, not validation. You must review titles/snippets and discard irrelevant results using your judgment. Don't assume all results match your criteria. For the most promising results, use `web_fetch_exa` to read the full content.
    
    ```
    web_fetch_exa {
      "urls": ["https://promising-url-1.com", "https://promising-url-2.com"],
    }
    ```
    # Synthesizing Research into Narrative
    
    When the task calls for a narrative answer (not a list or table), this file covers how to synthesize findings from multiple sources into a coherent, well-structured response.
    
    ## When Synthesis Applies
    
    Synthesis is the right output format when:
    - The user is asking "what do people say about X" or "what's the current state of Y"
    - The answer requires integrating perspectives from multiple sources
    - The output should be prose with citations, not a table of entities
    
    ## Structure
    
    ### Lead with the answer
    
    Put the core finding or conclusion first. The user should get value from the first paragraph alone.
    
    ### Organize by theme, not by source
    
    Bad: "Source A says X. Source B says Y. Source C says Z."
    Good: "Theme 1: [insight supported by A, B]. Theme 2: [insight supported by C, with counterpoint from A]."
    
    ### Surface disagreement explicitly
    
    When credible sources disagree, don't collapse to consensus. Present both sides with their evidence:
    - "On [topic], [position A] (supported by [sources]) vs [position B] (supported by [sources]). [When each applies or why they diverge]."
    
    ### Include confidence signals
    
    - How many independent sources support a claim?
    - How fresh is the evidence?
    - Are the sources practitioners or commentators?
    
    ## Thematic Clustering
    
    When dealing with many reactions or perspectives (e.g. "what are people saying about X"):
    
    1. Read through all results
    2. Identify recurring themes (not just topics -- themes have a stance or direction)
    3. Group results by theme
    4. For each theme: state the theme, cite 2-3 representative sources, note the volume
    5. Flag outlier themes that appear only once but carry important signal
    
    ## Citation Practice
    
    - Every factual claim gets a source URL
    - Prefer inline citations: "Engineers report 3x latency reduction ([source](url))"
    - For quotes, include the exact text and attribute it
    
    ## Common Mistakes
    
    - **Source-by-source summaries**: Feels comprehensive but is unreadable and doesn't synthesize
    - **Collapsing disagreement**: Picking a winner instead of presenting the landscape
    - **Missing recency**: Treating 2023 sources as current for fast-moving topics
    - **Over-synthesis**: Producing a full essay when the user asked a narrow question
    # Evaluating Source Quality
    
    When assessing sources during search and extraction, tag quality signals in your output so results can be weighted and ranked downstream.
    
    ## Noise Signals -- Filter Out First
    
    Before deep-reading, check for these disqualifiers:
    
    | Signal | What to look for |
    |--------|-----------------|
    | No skin in the game | Theorists who don't do the work -- no portfolio, no shipped products, no verifiable results |
    | Misaligned incentives | Paid to sell, not to be right (sponsored content, vendor blogs, affiliate-heavy) |
    | Circular credentials | Validated only by peers in the same bubble -- no external evidence of impact |
    | Positive-only advice | No tradeoffs, no failure modes discussed -- "just do X" with no caveats |
    | Temporal decay | Shifted from doing to teaching/advising. Check: are they still actively building/practicing? |
    
    ## Practitioner vs Commentator
    
    The most important distinction. Practitioners do the work; commentators write about the work.
    
    **Practitioner signals:** shipped products, open-source contributions, case studies with specific numbers, "we built X and here's what happened"
    
    **Commentator signals:** roundup posts, "top 10" lists, content primarily linking to others' work, no first-hand experience described
    
    Note this distinction in your quality tags.
    
    ## Verification Searches
    
    When validating a source's credibility (for expert-finding and best-of queries):
    
    ```
    // Who cites them?
    web_search_exa { "query": "[name] recommended by experts practitioners", "numResults": 5 }
    
    // Track record?
    web_search_exa { "query": "[name] results portfolio case study shipped", "numResults": 5 }
    
    // Criticism?
    web_search_exa { "query": "[name] criticism overrated wrong", "numResults": 5 }
    ```
    
    Only run verification searches when the task specifically calls for evaluating source credibility. For standard search tasks, just tag what you observe from the content you already have.
    
    ## Tagging in Output
    
    For each source, include a short free-form `quality` string describing what you observed -- e.g. "shipped the product, writes from direct experience" or "roundup blog, no original work shown, links to others." Don't classify into categories. Just describe what you see so the signal is preserved for downstream ranking.

    As part of our internal research, we recently took the new dataset for a spin - looking at one of the new key features - Event Relevance . Event Relevance provides information on the prominence of an event within a document and goes beyond our previous Relevance analytic that focused purely on the importance of a detected entity. As part of our analysis, we also considered the significance of event novelty by consulting our Event Similarity Day score. 
    
     As shown below, we generally find that high event relevance events (with a 90 to 100 score) significantly outperform low relevance events. However, the latter seem more predictive for small cap vs. large cap companies - possibly driven by the fact that it’s more difficult for smaller companies to make headlines or to be the focus of a news story than it is for larger companies. 
    
     
    
     We also reconfirm that more novel events provide stronger risk-adjusted performance across our four size & region universes. However, this comes with the tradeoff of lower event volume as we filter more aggressively on the number of days required since a similar event was detected in the past (up to 365 days).

    Title: GLiNER2.5
    URL: https://docs.fastino.ai/concepts/gliner
    Published: N/A
    Author: N/A
    Highlights:
    # GLiNER2.5
    
    > Learn when and how to use GLiNER2.5 Multi for multilingual, schema-driven information extraction.
    
    GLiNER2.5 Multi is Fastino's multilingual, multi-task information-extraction model. Use one schema to extract entities, classify text, build structured records, identify relations, and attach attributes to spans.
    
    ## When to use GLiNER 2.5
    
    Use GLiNER2.5 Multi when extraction or multilingual coverage is central to the task:
    
    - Entity extraction - pull people, organizations, products, locations, or domain-specific entities (medications, dosages, clauses) out of free text, with character offsets and confidence scores.
    - Structured records - turn "Alice bought apples and Bob bought oranges" into `[{"buyer": "Alice", "item": "apples"}, {"buyer": "Bob", "item": "oranges"}]`, keeping each instance's fields linked.
    - Relation and knowledge-graph extraction - extract typed entity-relation graphs (`works_for`, `located_in`) for agent memory or a knowledge base.
    - Span attributes - tag each extracted entity with an attribute, such as per-person sentiment, in the same pass as extraction.
    - Long documents - process an encoded context of up to 4,096 tokens, with chunking and offset remapping for longer documents.
    - Multiple tasks at once - combine entities, classification, structures, and relations in a single schema-constrained call instead of chaining several model requests.
    - Consistent outputs - use constrained classification or joint entity-relation decoding when labels and relation endpoints must agree.
    
    GLiNER2.5 Multi also supports classification. Choose GLiNER-2.5-Decide when the input is English and classification itself—intent, routing, sentiment, priority, moderation, or scoring—is the primary workload.
    
    ## How to use GLiNER 2.5
    
    Call the multilingual checkpoint through Fastino's OpenAI-compatible inference endpoint. Put the text in a user message and describe the task in `schema`:
    
    ```bash
    curl -X
    
    ...
    
    "model": "fastino/gliner2.5-multi-v1",
    
    ...
    
    }
    
    ...
    
    { "name": "location", "description": "city, region, or place" }
          ]
        }
      }'
    
    ```
    
    Add `classifications`, `structures`, or `relations` keys to the same `schema` to run several tasks over the same text in one call. See the Inference API reference for the full request and response contract, including structured records and relation schemas.
    
    ...
    
    Use constrained classification when several answers must form one valid decision. Unlike classic `classifications`, which selects each task independently, the constrained decoder searches for a joint assignment that satisfies declared rules.
